2. इसके द्वारा यह सूचित किया जाता है कि कम्पनी अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 248 (2) के तहत कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार को उपर्युक्त 
कम्पनियों के नाम कम्पनी रजिस्टर से इस आधार पर नाम हटाने का आवेदन प्राप्त हुआ है कि कम्पनी के निगमन के एक वर्ष के भीतर कारोबार 
आरंभ करने में विफल रहे हैं या इस आधार पर कि कम्पनी पूर्ववर्ती 2 वित्तीय वर्षों से कारोबार नहीं कर पाई है और इस अवधि के भीतर कम्पनी 
अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 455 के तहत निष्क्रिय कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त करने का आदेश का आवेदन नहीं किया है या कम्पनी ने निष्क्रिय कम्पनी 
की स्थिति प्राप्त कर ली है, पर वे कम्पनी के रूप में पंजीकरण नहीं रखना चाहते और अतः कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार से अपना/अपने नाम हटाने का अनुरोध 
किया है। 

3. तदनुसार, कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार उपर्युक्त कम्पनियों के नामों को कम्पनियों के रजिस्टर से हटाने का प्रस्ताव करता है। 


4. यदि किसी व्यक्ति/संस्था को कम्पनी को कम्पनी रजिस्ट्रार से कम्पनियों का नाम हटाने के प्रस्ताव से आपत्ति है तो वह व्यक्ति/संस्था 
इस सूचना के प्रकाशन की तारीख से 30 (तीस) दिनों के भीतर उपर्युक्त कार्यालय के पते पर अपनी आपत्ति भेज सकते हैं ।

कम्पनियों के नाम कम्पनी रजिस्टर से इस आधार पर नाम हटाने का आवेदन प्राप्त हुआ है कि कम्पनी के निगमन के एक वर्ष के भीतर कारोबार

अधिनियम, 2043 की धारा 455 के तहत निष्क्रिय कम्पनी की स्थिति प्राप्त करने का आदेश का आवेदन नहीं किया है या कम्पनी ने निष्क्रिय कम्पनी

G.S.R. 35.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution and in 
supersession of the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy (Cook) Recruitment Rules, 20l8, except as 
respects things done or omitted to be done before such supersession, the President hereby makes the following rules 
regulating the method of recruitment to the post of Cook, in the Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy, 
Hyderabad under the Ministry of Home Affairs, namely:- 


l. Short title and commencement.— (l) These rules may be called the Ministry of Home Affairs, Sardar 
Vallabhbhai Patel National Police Academy, Cook, (Group ‘C’ Post) Recruitment Rules, 2026. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Number of post, classification and level in pay matrix.— The number of the said post, its classification and the 
level in the pay matrix attached thereto, shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to these 
tules. 


3. Method of recruitment, age-limit, educational qualifications, etc.— The method of recruitment, age-limit, 
qualifications and other matters relating to the said post shall be as specified in columns (5) to (3) of the said 
Schedule. 


4. Disqualification.— No person,— 


(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having a spouse living; or 
(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 


shall be eligible for appointment to the said post: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the personal 
law applicable to such person and other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for doing so, exempt 
any person from the operation of this rule. 


5. Power to relax.— Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do, it 
may, by order and for reasons to be recorded in writing, relax any of the provisions of these rules with respect to any 
class or category of persons. 


6. Saving.— Nothing in these rules shall affect reservation, relaxation of age-limit and other concessions required to 
be provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, the Other Backward Classes, ex-Servicemen and other 
special categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government from time to time in 
this regard.

G.S.R. 38.—In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution and in 
supersession of the Central Water Commission Head Draftsman Recruitment Rules, 200l, except as respects things 
done or omitted to be done before such supersession, the President hereby makes the following rules regulating 
the method of recruitment to the post of Chief Draughtsman in the Central Water Commission under the Department 
of Water Resources, River Development and Ganga Rejuvenation, Ministry of Jal Shakti, namely : 


. Short title and commencement. — (l) These rules may be called the Department of Water Resources, River 
Development and Ganga Rejuvenation, Central Water Commission, Chief Draughtsman, Recruitment Rules, 2026. 


(2) They shall come into force on the date of their publication in the Official Gazette. 


2. Number of posts, classification and level in pay matrix. —The number of post, its classification and level in 
the pay matrix attached thereto, shall be as specified in columns (2) to (4) of the Schedule annexed to these rules.

4. Disqualification. — No person, — 
(a) who has entered into or contracted a marriage with a person having a spouse living; or 
(b) who, having a spouse living, has entered into or contracted a marriage with any person, 
shall be eligible for appointment to the said post: 


Provided that the Central Government may, if satisfied that such marriage is permissible under the 
personal law applicable to such person and the other party to the marriage and that there are other grounds for so 
doing, exempt any person from the operation of this rule. 


5. Power to relax. —Where the Central Government is of the opinion that it is necessary or expedient so to do, it may, by 
order, for reasons to be recorded in writing and in consultation with the Union Public Service Commission, relax any of the 
provisions of these rules with respect to any class or category of persons. 


6. Saving. - Nothing in these rules shall affect reservation, relaxation of age-limit and other concessions required to be 
provided for the Scheduled Castes, the Scheduled Tribes, Other Backward Classes, Ex-servicemen and other special 
categories of persons in accordance with the orders issued by the Central Government from time to time in this regard.

AWARD 
The present reference has been made by the Central Government vide Order No. L-l02/29/200l-IR(C-I) dated 


0.08.200l, in exercise of the powers conferred under clause (d) of sub-section (l) read with sub-section (2A) of 


Section l0 of the Industrial Disputes Act, [947, on the following terms: 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7239 


“ Whether the action of the management of M/s. Air India is dismissing Sh. V.N. 
Gangurde, Sr. Cleaner from service w.e.f. /9.2.2000 is just, fair and legal? If not to 
what relief is the workman entitled?” 


Notice of the reference was issued to both parties. The workman initially appeared and filed his Statement of Claim. 
The management also appeared through its learned counsel and filed its written statement along with relevant 
documents. 


However, thereafter, despite service of notice and repeated opportunities, none appeared on behalf of the workman. 
The workman failed to prosecute his case. 


Accordingly, the matter proceeded ex-parte against the workman. 


The management led evidence and placed on record: |. Charge-sheets issued to the workman, 2. Domestic enquiry 
proceedings 3. Enquiry report 4. Order of dismissal. 


It is pertinent to note that the workman did not file any evidence in support of his case. He neither entered the witness 
box nor produced any oral or documentary evidence. 


Thus, the averments made in the Statement of Claim remain unsubstantiated. 
Findings 


From the material on record, it is evident that: 


* The workman remained habitually absent without leave, 

* A proper and fair domestic enquiry was conducted, 

* Adequate opportunity was granted to the workman, 

* The workman failed to participate in the enquiry, 

. The Enquiry Officer found the charges proved, 

* The competent authority imposed punishment of dismissal after due consideration. 


Since the workman chose not to contest the proceedings and failed to lead any evidence, the case of the management 
remains unchallenged and unrebutted. 


It is well settled that: 


. In Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal (AIR 955 SC 425), it was held that a party who remains 
absent cannot later complain. 

* In Vidhyadhar ४. Manikrao ((999) 3 SCC 573), the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that failure to 
enter the witness box leads to adverse inference. 

* In Manager, RBI v. S. Mani (2005) 5 SCC 00), it was held that the burden of proof lies on the 
claimant. 

* In Workmen of Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. v. Management ((973) | SCC 8[3), it was held that if 


the domestic enquiry is fair and proper, the Tribunal should not interfere. 


* In U.P. State Road Transport Corporation v. Vinod Kumar (2008) | SCC I5), it was held that 
habitual absence is a serious misconduct justifying dismissal. 


Thus, in absence of any evidence from the workman and in view of the settled law, the claim cannot be sustained. 
Conclusion 
In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, this Tribunal holds that: 

* The domestic enquiry is fair and proper, 

. The findings of the Enquiry Officer are legal and justified, 


* The misconduct of the workman stands proved, 


7240 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST , 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


* The punishment of dismissal is proportionate, 
* The workman has failed to prove his case. 
AWARD 


The reference is answered in favour of the management and against the workman. 

It is held that the action of the management of M/s. Air India Ltd. in dismissing Shri V.N. Gangurde from service 
w.e.f. 9.02.2000 is just, fair and legal. 

The workman is not entitled to any relief. 

The reference stands disposed of accordingly.

In exercise of powers conferred under clause (d) of Sub-section (l) and Sub-section (2A) of Section 0 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 947 (/4 of 947), the Government of India through the Ministry of Labour, vide its Order 
No. L-2202/25/209-IR(CM-II) dated 9.03.20I9 has been pleased to refer the following dispute between the 
employer, that is the Management of Lachipur Colliery under Kajora Area of Eastern Coalfields Limited and their 
workman for adjudication by this Tribunal. 


SCHEDULE 


“ Whether the action of the management of Lachipur Colliery of Eastern Coalfields Ltd in denial of 
employment to Sri Prayag Raj Pasi, S/o Lt. Shanta Devi on compassionate ground is justified or not. If not, what 
relief the workman is entitled to? ” 


l. On receiving Order No. L-2202/25/20I9-IR(CM-II) dated 9.03.20l9 from the Government of India, 
Ministry of Labour, New Delhi for adjudication of the dispute, a Reference case was registered on 02.04.209 and an 
order was passed for issuing notice to the parties through registered post, directing them to appear and submit their 
written statements along with relevant documents in support of their claim. 


2. The president of Koyala Mazdoor Congress filed written statement on behalf of Prayagraj Pasi on 
3.02.2023. In a nutshell, the fact of the case as disclosed in the written statement of the union is that Sunta Devi was 
a permanent employee of Eastern Coalfields Limited (hereinafter referred to as ECL) posted at Lachipur Colliery 
under Kajora Area. She died in harness on 08.03.993. Prayagraj Pasi, the dependent son applied before the 
management of the employer company for providing employment to him against the death of his mother. The 
dependent son being a minor at the time of his mother’s death, the management of ECL did not process the proposal 
for employment. After attaining majority, once again the son applied before the management of ECL for his 
employment but the management did not consider the prayer. An Industrial Dispute was raised by the union before 
the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), Raniganj at Durgapur over this matter and in the conciliation proceeding 
both parties agreed to sign a Memorandum of Settlement on !.05.20I. Consequent thereof the dependent son 
submitted relevant documents before the management in support of his claim for employment but management did 
not consider his claim and once again an Industrial Dispute was raised. According to the union the minor son of the 
deceased employee had no knowledge about the rules and regulations applicable to him for his employment as a 
dependent of his deceased mother. The dependent son has no source of income to maintain his livelihood and belongs 
to a weaker section of the society. The union in their written statement has prayed for providing employment to 
Prayagraj Pasi in place of his deceased mother as per provisions of the National Coal Wage Agreement (hereinafter 
referred to as NCWA),. 


3. Management contested the case and filed their written statement on 43.02.2023. Management of ECL 
admitted that Sunta Devi was an employee at Lachipur Colliery and expired on 08.03.993. According to them 
Prayagraj Pasi, claiming to be the son of Sunta Devi submitted an app on 3.02.202, after passage of eighteen (8) 
years from the date of death of Sunta Devi. On scrutiny management found that Sunta Devi was twenty-three (23) 
years as on !.05.989 and the date of birth of Prayagraj Pasi being 0.06.977, the difference of his age with his 
mother was only eleven (Il) years which was doubtful. Furthermore, management contended that the Industrial 
Dispute was raised before the 


Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Raniganj in the year 208 i.e., after twenty-five (25) years from the date of 
death of Sunta Devi and thereafter referred to this Tribunal after twenty-six (26) years from the date of her death. It 
disclosed that the Competent Authority denied the claim for employment of Prayagraj Pasi due to delay in submitting 
application. It is stated in the written statement that the dependent of Sunta Devi was asked to submit reasons for 
delay in submitting his claim for employment, but no suitable reply has been submitted. The main ground on which 
management denied employment to Prayagraj Pasi is due to delay in submitting application of employment and 
placed reliance upon the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the case of Eastern Coalfields Limited 
Vs. Anil Badyakar and Others [Civil Appeal No. 3597 of 2009] and a decision of the Hon'ble High Court at 
Calcutta in the case of Nunibala Mondal @ Nuni Mondal and Another Vs. Eastern Coalfields Limited and 
Others [W.P. No. 660(W) of 206], wherein it is claimed that the Hon'ble High Court, Calcutta, recognized that the 
delay of five or six years is fatal in matter of compassionate employment. Management urged that the Industrial 
Dispute has no merit and is fit to be dismissed.

(iv) Copy of Indemnity Bond submitted by the petitioner in respect of his claim, as Exhibit M-4. 


(५) Copies of three letters issued to Prayagraj Pasi dated 05.0.206, 06.08.20i8 and 0.0.209, 
seeking reason for delay in submitting claim as Exhibits M-5, M-6 and M-7. 


[भाग [lave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण L0, 948 7243 


7. In cross-examination the management witness admitted that in the year 20] petitioner raised the Industrial 
Dispute before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (C), Raniganj at Durgapur and a Memorandum of Settlement was 
entered between the management and union on |.05.20l! (Exhibit W-4). It further transpires from his testimony that 
as per Memorandum of Settlement it was agreed that Prayagraj Pasi would submit the documents within fifteen days 
but he failed to comply the same. The witness deposed that the documents were submitted by the petitioner on 
2.02.202. It transpires from the evidence of management witness that no verification of documents was done by the 
management thereafter and witness also denied that the petitioner is entitled to employment as a dependent of his 
mother. During cross-examination witness also denied the suggestion that the petitioner submitted his first application 
for employment in the year 2004. 


8. The moot point for consideration in this Reference is whether the action of the management of Lachipur 
Colliery, denying employment to Prayagraj Pasi is justified. If not, to what relief he is entitled to. 


9. Mr. Rakesh Kumar, union representative advancing his argument in support of petitioner’s claim for 
employment submitted that Sunta Devi, an employee of ECL died on harness on 08.03.993 and her minor son 
applied for his employment under ECL on 8.06.2004, on attaining majority. The management did not refer him for 
screening or medical examination before the Initial Medical Examination Board. Due to non-consideration of claim 
for employment an Industrial Dispute was raised and over this issue a Memorandum of Settlement under Section 
2(3) of Industrial Disputes Act, !947 was reached between the representative of management and union. A Form ‘H’ 
(Exhibit W-4) was executed where the management agreed that it shall examine the documents and after verifying the 
genuineness of the case, if satisfied, they will forward the 


application to the ECL Headquarters for examination and taking decision by the Competent Authority. Mr. Kumar 
argued that even after reaching such understanding management did not consider the prayer for employment and 
Prayagraj Pasi submitted his application with enclosure (Exhibit W-l) for his employment. It is argued that till date 
management has neither considered no rejected the claim for employment of the dependent son. Therefore, 
management should be directed to provide employment to the son as per provisions of NCWA. 


0. Mr. P. K. Das, learned advocate for the management argued that Sunta Devi died on 08.03.993. At the 
relevant time there was no provision for maintaining the name of minors in the Live Roster of the company, as such 
no right was created in favour of Prayagraj Pasi as a dependent of deceased employee. In the instant case the first 
application for employment was submitted by Prayagraj Pasi on 3.02.20I2 (Exhibit -). Since the application was 
filed after inordinate delay of eighteen (8) years from the date of death of Sunta Devi, management of ECL did not 
consider the claim. It is further argued that in the Service Record the age of Sunta Devi was recorded as twenty-three 
(23) years as on !.05.989. According to the Birth Registration Certificate of Prayagraj Pasi (Exhibit M-3) his date 
of birth appears as 0.06.[977, as such the difference of age between the mother and the son is only eleven (i) years 
which is highly improbable and doubtful. Learned advocate argued that there is no merit in his claim for employment 
and the same has been defeated due to delay. 


ll. I have considered the rival contention of the union and the management of ECL. Perused the pleadings of the 
parties and evidence adduced. The materials on record reveal that Sunta Devi was an employee of ECL and she died 
in harness on 08.03.993. At the time of death of Sunta Devi in the year 993 the provisions of NCWA-V were 
applicable except for the provisions under Clause 9.5.0(iii) which was made applicable with effect from 22.02.996, 
by virtue of the Implementation 


Instruction No. 8 of NCWA-V. Accordingly, the provisions for maintaining the name of a minor male dependent, 
fifteen ([5) years and above in age was effective from 22.02.996. No right of employment therefore accrued in 
favour of Prayagraj Pasi on death of his mother on 08.03.]993 under the provisions of NCWA. 


2. According to the union the first application for employment was submitted by the dependent son of Sunta 
Devi was in the year 2004 i.e., eleven (l) years after the death of his mother, which is indeed a delayed application. 
The Birth Registration Certificate of Prayagraj Pasi (Exhibit M-3) reveals that his date of birth is 0.06.977. 
Therefore, he attained majority on !0.06.995 and the application claiming employment was an afterthought, which is 
submitted nine (9) years after attaining majority. It has been argued on behalf of the management that a difference of 
eleven (ll) years of age between the deceased employee and the claimant gives rise to an air of doubt whether 
Prayagraj Pasi is actually the son of Sunta Devi and such discrepancy of vital facts defeats the case of the union. On 
assessing such facts, it appears to me that genuineness of relationship between the claimant and the deceased 
employee could be established through police verification and examining the Service Record of the deceased 
employee. In absence of any cogent evidence to disprove the genuineness of relationship, appearing in the Service 
Record the argument advanced by Mr. P. K. Das, learned advocate for the management, based upon conjecture and 
surmise, is unfounded and unaccepted. Considering the fact and circumstances of this case, I hold that inordinate and 
unreasonable delay in submitting application for compassionate employment has not been accepted by the 
management. Record reveals that Prayagraj Pasi is now above forty-eight (48) years of age and I find no illegality in 
the action of the management in denying employment to the claimant. The Industrial Dispute is therefore decided 
against the union. 


Hence,

4. Now as regards the oral testimony of ०७४-] Kanti Dubey, he has deposed that he was working 
since !987 as General Clerk in East Bhagatdih Colliery and he has got exhibited the documents of 
the management namely Office Order dated 0.02.992 (Exhibit M-), Office Order dated 
30.0i.992 (Exhibit M-I/l) and Office Order dated 0/25.02.998 (Exhibit M-I/2). In cross- 
examination he has only stated that the concerned workmen and few others were sent for training of 
one year as S.D.L. Operator and thereafter it appears that he does not have any knowledge if any 
suitability test was conducted thereafter or not. 


5. As regards the documentary evidence submitted on behalf of the Management, Exhibit M-I is 
the Office Order dated 0.02.992 of the Agent Kustore Colliery and on its perusal it appears that 
the concerned workmen were selected by the Headquarter as General Mazdoor Category-I and they 
were posted at Alkusa Colliery. It has also been mentioned therein that they will be imparted one 
year training under S.D.L. they will get the basic wages of Category-I and they will not be entitled to 
any wage protection and accordingly they were relieved since 06.02.992 from Kustore Colliery and 
they were directed to contact the Agent of Alkusa Colliery after their duty along with identification 
certificate and attested photograph. Exhibit M-I/l is the Office Order dated 27/30.0.992 of the 
Dy. Chief Personnel Manager Kustore Area of the BCCL and on its perusal it transpires that this is 
related to the six workmen namely Chandi Charan Das, Parmeshwar Bhuiya, Shyam Sundar Ram, 
Bharat Kr. Das, BanshiDhar Oraon and Shiv Shankar Das and it has been mentioned therein that 
these Miners/Loaders of Kustore & East Bhagatdih Colliery who have been selected for the post of 
General Mazdoor Category-I as approved for the post vide letter dated 3/5.0.992 are hereby 
directed to report their duties to the Agent Alkusa Colliery for putting them on the job training as 
S.D.L. Operator and maintenance for the period of one year from the date of their joining at Alkusa 
Colliery on receipt of this letter. They will be paid Category-I wages without any protection of pay 
and after that their placement in the Category/Grade as per nature of job will be finalized after 
suitability test. On being released by their present controlling officer they are directed to report their 
duties to the Agent, Alkusa Colliery along with their identification certificate bearing their recent 
passport size photograph duly attested by their present controlling officer. This regularization is 
subject to verification of their Matriculation and other education and technical qualifications. 
Exhibit M-/2 is the office order dated 25.02.998 of the Dy. CME/Project Officer, Alkusa 
Colliery. This office order is related to the concerned workmen (Shiv Shankar Das and Shyam 
Sundar Ram) as well as others named therein and it shows the fixation of their wages in Category-VI 
after their regularization in $.D.L. Operator. 


6. On perusal of the schedule of the reference order it is evident that this Tribunal has to decide 
whether the action of the management of Kustore Area of BCCL in not regularizing Sri Parmeshwar 
Bhuiya& Four Others of Kustore Area in the post of SDL Operator w.e.f. Jan. 93 after the 
completion of their training period is justified or not. It is very clear from the first document of the 
workmen i.e. office order dated 27/30.0!.992 as well as Exhibit M-I/l which is also just the same, 
that from the date of joining at Alkusa Colliery the concerned workmen will be given training as 
S.D.L. Operator and maintenance for a period of one year from the date of their joining and 
thereafter their placement in the Category/Grade as per nature of job will be finalized after suitability 
test and in the meantime they will be paid Category-I wages without any protection of pay but WW- 
l Shiv Shankar Das has denied the same in Paragraph-3 of his cross-examination though in 
Paragraph-4 he has admitted that suitability test for regular $.D.L. Operator was conducted in the 
year 994 and after he passed the same, he was appointed as regular S.D.L. Operator in the year 
997 and at that time he was in General Mazdoor Category-I and on 25.07.998 he was given 
promotion and pay scale of S.D.L. Operator Category-VI. 


7. Thus as the Office Order dated 27/30.0.992 (Exhibit M-I/I) itself states that after completion 
of training of one year, their placement in the Category/Grade as per nature of the job will be 
finalized after suitability test that was admittedly conducted in the year क्‍994 as admitted in 
Paragraph-4 of his cross-examination by WW-I, the demand of the workmen regarding their 
regularization in the post of $.D.L. Operator w.e.f. January, 993 itself is not at all justified. 


8. Thus on the basis of the above discussions of the facts, circumstances and materials available on 
the case record this Tribunal comes to the conclusion that the action of the management of Kustore 
Area of BCCL in not regularizing Sri Parmeshwar Bhuiya & four others of Kustore Area in the post 
of S.D.L. Operator w.e.f. January 993 after the completion of their training period is not at all 
justified and they are not entitled to relief as claimed. The reference is answered accordingly.

COMMON AWARD 


Petitioner Workman Ms. 3. Aruna has filed the petition under 2(A)(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 
challenging the action of respondent Management whereby her service has been terminated by the Respondent and 
prayed to set aside her termination order from service of Respondent and also prayed to grant her regularization in 
the service of Respondent as Typist. This petition was registered as LC No.8/204. 


Thereafter, the Government of India, Ministry of Labour vide order No. L-!0]2/29/204-IR(CM-I 
dated 77 October, 204 has referred the Industrial Dispute u/s l0 of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 for 
adjudication to this Tribunal with the following Schedule:- 


SCHEDULE 


“Whether the action of the management in not regularizing the services of Ms. B. Aruna in the post of 
Typist is justified? To what relief the workman is entitled to ?” 


This reference got registered as ID No.223/20l4. Petitioner has filed memo and prayed to club both the 
cases i.e., LC No.8/20i4 and ID No.223/20l4. Since both industrial disputes contain same cause of action and 
pertain to the same workman Ms. B. Aruna, therefore, it is being heard and decided by the common award after 
clubbing together. 


2: Notices were issued to the Respondent, Respondent has filed counter. 
3. The averments made in the claim statement are as follows: 


As per averments of claim statement filed by the workman Ms. B. Aruna, she was initially appointed by the 
Respondent on the post of Typist on casual basis on 3.8.!998 and was engaged in a routine of !79 days and though 
the period was extended by the Respondent from time to time. Respondent through proceedings dated 2.2.20I] 
has terminated the services of Petitioner with effect from 2..202 without assigning any reasons and in violation of 
the provisions contained under ID Act. Further, Petitioner submitted that she was asked to attend the duties at par 
with the regular employee’s and she was also issued Identity Card and daily wages were paid to her from time to 
time. She was also paid bonus and other facilities of ESI as per the rules in force. Further, it is submitted that the 
management created artificial breaks in the services of Petitioner after completion of every !79 days of service only 
to deprive the regularization of the Petitioner into the services. Further, it is averred that the Management cannot 
exploit the services of the unemployed youth like the Petitioner and throw them out without following any legal 
principle and engaging other persons as Typists on casual basis. Petitioner averred that management has adopted 
unfair labour practice by giving Petitioner artificial break after completion of every 79 days without regularising the 
services of the Petitioner. Further Petitioner submitted that against her termination order Petitioner approached the 
Hon’ble High Court of Andhra Pradesh by filing the W.P. No. 398 of 20I2 and Hon’ble Court vide order dated 
7.3.20l3 had issued the direction to Respondent to engage the services of the Petitioner continuously without 
affecting any artificial break so long it is felt necessary for engaging their services without resorting to engaging the 
services of the freshers. Petitioner averred that she was eligible and entitled for regularization of services on the 
post of Typist with effect from initial appointment. Petitioner has prayed to set aside her termination order and to 
grant her regularization in the services of Respondent from the initial date of her appointment. 


4. Per contra, The Respondent in the counter, has contented that the various contentions and allegations made 
by the workman in her claim statement are denied. Admittedly the workman was engaged only on casual daily basis 
and such engagement was subject to availability of work on each day and work was offered on rotation basis to all 
such persons who are willing and make themselves available. As such there is no violation of any statutory rule or 
constitutional provisions in the matter. The engagement of the workman as casual Typist was purely on casual daily 
rated basis subject to availability of work. | The workman having been fully aware of the nature of her engagement 
and the consequences flowing from it, cannot now make claims to the contrary. Respondent contended that to meet 
certain exigencies and contingencies and whenever additional hands were required due to temporary increase in work 
load etc., the Company resorted to engagement of casual daily rated workers, from among those persons who were 
willing and making themselves available for work. Such causals were engaged in certain jobs like typist, drivers, 
helpers etc. on the basis of requirement. The rules of recruitment are not followed while engaging persons as daily- 
rated causal workers as is being done in the case of regular appointments. They are not selected in the manner in 
which regular employees are selected. Further, it is contended that it is open to the causal daily rated employees not 
to report for work on any day. Like-wise, the company is also not under obligation to offer them casual employment 
when there is no requirement. The casual workers are not holding any post in the company and cannot be equated 
with regular workmen or claim regularization of their services. Further, Respondent submitted that such causal daily 
rated employees are offered employment subject to availability of work have no right much less legal right to any 
post. They cannot claim back door entry into regular service bypassing the Rules. Hon’ble Supreme Court of India 
and Hon’ble High Court of Telangana have repeatedly held in umpteen number of cases that a person employed on 


7256 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


causal basis cannot lay any claim for benefits whatsoever, much less regularization in service on the basis of such 
casual employment. 


Further, Respondent submitted that the workman had worked as a causal Typist for a period of 90 days 
initially during the period from 3.8.98 to 3.0.98 and thereafter she had never approached the Management for such 
employment till the year 2003. Only in the year 2003 she again approached the Management and the Management 
had engaged the workman as a casual typist in accordance with the scheme of casual engagement workmen as 
approved by the Hon’ble High Court of A.P. vide order dated 9.0.200l passed in a batch of 28 Writ Petitions 
No.I6/200I etc.. According to scheme, workman was engaged as casual Typist for 80 days during the period 
from June, 2003 to 23.2.2004, l65 days during the period from 5.3.2005 to l6.9.2005, [73 days during the period 
28.9.2006 to 9.4.2007, 79 days during the period from 0.4.2008 to 24.0.2008 and 80 days during the period from 
24.2.2009 to 26.6.20l0. The Respondent contended that allegation of Petitioner that the company was giving 
artificial breaks by engaging her only for a period of 79 days in a year is not correct. Further, it is contended that a 
person engaged on casual basis is not entitled to claim either continuity or regularization in service. 


Respondent contended that the company is a public sector undertaking functioning under the control of the 
Ministry for Civil Aviation , Government of India, New Delhi and recruitment to various posts against regular 
vacancies is subject to the rules of recruitment and also subject to statutory provisions and guidelines of the Central 
Government, regarding reservations to SC/ST/OBC etc. as per statutory provisions. Some individuals who had 
worked as casual workers had filed a batch of 28 Writ Petitions No.l6 of 200 etc. before the Hon’ble High Court 
of A.P. praying for orders for regularization of their services against permanent vacancies. The company, as it was 
called as Indian Airlines Limited, filed counter affidavits in the said cases and Hon’ble High Court having considered

Now, let us examine whether the alleged termination of the Petitioner from the services by the Respondent is 
covered under the definition of Retrenchment as provided u/s 2 (00) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. 


Section 2(00) provides:- 


Section 2(00) "retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not include — 


(a) voluntary retrenchment of the workman; or 


(b) retrenchment of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the 
employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulated in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of employment between 
the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract being terminated under a stipulation in 
that behalf contained therein" 


Thus, in view of the definition of Retrenchment as contained u/s 2 (00)(bb) of I.D. Act, !947 in the instant matter the

Further, Respondent contended that from May, [997, there has been a ban on recruitment and hence the Respondent

3. Before delving into the question of legality of action of Respondent in not regularizing the Petitioner on the 
post of Typist it would be apposite to discuss the precedents of Hon’ble Supreme Court on the aspect of 
regularization of employee on the permanent post by the employer. 


4. In this context, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Regional Manager, SBI Vs Mahatma Mishra on ।* 
November, 2006 have held :- 
“Yet again in National Fertilizers Ltd. & Ors. v. Somvir Singh [(2006) 6 SCALE 07॥, it was held: 


"Regularization, furthermore, is not a mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following the Rules, the 
same being a nullity the question of confirmation of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation 
would not arise" 


It was further opined : 


‘Tt is true that the Respondents had been working for a long time. It may also be true that they had not been paid 
wages on a regular scale of pay. But, they did not hold any post. They were, therefore, not entitled to be paid salary 
ona regular scale of pay. Furthermore, only because thess Respondents have worked for some time, the same by itself 
would not be a ground for directing regularization of their services in view of the decision of this Court in Uma 
Devi (supra)."" 


Furthermore, the High Court, in our opinion, committed a serious error in passing an order only on the basis of 
sympathy although it was held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief.”’ 


“70. Yet again, recently in Ramakrishna_Kamat_v. State _of Karnataka this Court rejected a similar plea for 
regularisation of services stating: (SCC pp. 377-78, para 7) 'We repeatedly asked the learned counsel for the 
appellants on what basis or foundation in law the appellants made their claim for regularisation and under what 
rules their recruitment was made so as to govern their service conditions. They were not in a position to answer 
except saying that the appellants have been working for quite some time in various schools started pursuant to 
resolutions passed by Zila Parishads in view of the government orders and that their cases need to be considered 
sympathetically. It is clear from the order of the learned Single Judge and looking to the very directions given, a very 
sympathetic view was taken. We do not find it either just or proper to show any further sympathy in the given facts 
and circumstances of the case. While being sympathetic to the persons who come before the court the courts cannot at 
the same time be unsympathetic to the large number of eligible persons waiting for a long time in a long queue 
seeking employment.’ " 


Thus, as per the law laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above the regularization of a workman is not a 
mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following rules is being nullity and question of confirmation 
of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation would not arise. Thus, admittedly in the instant 
case Petitioner was neither recruited nor appointed on any post by the Respondent management under any Rules. 
Petitioner herein was engaged casually to work for a fixed term under the schemes to engage casual workmen for 
work as approved by Hon'ble High Court. Thus, Petitioner was engaged on casual basis for fixed term and on expiry 
of fixed term another workman was engaged. The Petitioner was never appointed or engaged on any post 
continuously. Therefore, she can not claim for regularization merely on the basis of working days or period. 
5. Further, in the case of Krishan Gopal Vs ONGC 2020 SC-78 Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
broad principle in respect of granting regularization to an employee. The Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 
# 24 The divergence between the decisions in Bijli Mazdoor Sangh and Maharashtra SRTC was sought to be 
reconciled in a two judge Bench decision of this Court in Hari_Nandan_Prasad_v_ Employer I/R_to 
Management of Food Corporation of India20 (“FCI’’). Justice A K Sikri, speaking for the two judge Bench 
held: 


“39. On a harmonious reading of the two judgments discussed in detail above, we are of the opinion that 
when there are posts available, in the absence of any unfair labour practice the Labour Court would not give 
direction for regularisation only because a worker has continued as daily- wage worker/ad hoc/temporary 
worker for number of years. Further, if there are no posts available, such a direction for regularisation 
would be impermissible. In the aforesaid circumstances giving of direction to regularise such a person, only 
on the basis of number of years put in by such a worker as daily-wager, etc. may amount to back door entry 
into the service which is an anathema to Article /4 of the Constitution. Further, such a direction would not 
be given when the worker (2005) 6 SCC 75] (2074) 7 SCC 7909 concerned does not meet the eligibility 
requirement of the post in question as per the recruitment rules. However, wherever it is found that similarly 
situated workmen are regularised by the employer itself under some scheme or otherwise and the workmen

in question who have approached the Industrial/Labour Court are on a par with them, direction of 
regularisation in such cases may be legally justified, otherwise, non-regularisation of the left-over workers 
itself would amount to invidious discrimination qua them in such cases and would be violative of Article 
4 of the Constitution. Thus, the industrial adjudicator would be achieving the equality by upholding Article 
4, rather than violating this constitutional provision.” 


23 The following propositions would emerge upon analyzing the above decisions: 


(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to 
order regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions 
contained in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the 
Status of permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair 
labour practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to 
employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular 
workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts 
are available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number 
of years of service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would 
be open to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been 
regularised to make a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit 
would amount to a violation of Article ।4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 709 of the Vth Schedule 
of the ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing 
them for years, with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


6. Further, in the case of ZP Engg. Devi and another Vs. Digambara Rao (2004) 6 SCC 262 Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have held:- 


“It may not be out of place to mention that completion of 240 days of continuous service in a year may not by itself 
be a ground for directing an order of regularization. It is not also case of Respondent that they were appointed in 
accordance with extant rules. No direction for regularization of their services was therefore be issued.” 


ine Thus, in view of the law laid down of the Hon’ble Supreme court, as discussed in preceding paragraphs, 
Petitioner has failed to produce any evidence in support of her plea that employer has indulged in an unfair labour 
practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such post which available or and by continuing Petitioner 
workman on temporary or daily wages basis. There is no evidence on record that Petitioner was recruited and 
appointed to any post in accordance with extant rules. Therefore, in view of fore gone discussion and law laid down 
by the Apex Court as discussed above, Petitioner workman is not entitled for regularization in the services of 
Respondent management from the date of her initial appointment as he claims. Thus, the action of Respondent in not 
regularizing the workman on the post of Typist is legal and justified. 
This issue is decided against the Petitioner and in favour of Respondent. 

8. Issue No.III:- In view of the finding and discussion at Issue No.I and Issue No.II, Petitioner is not 
entitled for any regularization and re-instatement in the service of Respondent and her claim is liable to be dismissed. 


Thus, the claim statement filed by the Petitioner is liable to be dismissed.

Now, let us examine whether the alleged termination of the Petitioner from the services by the Respondent is 


covered under the definition of Retrenchment as provided u/s 2 (00) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. 


Section 2(00) provides:- 


Section 2(00) "retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not include — 


(a) voluntary retrenchment of the workman; or 


(b) retrenchment of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the 
employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulated in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of employment between 
the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract being terminated under a stipulation in 
that behalf contained therein" 


Thus, in view of the definition of Retrenchment as contained u/s 2 (00)(bb) of I.D. Act, 947 in the instant matter the 
services of the workman has been terminated as a result of non- renewal of the Contract’ of employment between 
employer and workman concerned on its expiry of term as manifested by the documents #.४४] to Ex.W8. Thus, 
alleged termination of the Petitioner from service is not covered under definition of retrenchment as provided under 
Sec.2(00) of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 and provision of Sec.25F of I.D. Act, !947 is not applicable to his case. 
However, Petitioner workman has argued that he was rendering continuous service and there was never any break

4. In this context, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Regional Manager, SBI Vs Mahatma Mishra on ।*' 
November, 2006 have held :- 


“Yet again in National Fertilizers Ltd. & Ors. v. Somvir Singh [(2006) 6 SCALE 07॥, it was held: 

"Regularization, furthermore, is not a mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following the Rules, the 
same being a nullity the question of confirmation of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation 
would not arise" 

It was further opined : 

‘Tt is true that the Respondents had been working for a long time. It may also be true that they had not been paid 
wages on a regular scale of pay. But, they did not hold any post. They were, therefore, not entitled to be paid salary 
on a regular scale of pay. Furthermore, only because thess Respondents have worked for some time, the same by itself 
would not be a ground for directing regularization of their services in view of the decision of this Court in Uma 
Devi (supra)."" 

Furthermore, the High Court, in our opinion, committed a serious error in passing an order only on the basis of 
sympathy although it was held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief.” 

“70. Yet again, recently in Ramakrishna_Kamat_v. State _of Karnataka this Court rejected a similar plea for 
regularisation of services stating: (SCC pp. 377-78, para 7) 'We repeatedly asked the learned counsel for the 
appellants on what basis or foundation in law the appellants made their claim for regularisation and under what 
rules their recruitment was made so as to govern their service conditions. They were not in a position to answer 
except saying that the appellants have been working for quite some time in various schools started pursuant to 
resolutions passed by Zila Parishads in view of the government orders and that their cases need to be considered 
sympathetically. It is clear from the order of the learned Single Judge and looking to the very directions given, a very 
sympathetic view was taken. We do not find it either just or proper to show any further sympathy in the given facts 
and circumstances of the case. While being sympathetic to the persons who come before the court the courts cannot at 
the same time be unsympathetic to the large number of eligible persons waiting for a long time in a long queue 
seeking employment.'" 

Thus, as per the law laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above the regularization of a workman is not a 
mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following rules is being nullity and question of confirmation 
of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation would not arise. Thus, admittedly in the instant 
case Petitioner was neither recruited nor appointed on any post by the Respondent management under any Rules. 


7270 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST , 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


Petitioner herein was engaged casually to work for a fixed term under the schemes to engage casual workmen for 
work as approved by Hon'ble High Court. Thus, Petitioner was engaged on casual basis for fixed term and on expiry 
of fixed term another workman was engaged. The Petitioner was never appointed or engaged on any post 
continuously. Therefore, he can not claim for regularization merely on the basis of working days or period. 


4. Further, in the case of Krishan Gopal Vs ONGC 2020 SC-78 Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
broad principle in respect of granting regularization to an employee. The Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 
# 24 The divergence between the decisions in Bijli Mazdoor Sangh and Maharashtra SRTC was sought to be 
reconciled in a two judge Bench decision of this Court in Hari_Nandan_Prasad_v_ Employer I/R_to 
Management of Food Corporation of India20 (“FCI’’). Justice A K Sikri, speaking for the two judge Bench 
held: 


“39. On a harmonious reading of the two judgments discussed in detail above, we are of the opinion that 
when there are posts available, in the absence of any unfair labour practice the Labour Court would not give 
direction for regularisation only because a worker has continued as daily- wage worker/ad hoc/temporary 
worker for number of years. Further, if there are no posts available, such a direction for regularisation 
would be impermissible. In the aforesaid circumstances giving of direction to regularise such a person, only 
on the basis of number of years put in by such a worker as daily-wager, etc. may amount to back door entry 
into the service which is an anathema to Article /4 of the Constitution. Further, such a direction would not 
be given when the worker (2005) 6 SCC 757 (2074) 7 SCC 7909 concerned does not meet the eligibility 
requirement of the post in question as per the recruitment rules. However, wherever it is found that similarly 
situated workmen are regularised by the employer itself under some scheme or otherwise and the workmen 
in question who have approached the Industrial/Labour Court are on a par with them, direction of 
regularisation in such cases may be legally justified, otherwise, non-regularisation of the left-over workers 
itself would amount to invidious discrimination qua them in such cases and would be violative of Article 
44 of the Constitution. Thus, the industrial adjudicator would be achieving the equality by upholding Article 
44, rather than violating this constitutional provision.” 


23 The following propositions would emerge upon analyzing the above decisions: 


(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to 
order regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions 
contained in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the 
Status of permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair 
labour practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to 
employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular 
workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts 
are available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number 
of years of service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would 
be open to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been 
regularised to make a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit 
would amount to a violation of Article /4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 709 of the Vth Schedule 
of the ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing 
them for years, with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


5. Further, in the case of ZP Engg. Devi and another Vs. Digambara Rao (2004) 6 SCC 262 Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have held:- 


“It may not be out of place to mention that completion of 240 days of continuous service in a year may not by itself 
be a ground for directing an order of regularization. It is not also case of Respondent that they were appointed in 
accordance with extant rules. No direction for regularization of their services was therefore be issued.” 

6. Thus, in view of the law laid down of the Hon’ble Supreme court, as discussed in preceding paragraphs, 
Petitioner has failed to produce any evidence in support of his plea that employer has indulged in an unfair labour 
practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such post which available or and by continuing Petitioner 
workman on temporary or daily wages basis. There is no evidence on record that Petitioner was recruited and 
appointed to any post in accordance with extant rules. Therefore, in view of fore gone discussion and law laid down

by the Apex Court as discussed above, Petitioner workman is not entitled for regularization in the services of 
Respondent management from the date of his initial appointment as he claims. Thus, the action of Respondent in not 
regularizing the workman on the post of Peon is legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the Petitioner and in favour of Respondent.

has not fulfilled the condition precedent for seeking protection against Retrenchment as provided under the provision 
of Sec.25F of I.D. Act, 947. Since Petitioner failed to fulfill condition of one year of continuous service before the 
date of her termination. 


Now, let us examine whether the alleged termination of the Petitioner from the services by the Respondent is 
covered under the definition of Retrenchment as provided u/s 2 (00) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. 


Section 2(00) provides:- 


Section 2(00) "retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not include — 

(a) voluntary retrenchment of the workman; or 

(b) retrenchment of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the 
employer and the workman concerned contains a Stipulated in that behalf; or 

(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of employment between 
the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract being terminated under a stipulation in 
that behalf contained therein" 

Thus, in view of the definition of Retrenchment as contained u/s 2 (00)(bb) of I.D. Act, !947 in the instant matter the 
services of the workman has been terminated as a result of non- renewal of the Contract’ of employment between 
employer and workman concerned on its expiry of term as manifested by the documents ४5.0७७] to Ex.W7. Thus, 
alleged termination of the Petitioner from service is not covered under definition of retrenchment as provided under 
Sec.2(00) of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 and provision of Sec.25F of ID. Act, 947 is not applicable to her case. 
However, Petitioner workman has argued that she was rendering continuous service and there was never any break 
except weekly off to which she is entitled but the management has created the artificial break after every 79 days of 
service only to deprive the regularization of workman. 


In this context, Respondent has contended that casual worker who had worked, filed a batch of 28 Writ Petitions 
No.l6 of 200] etc.. before the Hon’ble High Court of A.P. praying for orders of regularization of their services 
against permanent vacancies. |The company, as it was called as Indian Airlines Limited, filed counter affidavits in 
the said cases and Hon’ble High Court having considered the aspect that a number of cases were filed by casual 
workers including workman, working in different jobs has directed Indian Airlines Limited to evolve a scheme for 
empanelment, engagement and also for absorption in future vacancies whenever they occur. A scheme was 
accordingly formulated and submitted to the Hon’ble High Court and upon considering the said scheme, the Hon’ble 
Court dismissed the batch of WPs filed by casuals vide a common order dated 9.[0.200] and has approved scheme 
framed by Indian Airlines for empanelment and engagement of casuals. The said scheme of engagement of casuals 
on rotation basis was further upheld by the Division Bench of AP High Court vide order dated 0.08.2009 passed in a 
batch of cases in Writ Appeals No.24/2002, etc. Further, Respondent contended that the workman herein was such 
causal worker whose name figured in the pool of causal Typist prepared in the year 200l, as she had worked for a 
term before formation of the panel on 9.!0.200l, and thus she became eligible to be considered for casual 
engagement provided she offer her services as a causal worker and subject to requirement for such casual engagement 
by the Company, in terms of the said order passed by the Hon’ble High Court. As workman herein could not secure 
a permanent employment elsewhere she had subsequently approached the company offering her services as a casual 
worker and thus she was engaged as a casual worker on certain occasions subsequently to the year 200 in 
accordance with the terms of the said schemes approved by the Hon’ble AP High Court. 


Further, Respondent contended that there is no such term as automatic absorption of causals as per the provisions of 
the scheme approved by the Hon’ble High Court. It would be apposite to reproduce the extract of the relevant terms 
of the schemes approved High Court vide the common order dated 9.0.200 as hereunder: - 

“6. after scrutinizing the records of such of the casual workers who report on response to the intimations within the 
period specified will be engaged on casual basis on rotation till such time the vacancies are available. In order to 
provide an equal opportunity to all the ex-casuals the engagement of an individual will be restricted to 90 days or 769 
days only as the case may be and after completion of the term by an individual, the next person will be offered causal 
employment on the same basis. In case of any individual drops out, the next person failing to report will be struck off 
from the panel as aforesaid. 

7. The engagement of causals will be continued only till the requirement of the company. In case of the company’s 
deciding to fill up any vacancies on regular basis as per the recruitment and promotion rules, they will be considered 
subject to their fulfilling the eligibility criteria fixed for the respective posts on regular basis.” 


[भाग [lave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7277 


Further, it is contended that the workman was given an opportunity of working as a casual in accordance with the 
provisions of the above said scheme and by working as casual on certain occasions she had not acquired any right to 
claim regularization. The engagement of a casual is restricted to a maximum of 80 days as per the scheme in order 
to give an opportunity to the other individuals in the panel who were willing to work on casual basis in terms of the 
scheme. The workman had chosen to offer her services for engagement as a casual worker voluntarily and there was 
no demand by the Company or particularly engaging the workman on casual basis as there were other individuals 
available in the panel casuals. Respondent contended that the allegation of workman that the company has created 
artificial breaks in her service is false. The casual workers, so engaged, are issued with identity card in connection 
with work requirement and are paid bonus, ESI contribution as required under the applicable laws and that does not 
give workman any right for regularization. In view of fore gone discussion and on going evidence on record as well 
as direction of Hon'ble High Court as quoted in preceding paragraph, I am of the considered view that the action of 
Respondent management in terminating the services of the Petitioner workman is legal and justified. In view of order 
of Hon'ble High Court the plea of the Petitioner that Respondent has created artificial break in the service of workman 
after every 79 days is untenable. 


Thus, Issue No.I is decided against the Petitioner and in favour of Respondent. 


9. Issue No.II:- This issue pertains to question whether the action Respondent in not regularizing the service of 
Petitioner in the post of Typist is justified. 


0. In this context, Petitioner witness १४५४] in her chief statement of affidavit has stated that, she has rendered 
continuous service and there was no break in her service. WWI has deposed that Respondent used to create the 
artificial breaks after completing !79 days of service only with the malafide intention to deprive her from 
regularization of service and to show that the worker has not completed 240 days of service. Further, it is submitted 
that giving artificial breaks in the service was with the intention to deprive the regularization of her service and such 
action of Respondent is illegal, unjust, contrary to law, victimization and amounts to unfair labour practice. 


Il. Undisputedly, Petitioner workman was engaged by the Respondent management for the work on casual 
basis for a fixed period intermittently from time to time during the period. Petitioner had not filed any document to 
show that he was appointed by Respondent on the post of Typist. Further, Petitioner has not filed any documentary 
evidence i.e., any appointment order, salary slip or any other document in support of her claim that she was recruited 
and appointed by Respondent on the post of Typist. The documents Ex.W] to Ex.W7 are the engagement letters of 
workman for different periods upto maximum term of |80 days. 


2. Per contra, Respondent has contended that the workmen/Petitioner had filed a W.P.No.38082 /20I2 before 
the Hon'ble High Court of AP praying to regularize their services in the respective post from the initial date of their 
appointment, to retain and continue them in the respective post with all consequential benefits and attendant benefits 
and pending disposal of this Writ Petition to continue them in their respective post without effecting any artificial 
breaks. The Writ Petition No.38082 /20l2 came up for final hearing along with batch of the l5 writ petitions and on 
07.03.20i3 the Hon'ble High Court directed Air India Limited to engage the services of the Petitioner and others 
continuously without effecting any artificial breaks so long as it is felt necessary for engaging the services, without 
resorting to engaging the service of freshers. The writ petitions were dismissed by Hon’ble Court, same workman 
was pursuing her claim for regularization by filing industrial dispute case before Labour Court. 


Further, Writ Appeals including WA No.882/20]3 in respect of WP No. 38082/202 were filed before the division 
bench challenging the order and Hon'ble Division Bench ordered that they do not see any necessity or reason to 
modify the order passed by the learned Single Judge, as he had already granted the necessary leave to engage the 
services of the Writ Petitioners, on casual basis, till such time the quantum of work undertaken by the Air India 
required any such engagement and if there is no requirement of man-power, freedom and liberty is already preserved 
not to engage the casual employees. 


Further, Respondent contended that from May, [997, there has been a ban on recruitment and hence the Respondent 
Airline could not make permanent appointments to any post except certain posts of critical nature or in case of 
operational requirements and that too mostly on fixed term contract basis after 20l2. In any case, appointments to 
various posts can be made only as per recruitment procedure. 


3. Before delving into the question of legality of action of Respondent in not regularizing the Petitioner on the 
post of Typist it would be apposite to discuss the precedents of Hon’ble Supreme Court on the aspect of 
regularization of employee on the permanent post by the employer. 


4. In this context, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Regional Manager, SBI Vs Mahatma Mishra on * 
November, 2006 have held :- 
“Yet again in National Fertilizers Ltd. & Ors. v. Somvir Singh [(2006) 6 SCALE 707॥, it was held: 


7278 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST I, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


"Regularization, furthermore, is not a mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following the Rules, the 
same being a nullity the question of confirmation of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation 
would not arise" 
It was further opined : 
‘Tt is true that the Respondents had been working for a long time. It may also be true that they had not been paid 
wages on a regular scale of pay. But, they did not hold any post. They were, therefore, not entitled to be paid salary 
on a regular scale of pay. Furthermore, only because thess Respondents have worked for some time, the same by itself 
would not be a ground for directing regularization of their services in view of the decision of this Court in Uma 
Devi (supra)."" 
Furthermore, the High Court, in our opinion, committed a serious error in passing an order only on the basis of 
sympathy although it was held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief.” 
“70. Yet again, recently in Ramakrishna_Kamat_v. State _of Karnataka this Court rejected a similar plea for 
regularisation of services stating: (SCC pp. 377-78, para 7) 'We repeatedly asked the learned counsel for the 
appellants on what basis or foundation in law the appellants made their claim for regularisation and under what 
rules their recruitment was made so as to govern their service conditions. They were not in a position to answer 
except saying that the appellants have been working for quite some time in various schools started pursuant to 
resolutions passed by Zila Parishads in view of the government orders and that their cases need to be considered 
sympathetically. It is clear from the order of the learned Single Judge and looking to the very directions given, a very 
sympathetic view was taken. We do not find it either just or proper to show any further sympathy in the given facts 
and circumstances of the case. While being sympathetic to the persons who come before the court the courts cannot at 
the same time be unsympathetic to the large number of eligible persons waiting for a long time in a long queue 
seeking employment.'" 
Thus, as per the law laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above the regularization of a workman is not a 
mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following rules is being nullity and question of confirmation 
of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation would not arise. Thus, admittedly in the instant 
case Petitioner was neither recruited nor appointed on any post by the Respondent management under any Rules. 
Petitioner herein was engaged casually to work for a fixed term under the schemes to engage casual workmen for 
work as approved by Hon'ble High Court. Thus, Petitioner was engaged on casual basis for fixed term and on expiry 
of fixed term another workman was engaged. The Petitioner was never appointed or engaged on any post 
continuously. Therefore, she can not claim for regularization merely on the basis of working days or period. 
5. Further, in the case of Krishan Gopal Vs ONGC 2020 SC-78 Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
broad principle in respect of granting regularization to an employee. The Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 
# 24 The divergence between the decisions in Bijli Mazdoor Sangh and Maharashtra SRTC was sought to be 
reconciled in a two judge Bench decision of this Court in Hari_Nandan_Prasad_v_ Employer I/R_to 
Management of Food Corporation of India20 (“FCI’’). Justice A K Sikri, speaking for the two judge Bench 
held: 
“39. On a harmonious reading of the two judgments discussed in detail above, we are of the opinion that 
when there are posts available, in the absence of any unfair labour practice the Labour Court would not give 
direction for regularisation only because a worker has continued as daily- wage worker/ad hoc/temporary 
worker for number of years. Further, if there are no posts available, such a direction for regularisation 
would be impermissible. In the aforesaid circumstances giving of direction to regularise such a person, only 
on the basis of number of years put in by such a worker as daily-wager, etc. may amount to back door entry 
into the service which is an anathema to Article /4 of the Constitution. Further, such a direction would not 
be given when the worker (2005) 6 SCC 757 (2074) 7 SCC 7909 concerned does not meet the eligibility 
requirement of the post in question as per the recruitment rules. However, wherever it is found that similarly 
situated workmen are regularised by the employer itself under some scheme or otherwise and the workmen 
in question who have approached the Industrial/Labour Court are on a par with them, direction of 
regularisation in such cases may be legally justified, otherwise, non-regularisation of the left-over workers 
itself would amount to invidious discrimination qua them in such cases and would be violative of Article 
44 of the Constitution. Thus, the industrial adjudicator would be achieving the equality by upholding Article 
44, rather than violating this constitutional provision.” 


23 The following propositions would emerge upon analyzing the above decisions: 

(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to 
order regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions 
contained in Article /4 of the Constitution; 

(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the 
Status of permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair 
labour practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to 
employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular 
workmen on lower wages; 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण L0, 948 7279 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts 
are available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number 
of years of service; 
(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would 
be open to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been 
regularised to make a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit 
would amount to a violation of Article ।4, and 
(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 79 of the Vth Schedule 
of the ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing 
them for years, with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 

6. Further, in the case of ZP Engg. Devi and another Vs. Digambara Rao (2004) 6 SCC 262 Hon’ble 


Supreme Court have held:- 


“It may not be out of place to mention that completion of 240 days of continuous service in a year may not by itself 

be a ground for directing an order of regularization. It is not also case of Respondent that they were appointed in 
accordance with extant rules. No direction for regularization of their services was therefore be issued.” 
7. Thus, in view of the law laid down of the Hon’ble Supreme court, as discussed in preceding paragraphs, 
Petitioner has failed to produce any evidence in support of her plea that employer has indulged in an unfair labour 
practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such post which available or and by continuing Petitioner 
workman on temporary or daily wages basis. There is no evidence on record that Petitioner was recruited and 
appointed to any post in accordance with extant rules. Therefore, in view of fore gone discussion and law laid down 
by the Apex Court as discussed above, Petitioner workman is not entitled for regularization in the services of 
Respondent management from the date of her initial appointment as he claims. Thus, the action of Respondent in not 
regularizing the workman on the post of Typist is legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the Petitioner and in favour of Respondent. 


8. Issue No.III:- In view of the finding and discussion at Issue No.I and Issue No.II, Petitioner is not 
entitled for any regularization and re-instatement in the service of Respondent and her claim is liable to be dismissed. 


Thus, the claim statement filed by the Petitioner is liable to be dismissed. 
AWARD 


l. In view of finding given at Issue No.I, वा and III, the claim petition filed by the Petitioner in LC No.7/204 
challenging her termination order claiming regularization is hereby dismissed. 


2. The action of the management in not regularizing the services of Ms. S. Gayatri Devi D/o Sri M.N. 
Damodaram in the post of Typist is held justified. As such, the workman is not entitled to any relief as 
prayed for. The reference ID No.226/20]4 is answered accordingly.
