The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No. L-4202/27/202-IR(DU) dated 
08/02/2023 passed in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of section (l) read with sub-section (2A) of 
Section l0 of the Industrial Dispute Act 947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as 
under: 


“Whether the dispute raised by Sh. Bandu Navnath Babar vide letter dated 23.02.202I against the 
management of M/s b4S Solutions Pvt. Ltd., Pune for alleged illegal transfer from Latur to Pune is covered 
under the industrial Dispute under the jurisdiction of the Central Government under ID Act, /9472 If yea, 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 728] 


whether the action of the management of M/s b4S Solutions Pvt. Ltd., Pune to transfer Sh. Bandu Navnath 
Babar from Latur to Pune is proper, Legal and justified? If not. To what relief the concerned applicant is 
entitled to? What direction, if any, is necessary in the matter?’ 


In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 
case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (7) and others /987 (29) FLR 94 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred 
by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (II), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (776) FLR 7764 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries vy. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 7964 (49) FLR 38 and 
Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. /996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the 
workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not 
necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation 
made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2070 (726) FLR 59; 


Management is submits as under:- 


I.The second Party Workmen Sh. Bandu Navnath Babar has tendered his resignation from the services of the First 
Party Company with effect from 30.03.202] 


2.Second party workman also has submitted a letter dated 05.06.2023 in which has informed the First party that he is 
withdrawing the Industrial Dispute bearing No. Reference CGIT — 25 of 2023 which is pending adjudication in this 
Hon’ble Tribunal, he has stated in said letter that h would be filing application this effect before this Hon’ble 
Tribunal within 4 days. 


3.Even otherwise the Second party workman has remained absent with effect from 20" October 2020 to 077 
April2023. His name therefore was removed from the services of the company on 07" April,2023 on ground that he 
had abandoned his services. A copy of letter dated 7" April, 2023 issued by First Party Company to second party 
workman is annexed with this application. Now in view of the resignation by Second Party, Second party’s discharge 
stands converted to acceptance of resignation. 


4.The First Party Employer therefore state and submits that no cause of action survives in the Industrial Dispute now 
and the adjudication proceedings in this case become infructuous. 


5.Therefore the First party company respectfully prays that the Industrial Dispute may be disposed of for want of 
cause of action 


Since no statement of claim has been filed by the union in support of his case, the claim is liable to be dismissed. 
For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the union is not entitled for any relief. 
Accordingly, the reference stands answered in terms aforesaid.

Now, let us examine whether the alleged termination of the Petitioner from the services by the Respondent is 
covered under the definition of Retrenchment as provided u/s 2 (00) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. 


Section 2(00) provides:- 


Section 2(00) "retrenchment" means the termination by the employer of the service of a workman for any reason 
whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, but does not include - 


(a) voluntary retrenchment of the workman; or 


(b) retrenchment of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the 
employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulated in that behalf; or 


(bb) termination of the service of the workman as a result of the non-renewal of the contract of employment between 
the employer and the workman concerned on its expiry or of such contract being terminated under a stipulation in 
that behalf contained therein" 


Thus, in view of the definition of Retrenchment as contained u/s 2 (00)(bb) of I.D. Act, !947 in the instant matter the 
services of the workman has been terminated as a result of non- renewal of the Contract’ of employment between 
employer and workman concerned on its expiry of term as manifested by the documents 75.४७] to Ex.W8. Thus, 
alleged termination of the Petitioner from service is not covered under definition of retrenchment as provided under 
Sec.2(00) of Industrial Disputes Act, 947 and provision of Sec.25F of I.D. Act, 947 is not applicable to his case.

4. In this context, Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Regional Manager, SBI Vs Mahatma Mishra on ।* 
November, 2006 have held :- 


“Yet again in National Fertilizers Ltd. & Ors. v. Somvir Singh [(2006) 6 SCALE 707॥, it was held: 

"Regularization, furthermore, is not a mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following the Rules, the 
same being a nullity the question of confirmation of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation 
would not arise" 

It was further opined : 

‘Tt is true that the Respondents had been working for a long time. It may also be true that they had not been paid 
wages on a regular scale of pay. But, they did not hold any post. They were, therefore, not entitled to be paid salary 
on a regular scale of pay. Furthermore, only because thess Respondents have worked for some time, the same by itself 
would not be a ground for directing regularization of their services in view of the decision of this Court in Uma 
Devi (supra)."" 

Furthermore, the High Court, in our opinion, committed a serious error in passing an order only on the basis of 
sympathy although it was held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief.” 

“70. Yet again, recently in Ramakrishna_Kamat_v. State _of Karnataka this Court rejected a similar plea for 
regularisation of services stating: (SCC pp. 377-78, para 7) 'We repeatedly asked the learned counsel for the 
appellants on what basis or foundation in law the appellants made their claim for regularisation and under what 
rules their recruitment was made so as to govern their service conditions. They were not in a position to answer 
except saying that the appellants have been working for quite some time in various schools started pursuant to 
resolutions passed by Zila Parishads in view of the government orders and that their cases need to be considered 
sympathetically. It is clear from the order of the learned Single Judge and looking to the very directions given, a very 
sympathetic view was taken. We do not find it either just or proper to show any further sympathy in the given facts 
and circumstances of the case. While being sympathetic to the persons who come before the court the courts cannot at 
the same time be unsympathetic to the large number of eligible persons waiting for a long time in a long queue 
seeking employment.’ " 

Thus, as per the law laid down by Hon’ble Supreme Court as discussed above the regularization of a workman is not a 
mode of appointment. If appointment is made without following rules is being nullity and question of confirmation 
of an employee upon the expiry of the purported period of probation would not arise. Thus, admittedly in the instant 
case Petitioner was neither recruited nor appointed on any post by the Respondent management under any Rules. 
Petitioner herein was engaged casually to work for a fixed term under the schemes to engage casual workmen for 
work as approved by Hon'ble High Court. Thus, Petitioner was engaged on casual basis for fixed term and on expiry 
of fixed term another workman was engaged. The Petitioner was never appointed or engaged on any post 
continuously. Therefore, he can not claim for regularization merely on the basis of working days or period. 


4. Further, in the case of Krishan Gopal Vs ONGC 2020 SC-78 Hon’ble Supreme Court has laid down the 
broad principle in respect of granting regularization to an employee. The Hon’ble Supreme Court have held:- 


# 24 The divergence between the decisions in Bijli Mazdoor Sangh and Maharashtra SRTC was sought to be 
reconciled in a two judge Bench decision of this Court in Hari_Nandan_Prasad_v_ Employer I/R_to 
Management of Food Corporation of India20 (“FCI’’). Justice A K Sikri, speaking for the two judge Bench 
held: 


“39. On a harmonious reading of the two judgments discussed in detail above, we are of the opinion that 
when there are posts available, in the absence of any unfair labour practice the Labour Court would not give 
direction for regularisation only because a worker has continued as daily- wage worker/ad hoc/temporary 
worker for number of years. Further, if there are no posts available, such a direction for regularisation 
would be impermissible. In the aforesaid circumstances giving of direction to regularise such a person, only 
on the basis of number of years put in by such a worker as daily-wager, etc. may amount to back door entry 
into the service which is an anathema to Article /4 of the Constitution. Further, such a direction would not 
be given when the worker (2005) 6 SCC 757 (2074) 7 SCC 799 concerned does not meet the eligibility 
requirement of the post in question as per the recruitment rules. However, wherever it is found that similarly 
situated workmen are regularised by the employer itself under some scheme or otherwise and the workmen 
in question who have approached the Industrial/Labour Court are on a par with them, direction of 
regularisation in such cases may be legally justified, otherwise, non-regularisation of the left-over workers 
itself would amount to invidious discrimination qua them in such cases and would be violative of Article 
4 of the Constitution. Thus, the industrial adjudicator would be achieving the equality by upholding Article 
44, rather than violating this constitutional provision.” 


23 The following propositions would emerge upon analyzing the above decisions: 


(i) Wide as they are, the powers of the Labour Court and the Industrial Court cannot extend to a direction to 
order regularisation, where such a direction would in the context of public employment offend the provisions 
contained in Article /4 of the Constitution; 


[भाग [ave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण L0, 948 7289 


(ii) The statutory power of the Labour Court or Industrial Court to grant relief to workmen including the 
Status of permanency continues to exist in circumstances where the employer has indulged in an unfair 
labour practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such posts are available and by continuing to 
employ workmen as temporary or daily wage employees despite their performing the same work as regular 
workmen on lower wages; 


(iii) The power to create permanent or sanctioned posts lies outside the judicial domain and where no posts 
are available, a direction to grant regularisation would be impermissible merely on the basis of the number 
of years of service; 


(iv) Where an employer has regularised similarly situated workmen either in a scheme or otherwise, it would 
be open to workmen who have been deprived of the same benefit at par with the workmen who have been 
regularised to make a complaint before the Labour or Industrial Court, since the deprivation of the benefit 
would amount to a violation of Article ।4, and 


(v) In order to constitute an unfair labour practice under Section 2(ra) read with Item 79 of the Vth Schedule 
of the ID Act, the employer should be engaging workmen as badlis, temporaries or casuals, and continuing 
them for years, with the object of depriving them of the benefits payable to permanent workmen. 


5. Further, in the case of ZP Engg. Devi and another Vs. Digambara Rao (2004) 6 SCC 262 Hon’ble 
Supreme Court have held:- 


“It may not be out of place to mention that completion of 240 days of continuous service in a year may not by itself 

be a ground for directing an order of regularization. It is not also case of Respondent that they were appointed in 
accordance with extant rules. No direction for regularization of their services was therefore be issued.” 
6. Thus, in view of the law laid down of the Hon’ble Supreme court, as discussed in preceding paragraphs, 
Petitioner has failed to produce any evidence in support of her plea that employer has indulged in an unfair labour 
practice by not filling up permanent posts even though such post which available or and by continuing Petitioner 
workman on temporary or daily wages basis. There is no evidence on record that Petitioner was recruited and 
appointed to any post in accordance with extant rules. Therefore, in view of fore gone discussion and law laid down 
by the Apex Court as discussed above, Petitioner workman is not entitled for regularization in the services of 
Respondent management from the date of his initial appointment as he claims. Thus, the action of Respondent in not 
regularizing the workman on the post of Helper is legal and justified. 


This issue is decided against the Petitioner and in favour of Respondent. 


7. Issue No.III:- In view of the finding and discussion at Issue No.I and Issue No.II, Petitioner is not 
entitled for any regularization and re-instatement in the service of Respondent and his claim is liable to be dismissed. 


Thus, the claim statement filed by the Petitioner is liable to be dismissed. 
AWARD 


l. In view of finding given at Issue No.I, वा and III, the claim petition filed by the Petitioner in LC No.4/204 
challenging his termination order and claiming regularization is hereby dismissed. 


2: The action of the management in not regularizing the services of Sri D. Srinivas S/o Late Sh. D-Ramaiah in 
the post of Helper(Canteen) is held justified. As such, the workman is not entitled to any relief as prayed for. 
The reference ID No.22/204 is answered accordingly. 


Award is passed accordingly. Transmit.

workmen are the members of Kustore Shramik Sahayog Samiti Ltd. and on demand by the

concerned workmen are the members of Kustore Shramik Sahayog Samiti Ltd and under the work 
order which is temporary in nature,their secretary supplied their services to do the temporary nature 
of job. They never worked under the direct control and supervision of the BCCL nor they were 
engaged by it at any point of time. They are the time rated workers and therefore there is no 
employer employee relationship between the management and the workmen and so their demand of 
regularization is not justified. Their attendance was marked by the Cooperative Society itself as has 
been admitted by ४७४५७-] in Paragraph-3 of his evidence and १४७४-२2 has also admitted that they were 
working through the cooperative society and therefore they cannot be regularized and prayed to hold

3. On perusal of the oral testimony of WW-! Suresh Prasad who is also one of the 
workmen it is evident that they were engaged at Simlabahal Colliery by Kustore Sahayog Samiti as 
General Mazdoor and worked till December 99], They were engaged in transportation work and

cashier of the company. Their attendance was marked by the Attendance Clerk but they stopped their 
work on their demand of equal wages to the regular workmen and they were doing permanent nature

record that have been issued by the same Secretary Sri Ramashray Gahlot of the Samiti.

appears relevant for this case.

to March 990. He has deposed that during his tenure the project work was going on at Simlabahal 
and some contract work was allotted to Kustore Shramik Sahayog Samiti and its workers were

reference case had not worked there. They were knowing the Secretary of the Society and on the 
identification of the Secretary the workers were allowed to work there. After the completion of the

correct. In cross-examination he has admitted that the attendance of the workers who used to work 
were being recorded either as surface worker or as worker working in underground mine. Their work 
were being supervised by the overman and mining sardar.They were being paid by cheque through 
Secretary of the Sahayog Samiti. Work order used to be issued to the Society by the Agent of the 
Colliery. He has denied the suggestion that all the concerned persons had worked at Simlabahal 
Colliery for more than 490/240 days in a calendar year and they have suppressed the attendance 
register. 


6. Admittedly the concerned workmen are the members of Registered Cooperative Society 
namely Kustore Shramik Sahayog Samiti Ltd. and to complete the work order allotted vide work

order no. SBC/BCCL/90/KSSSL-3 dated 0.0.l990(Exhibit ९४-३/॥) and work order no. 
SBC/BCCL/90/KSSSL-5(Exhibit W-3) issued by Dy. C.M.A., Simlabahal Colliery of BCCL, 
Bhalgora Area the concerned workmen were deployed by the Samiti for doing the work of cleaning, 
line packing, material transportation at XI Seam dip Section on contract basis and thus it is clear that 
the cooperative society which is a registered society, supplied its workers to the BCCL for 
completion of the job of the work order on contract basis and as is evident from Exhibit ४-॥ which 
is Attendance Chart, their attendance was marked by Ramashray Gahlot, the Secretary of the 
Cooperative Society itself and though the witnesses of the workmen have stated that they were being 
paid their wages by the management of BCCL but as no pay slip has been issued to them as admitted 
by WW-lI in cross-examination and so for want of any documentary evidence available on the case 
record from the side of the workmen regarding payment of wages to them by the BCCL it is clear 
that the wages of these concerned workmen were also paid to them by the Cooperative Society itself 
and though MW-2 has admitted in his cross-examination that their work was being supervised by the 
Over man and Mining Sardar only on this basis they can not automatically be treated as employees 
of BCCL because in such cases the work is supervised for safety and operational purposes and it is 
not decisive proof of the direct employment in mining operation and statutory supervision by the 
Mines Officials is mandatory under the Mining Laws and therefore this only can not be the basis to 
presume the employer-employee relationship specially when the concerned workmen have been 
supplied by the cooperative society/contractor, their attendance is being maintained and marked by 
them and their wages are being paid by them. 


7. Thus on the basis of the above discussions of facts, circumstances and materials available 
on the case record this Tribunal comes to the conclusion that there being no employer-employee 
relationship between the concerned workmen and the BCCL, the demand of the union for 
regularization by the management of Simlabahal Colliery under Bhalgora Area of M/s. BCCL of Sri 
Gopal Sharan Singh and 07 other workers is not justified and accordingly they are not entitled to 
any relief. The reference is answered accordingly.

The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No. L-420/8/2023-IR(DU) dated 
22/03/2023 passed in exercise of the powers conferred by clause (d) of section (l) read with sub-section (2A) of 
Section l0 of the Industrial Dispute Act 947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as 
under: 


“Whether the dispute raised by Tarapur Atomic Power Project 3 & 4 Employees Association, Palghar vide 
letter dated //७.96.2927 against the management of National Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) 3 
& 4, Tarapur Atomic Power Station (TAPS) over the issue of unfair labour practice by showing partiality or 
granting favour to unrecognized newly formed Trade Union Tarapur Anu-urja karamchari Sangh (TAKS) is 
industrial Dispute under Section 2(k) of I.D. Act, /9477 


If yes, whether the claim of Tarapur Atomic Power Project 3 & 4 Employees Association, Palghar vide letter 
dated //.96.2027 against the management National Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) 3 & 4, 
Tarapur Atomic Power Station (TAPS) over the issue of unfair labour practice by showing partiality or 
granting favour to unrecognized newly formed Trade Union Tarapur Anu-urja karamchari Sangh (TAKS) is 
proper, legal and justified under ID Act, /१477 If yes, to what relief the disputant Union is entitled and what 
directions if any, are necessary in the matter?” 

In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 


case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (7) and others 7/987 (29) FLR 94 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred 
by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (II), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (7768) FLR 7764 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 7/964 (49) FLR 38 and 
Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. /996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the 
workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not 
necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation 
made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail ifno evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2070 (726) FLR 59; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. A perusal 
of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led by the respondent. 
In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.” 


Since no statement of claim has been filed by the union in support of his case, the claim is liable to be dismissed. 
For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the union is not entitled for any relief. 
Accordingly, the reference stands answered in terms aforesaid. 
Award as above.

For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the union is not entitled for any relief.

The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No. RLCP/8(56)/2022 dated 03/[ 2/2024 
passed in exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (5) of section ]2 read with sub-section (2A) of Section l0 
of the Industrial Dispute Act 947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as under: 


“Whether the action of the management of Artificial Limb Centre, Pune in withholding of gratuity and 
regular pension of the workman i.e. shri Lokinder S Painoli is legal and justified? If not, to what relief the 
concerned workman is entitled to ?” 


In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 
case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (7) and others /9867 (29) FLR 94 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred 
by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


736 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (II), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (7768) FLR 7764 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 7/964 (49) FLR 38 and 
Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. /996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the 
workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not 
necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation 
made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail ifno evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2070 (726) FLR 529; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. A perusal 
of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led by the respondent. 
In the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.” 


Mr. B.K. Ashok, Learned Counsel for the Management, appeared and he prayed that the matter be dismissed for want 
of prosecution. 


Since no statement of claim has been filed by the union in support of his case, the claim is liable to be dismissed. 
For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the union is not entitled for any relief. 

Accordingly, the reference stands answered in terms aforesaid. 

Award as above.

AWARD 


The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No.B. RLCP-7(20)/202 dated 29™ 
September 2022 passed in exercise of the powers conferred by clause(d) of sub-section(/) sub-section (2A) of Section 
0 of the Industrial Dispute Act !947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as under: 


“Whether the termination of Shri Gautam Shivappa Sonawane, the workman by M/s. 
Property Solution (India) Pvt. Ltd, housekeeping Contractor of M/s. HDFC Bank without 
complying the provisions of Industrial Disputes Act, /947 is legal? If not, what relief the 
workman is entitled to?”’ 


Notice of the reference was duly issued to the workman. The record reveals that despite service of notice and repeated 
opportunities, none has appeared on behalf of the workman. Further, the workman has failed to file the Statement of 
Claim as mandated under Rule 0B of the Industrial Disputes (Central) Rules, 957. 


On the date fixed for hearing, none appeared for the workman. In the absence of the Statement of Claim, there are no 
pleadings, no facts, and no relief claimed before this Tribunal. 


It is well settled that the burden to prosecute an industrial dispute lies upon the workman who has raised the dispute. 
Filing of a Statement of Claim is not a mere formality but the foundation of adjudication. 


The Hon’ble Supreme Court in Sangham Tape Company v. Hans Raj, (2005) 9 SCC 33], has held that where a 
workman fails to pursue the reference or lead evidence, the Labour Court is justified in answering the reference 
against the workman. 


Similarly, in Tata Engineering & Locomotive Co. Ltd. v. Workmen, (98) 4 SCC 627, the Supreme Court observed 
that an industrial adjudicator cannot grant relief in the absence of pleadings and proof. 


The Hon’ble Delhi High Court in MCD v. Sukhvir Singh, 994 LLR 332 (Del) held that where the workman neither 
files a Statement of Claim nor appears to prosecute the dispute, the Labour Court has no option but to reject the 
reference. 


Likewise, the Bombay High Court in Shivaji Gundu Surwase v. Kranti Junior Adhyapak Mahavidyalaya, (though on 
merits), reiterated that relief under labour law must be founded on pleadings and evidence, and cannot be granted in 
vacuum. 


Findings 
In the present case: 
e = =The workman has not filed any Statement of Claim; 
e The workman has remained absent despite notice; 
e There is no material on record to adjudicate the dispute. 


This Tribunal cannot presume facts or grant relief in the absence of pleadings. Continuation of proceedings in such 
circumstances would amount to abuse of the adjudicatory process. 


In view of the above facts and settled legal position, the reference is answered against the workman. 
Accordingly, the claim of the workman is dismissed for non-prosecution. 
The reference is disposed of accordingly. 


No order as to costs.

AWARD 


The present reference has been made by the Central Government by its order No. RLCP-8(66)/2023 dated |2/0/2024 
passed in exercise of the powers conferred by Sub-section(5) of Section !2 read with sub-section(2A) of Section 0 of 
the Industrial Dispute Act 947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as under: 


“Whether the action of the Management of the Resident warden, Cadets Hostel (Boys) Armed Forces Medical 
College, Pune in terminating the services of Shir Narayan Rachandra Pujari is legal and justified? If not, to what 
relief the workman is entitled to?”’?” 


In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not field any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 
case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (7) and others 7967 (29) FLR 94 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence to 
prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred by 
the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (7), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (778) FLR 7764 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries v. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. /964 (49) FLR 38 and Meritech 
India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 7996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the workman 
the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not necessary for the 
employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation made by a party is on 
the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2070 (726) FLR 59; wherein it has been held as 
under: 


“The submission is that even if the petitioner failed to lead the evidence, burden was on the shoulders of the 
respondent to prove the termination order as illegal. He was required to lead evidence first which he failed. A perusal 
of the impugned award also does not show that any evidence either oral or documentary was led by the respondent. In 
the case of no evidence, the reference has to be dismissed.” 


Since no statement of claim has been filed by the union in support of his case, the claim is liable to be dismissed. 
For the foregoing reasons, the case is dismissed and the Workman is not entitled for any relief. 
Accordingly, the reference stands answered in terms aforesaid. 


Award as above.

0 of the Industrial Dispute Act !947. The terms of reference as per the schedule to the said order are as under: 


“Whether Whether dispute raised by Sh. Achyut Vishwanath Irpe vide letter dated 23.2.202] against the management 
of M/s. B4S Solutions Pyt. Ltd, Pune for alleged illegal transfer from Latur to Pune is covered under the Industrial 
Dispute under the jurisdiction of the Central Government under ID Act, 7/9472 If yes, whether the action of the 
management of M/s. b4S Solutions Pvt. Ltd., Pune to transfer Sh. Achyut Vishwanath Irpe from Latur to Pune is 
proper, legal and justified? If not, to what relief the concerned applicant is entitled to? What direction, if any, is 
necessary in the matter?” 


In view of the above said facts the claimant/workman has not filed any statement of claim/ evidence in support of his 
case on affidavit, in spite of several opportunities given to him and taking into consideration the law as laid by the 
Hon'ble High Court in the case of V. K. Raj Industries v. Labour Court (7) and others /9867 (29) FLR 94 as under: 


“It is well settled that if a party challenges the legality of an order, the burden lies upon him to prove illegality of the 
order and if no evidence is produced the party invoking jurisdiction of the Court must fail. Whenever a workman 
raises a dispute challenging the validity of the termination of service if is imperative for him to file written statement 
before the Industrial Court setting out grounds on which the order is challenged and he must also produce evidence 
to prove his case. If the workman fails to appear or to file written statement or produce evidence, the dispute referred 
by the State Government cannot be answered in favour of the workman and he would not be entitled to any relief.” 


In the case of M/s Uptron Powertronics Employees’ Union, Ghaziabad through its Secretary v. Presiding Officer, 
Labour Court (I), Ghaziabad and others 2008 (776) FLR 7764 Hon’ble Allahabad High Court has held as under: 


“The law has been settled by the Apex Court in case of Shanker Chakravarti v. Britannia Biscuit Co. Ltd., V.K. Raj 
Industries vy. Labour Court and Ors., Airtech Private Limited v. State of U.P. and Ors. 7964 (49) FLR 38 and 
Meritech India Ltd. v. State of U.P. and Ors. 7996 FLR that in the absence of any evidence led by or on behalf of the 
workman the reference is bound to be answered by the court against the workman. In such a situation it is not 
necessary for the employers to lead any evidence at all. The obligation to lead evidence to establish an allegation 
made by a party is on the party making the allegation. The test would be, who would fail if no evidence is led.” 


And by the Hon’ble Allahabad High Court in the case of District Administrative Committee, U.P. P.A.C.C.S.C. 
Services v. Secretary-cum-G.M. District Co-operative Bank Ltd. 2070 (726) FLR 59;

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour & Employment, O/o. Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner 
(Central) Chennai vide its order No.8/2/2022/PDY/Adj /Al dated 06.0.2022 has referred the following Industrial 
Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication:- 


“Whether the claim of applicant seeking absorption of his service in the Management of Superintendent of Post 
Offices , Kumbakonam Division is legal and valid? If not, to what relief the applicant is entitled to?” 


2. As per the claim of the Petitioner, his father R.Jeevandass, while working as Postman expired on 27.07.2005. 
The Petitioner, his Mother and Sister are the legal heirs of deceased. The Petitioner was engaged as an outsider at 
Kumbakonam Head Post Office from 07.06.!993 and completed more than 240 days work during the years 993 & 
994. Similarly placed persons were absorbed as GDS in Tamil Nadu Circle. The Petitioner also approached the 
Hon’ble CAT., Chennai for remedy and thereby direction was issued to the competent authority to consider the case 


7364 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SECc. 3(ii)] 


of the Petitioner for absorption, but, the authority has rejected his claim by order dated 3.03.2002 . The 
Respondent denied the work as outsider but no order was issued in writing. The Petitioner requested to appoint him 
on compassionate ground, but the Respondent did not consider the same. The candidates who were engaged after 
993 were permitted to work continuously and absorbed as GDS in regular vacancy. But, since the Petitioner had 
approached the CAT., Chennai, he was denied the work from May, 20l2. Thereafter the Petitioner’s efforts ended 
in vein and thus approached the Labour Court and Taluk Legal Services at Kumbakonam and on their advice, the 
Petitioner filed claim before the Assistant Labour Commissioner (Central), Pondicherry. The action of the 
Respondent in denying the Petitioner for regular appointment is illegal as per provisions of section 25F of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, 947. Therefore, he filed petition before the Assistant Labour Commissioner, (Central) 
Chennai and on failure of conciliation, he filed this claim petition before this Tribunal praying that an Award may be 
passed directing the Respondent to reinstate the Petitioner into service with continuity of service, back wages and 
all other attendant benefits. 


3. The Respondent in its reply stated that the Petitioner is not a permanent employee but a temporary 
employee. There is no employer-employee relationship exists and therefore, the Respondent need not to pay any 
compensation. The Petitioner has not completed 240 days of work during the year 4993-94 and he was appointed as 
outsider in leave vacancy place in Kumbakonam Division from the year 993 and he was engaged during !995 as 
provisional appointee and not on the basis of 240 days of completion of work as mentioned by the Petitioner. The 
Petitioner’s case is totally irrelevant with the case of three persons and could not be accepted. The Hon’ble CAT., 
Chennai has directed the Respondent department to complete the implementation of scheme of regularization of the 
dovetailed list candidates absorption for appointment as regular GDS, in pursuance of order dated 20.04.990 in 
(2.3.]0.6] /[9986. These instructions are pertaining to those who have already in the dovetailed list for regular 
appointment and completed 240 days of service for a period of 2 years as substitute for EF agent during the year 
993-94. The Petitioner has not completed 240 days of service. Therefore, the CAT order has no relevance to the 
Petitioner. The Petitioner has not fulfilled the eligibility criteria, therefore, he was not considered for regular 
absorption. All the pending compassionate cases, including the case of the Petitioner were re-examined with 
reference to relative merit points and placed before the Circle Relaxation Committee which scrutinized all the 
pending applications, but it did not recommend the case of the Petitioner. The Petitioner earned only 56 merit points 
while the relative merit points for the last recommended for the postman was 75 and for MTS it was 9] and due to 
non-availability of vacancies under 5% Direct Recruitment quota for compassionate appointment and the same was 
intimated to the Petitioner vide letter dated 28.06.20l2. The case was again placed before the Circle Relaxation 
Committee for examination for vacancy in 20l6-7, but the case of the Petitioner was not recommended by the 
Committee on the ground that non-availability of direct recruitment vacancy in the respective cadre under RRR 
quota and less indigent as per relative merit points. Therefore, the Petitioner is not entitled for any relief.

examined as ७५७४] and he has filed proof of affidavit and documents were marked as 75. ॥| to M5. 


4. Heard the learned counsel appearing on either side and perused the material available on record. 


5. To answer the reference, I have to consider the eligibility criteria of the Petitioner for absorption. The first 
criteria is continuous service for more than 240 days ina year. As per the case of the Petitioner he was engaged on 
07.06.993. This fact is admitted by the Respondent that the Petitioner was engaged on 07.06.993, but denied that he 
worked for 240 days on regular basis continuously. There is no material available on record to show that Petitioner 
has worked more than 240 days in the year 994-95. The judgement of the Hon’ble CAT., Chennai is available on 
record as Ex.W3. On perusal of the judgement, it appears that the workman worked as an outsider from 993 in the 
Post Office at Kumbakonam and after death of his father, he made a representation on 05.0.2006 seeking 
compassionate appointment. There is no appointment letter, there is no salary slip and no attendance register 
available on record. Therefore, it is not possible to ascertain that the Petitioner had worked for more than 240 days in 
the year 993-94. Therefore, this cannot be taken as reason for non-absorption of the Petitioner. 


6. The second ground raised by the Petitioner is absorption on compassionate ground. 
7. On this point, the Hon’ble CAT., Chennai has directed the Respondent/Management as under:- 


“Accordingly, we direct the Respondent to consider the case of the applicant for appointment on compassionate 
ground within a period of two months from the date of receipt of copy of this order.” 


8. The Respondent/Management has considered the case of the Petitioner in compliance with the Hon’ble CAT., 
Chennai order through Memorandum No. 82/GDS/OS dated 3.03.2002. As per the rules of the Respondent in 
Ex.W4 there was availability of 5% of direct recruitment vacancy in compassionate appointment quota and the 
Petitioner was considered as less indigent as per relative merit points, when compared to the applicants whose cases 
have been processed along with the case of the Petitioner. Therefore, the Chief Postmaster General, Tamil Nadu Circle 
by its order dated 24.2.203 rejected the claim of the Petitioner. 


9. On perusal of this order, two points mentioned by the Respondent authority which runs as under:- 


“Due to lack of relative indigency as per Relative Merit Points, when compared to the claimants whose cases have 
been processed along with his case and recommended. The relative merit point of Shri J.Oppiliappan was 56, while 
the RMP of the last recommended applicant for Postman cadre was 75 and MTS cadre was 9]; & 


2. There were no vacancies available to consider his case as the % of vacancies earmarked for compassionate 
appointment is only 5% of Direct Recruitment quota.” 


0. The Petitioner in this claim petition submitted that three persons were appointed by the Respondent. It is 
well settled law that compassionate appointment is not a vested right of any person. It is an exception of normal 
recruitment rules. Availability of vacancy is mandatory circumstances to get absorption along with related rules in 
existence at the time of scrutiny of representation made by the person concerned. In the case of Secretary, State of 
Karnataka Vs. Uma Devi, (in Civil Appeals Nos. 3595-362 of 999 dated 0.04.2006), it was held by the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court that compassionate appointment must remain exceptional and not routine. While deciding the 
representation of the workman discussed the policy allowing regularisation and passed order on the basis of 
existing norms and availability of vacancies. 


Il. Compassionate absorption is meant only for immediate relief and not for long term employment guarantee. 
Ex.W2 is informative letter written by the Superintendent of Post Offices, Kumbakonam to the Petitioner and it was 
informed that the service during the year |993-94 is not correct and it is found that the Petitioner has worked only for 


7366 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


225 days. Therefore, the Petitioner failed to satisfy the conditions .. including the Petitioner’s name in the dovetailed 
list. It is also informed that three substitutes engaged after 994 have been included in the dovetailed list on the basis 
of regular vacancy after resorting to regular appointment formalities, after properly notified the vacancies with 
eligibility conditions. Therefore, the Petitioner’s claim is not identical to three persons appointed by the Respondent. 
2. Availability of vacancies:- 

Absorption always is subject to vacant position posts and limited upto 5% quota for compassionate quota as per 
existing rules of the Respondent. The Respondent authority passed a detailed order considering the availability of 
vacancies upto 5% quota for compassionate appointments and eligibility criteria of the Petitioner in comparison to 
other persons who were claiming appointment on the basis of compassionate grounds. 


3. Thus, as per discussion above, the claim of the Petitioner seeking absorption in the service of the 
Respondent/Management is not legal and valid, since he has not completed 240 days of service in the year 993-94 
and he was less indigent as per relative merit points compared to other candidates whose applications were 
processed by the Respondent/Management and non-availability of 5% direct recruitment vacancy. 

4. Now, I have to consider the second point of schedule that if not, what relief the Petitioner is entitled? 

5. The Petitioner’s contention is that the Respondent denied the work as outsider GDS in May, 202, while 
he was working as GDS outsider from 993 to 20l2 for about 9 years. The Respondent/Management in its reply 
statement admitted this fact that the Petitioner was initially engaged during !995 as provisional appointee and not 
on the basis of completion of 240 days of work and the instructions given by Hon’ble CAT., Chennai are pertaining 
to those who already included in the dovetailed list for appointment who have completed 240 days of service fora 
period of 2 years as substitute for ED agent during the year !993-94 and nowhere denied that then Petitioner did 
not work upto the year 20!2. Thus, it may be presumed that [ Order 8 of Rule 4 of CPC], that the Respondent 
admitted this fact that the Petitioner worked from 995 to 20l2 for about !7 years and was removed from service 
without assigning any reasons. 

6. As per the provisions of section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947, if a workman has completed 
240 days of continuous service in a calendar year , then before terminating the workman, the employer must give one 
month notice or pay one month salary in lieu of notice and must pay retrenchment compensation i.e., |5 days 
salary of average pay for every calendar year. It is worth to mention here that the Petitioner fails to prove that he 
worked more than 240 days continuously in the year 993, but he succeeded to prove that he worked from the year 
995 to 202 with the Respondent/Management. Therefore, the Petitioner is entitled to get protection of section 25F 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, !947 . But, this protection was not provided by the Respondent and thus, violated the 
provisions of section 25F of the Act. No show cause notice was issued by the Respondent , no opportunity to defend 
the Petitioner was provided and no domestic enquiry was conducted and it was only oral termination of the 
workman. In these circumstances, the oral termination of the Petitioner from service is illegal, amounts to 
retrenchment and the employer failed to adopt due process of law while terminating the Petitioner from service. 


7. Now, I have to decide to what relief the Petitioner is entitled? 


8. The Petitioner was denied the work in the year of 20!2. The Petitioner mentioned his age as 50 in the proof 
of affidavit filed in the year 2025. Since this fact is established that oral termination of the Petitioner amounts to 
illegal and retrenchment, he is entitled for reinstatement into service. There is no proof available on record that the 
Petitioner was engaged to receive from any other source during the retrenchment period and he has not rendered any 
service to the respondent institution during the period of retrenchment, the Petitioner is entitled to get only 25% of 
back wages. 


AWARD 


The claim petition filed by the Petitioner is allowed to the extent that the Respondent/Management will 
reinstate the Petitioner into service within a period of two months after publication of this Award and pay the back 
wages @ 25%. Further, the Petitioner is entitled to get absorption when 5% compassionate appointment quota is 
available in favour of the Petitioner. Ordered accordingly.

2. As per the case of the Petitioner, her father was served as temporary employee in GPO.,Chennai and died 
while in service on 07.07.20l0. On considering the penury of the family, the Petitioner got appointment in GPO., 
Chennai during August, 20l0 and she was attached to speed post (Book now Pay later) section and was terminated

3. The Respondent/Management in its reply statement submitted that the Petitioner was only engaged as an 
outsider, based on the requirement as “piece rate worker”. It is further submitted that the Petitioner’s service was 
terminated due to certain action of omissions committed by the employee. It is further stated that she was in the habit 
of making false complaints against the co-employees of Respondent/Management. It is also stated that only if there is 
considerable volume of work/business, then the Petitioner will be called for work. The Petitioner is not a departmental 
employee and she was engaged on “piece rate work” based on requirement from time to time. The Respondent 
further submits that Petitioner’s service was discontinued during the year 202l in order to maintain decorum. 
discipline and healthy working atmosphere in the office premises, however, considering her family circumstances, she 
was given a chance to engage as piece rate worker on humanitarian ground. Even then, the Petitioner has continued to 
indulge in causing hardships, submitting complaints against the employees which disturbed the working environment 
in the Respondent office as well. Therefore, the claim raised by the Petitioner for reinstatement in service may be 
dismissed with costs.

4. Heard the learned counsel appearing on either side and perused the material available on record. 


5. The question that arises for determination is whether the Petitioner is entitled for reinstatement in service of 
the Respondent/Management in GPO, Chennai? 


6. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant stated that Petitioner was engaged in the O/o. 
Respondent/Management during the year 20l0 and was attached to speed post section which was merged with 
BPC (Business Post Center) in the year 204 and she was worked continuously till February, 202]. She was engaged 
again during August, 202! and worked till 3.I2.202l. The Petitioner has worked more than 240 days 
continuously in |2 calendar months and she was removed from service without assigning any reasons. 


7. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Respondent argued that the Petitioner was engaged as piece 
rate worker and she was disengaged during February, 202] because, she indulged in raising false and fabricated 
allegations and making rumours/complaints against the co-employees which caused unhealthy working atmosphere. 
It is further argued that though she was disengaged from February, 202], the Petitioner was again engaged in service 
in the month of August, 202]. But, she failed to maintain the decorum, & discipline, therefore, she was disengaged 
from service w.e.f. 3l.2.202]. 


8. On perusal of records, having gone through the pleadings of the parties and upon hearing the learned counsel 
on either side, this fact is established that the Petitioner was engaged in the year 20l0 and she worked continuously 
upto February, 202l. Again, she was engaged in the month of August, 202! and continued till 3.2.202. Thus, the 
Petitioner has completed 240 days continuously in the office of the Respondent/Management. The Respondent / 
Management claimed that Petitioner was engaged as piece rate worker. 


9. Thus, I have to consider the status of piece rate worker as mentioned by the respondent in its reply statement. 
The piece rate worker who is paid according to the quantity of work and may be considered as a worker, if there is 
employer-employee relationship exists between the respondent and workman and having supervisory control over the 
workman on day-to-day work of the workman. 


0. In the case of Divisional Manager, New India Assurance Corporation of India Ltd. Vs. A.Sankaralingam, 
AIR 2009 SC 309, whereby the Hon'ble Supreme observed that part time employees working under the control and 
supervision of the employer are workmen. 


ll. Further, in the cross examination, the management witness ४४], working as Inspector of Posts, Chennai has 
clearly admitted that the outsiders are controlled and supervised by the officers of Department of Posts. Therefore, it 
is established that the Petitioner was controlled and supervised by the officials of the Respondent/Management. 


2. On perusal of records, it appears that the Petitioner has completed qualifying period of more than 240 days 
continuously in !2 calendar months and she was under the control and supervision of the Respondent/Management. 
The Respondent inits reply statement admitted that the work performance of Petitioner was not upto the mark as 
she indulged in the habit of making false and fabricated complaints against the co-employees and creating unwanted 
rumours, which developed unhealthy working atmosphere in the respondent office. If the Respondent/Management 
admits that the Petitioner has committed any misconduct or misbehavior while on duty, it has to conduct domestic 
enquiry after leveling charges against the Petitioner and in case, the charges are proved/established and found guilty 
of misconduct during the enquiry, the Respondent/Management may proceed with for further action of imposing 
punishment on the Petitioner. But, in the present case admittedly, no enquiry was conducted prior to termination of 
the Petitioner from service and no opportunity to defend the Petitioner was provided; neither one month notice was 
given to the Petitioner nor paid one month salary in lieu of notice, I5 days salary of average pay for every calendar 
year. Without doing so, the Respondent/Management has violated the provisions of section 25F of the Act. In these 
circumstances, the termination of the Petitioner from service is illegal, amounts to retrenchment and the employer 
failed to adopt due process of law, while terminating the Petitioner from service. Thus, the Petitioner is entitled to get 
reinstatement into service of the Respondent / Management. 


3. Now, I have to consider entitlement of back wages to the Petitioner. 


4. This fact is established, as I discussed above, the Petitioner was removed from service without assigning any 
reasons; no opportunity to defend the Petitioner was provided; neither one month notice was given to the Petitioner 
nor paid one month salary in lieu of notice, [5 days salary of average pay for every calendar year. Therefore, the 
Petitioner was not at fault at the time of termination of her service. It is also proved that she was not able to perform 
any work of the Respondent/Management after she was disengaged from service. In such circumstances, the Petitioner 
is entitled to get 25% of back wages as per salary slip marked Ex.W2 & W3.

In view of the above discussion, the Petitioner is entitled to get reinstatement into service of the 
Respondent/Management of GPO., Chennai along with continuity of service and 25% of back wages. The 
Respondent/Management is directed to reinstate the Petitioner into service within a period of two months after 
publication of this Award and pay the back wages @ 25%. Ordered accordingly.

Submissions of respondent no.2:- 


3. While arguing the case, AR for respondent no.2 contended that respondent no.2 has engaged workman and 
other workmen, who have already filed reference bearing ID No.255/20i3 and during the pendency of the case,

Findings:- 
4. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by Sh. R P Rana (AR for workman), Sh. G S 
Sidhu (AR for respondent no.|) and Sh. K B Sharma (AR for respondent no.2). 


5. First question which arise for consideration is whether the applicant is workman as defined under Section 
2(s) of the Act. To my mind, the claimant is a workman within the definition of Section 2(s) of the Act. In this regard, 
reliance can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2077 
Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act 
which deals with the definition of "workman" has observed as under : 


"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of service, 
the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a 
workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in the plain 
language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person 
employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on 
fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observations that even if a person is engaged on temporary, part time or 
contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in that eventuality such a 
person would be covered by the definition of "workman" as provided in Section 2(s) of the Act. Thus, nature of 
appointment or source of appointment is not relevant to be a "workman" within the Act. Since, the workman was 
engaged on contract basis by respondent no.2 for the work of respondent no.!, thus it would be termed as workman 
under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


6. Next question which arises for consideration is whether respondent no.| is an industry. The Hon’ble Apex 
Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length 
with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test 
for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity 
(b) organised by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) 
for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is 
an “Industry” in that enterprise. Relevant part of judgment of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra) is 
reproduced as under-- 


“Does research involve collaboration between employer and employee? It does. The employer is the institution, the 
employees are the scientists, para-scientists and other personnel. Is scientific research service? Undoubtedly it is. Its 
discoveries are valuable contributions to the wealth of the nation. Such discoveries may be sold for a heavy price in 
the industrial or other markets. Technology has to be plate for and technological inventions and innovations may be 
patented and sold. In our scientific and technological age nothing has more cash value, as intangible goods and 
invaluable services, than discoveries. For instance, the discoveries of Thomas Alva Edison made him fabulously rich. 
It has been said that his brain had the highest cash value in history for he made the world vibrate with the miraculous 
discovery of recorded, sound. Unlike most inventors, he did not have to wait to get his reward in heaven; he received, 
it munificently on this gratified and grateful earth, thanks to conversion of his inventions into, money a plenty. 


[भाग [lave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7383 


Research benefits industry. Even though a research institute may be a separate entity disconnected from the many 
industries which funded the institute itself, it can be regarded as an Organisation, propelled by systematic activity, 
modeled on co-operation between employer and employee and calculated to throw up discoveries and inventions and 
useful solutions which benefit individual industries and the nation in terms of goods and services and wealth. It 
follows that research institutes, albeit run without profit-motive, are industries.” 


7. In the present case, respondent no.| is doing research work and as per 7२७४] Sh. Virender Lamba, black tea, 
rose water, stevia plant, harar, amla and other medicinal plants are sold in the institute. He has also admitted that vide 
Ex.WI to W7, various products of the institute have been sold to the customers. Thus, respondent no.lis engaged in 
systematic activity organized by cooperation between employer and employee (employees being workmen in the 
present case) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants. In this 
regard, it is carrying out research. In addition to this, from the research work, benefits are being driven by respondent 


no.l and as per observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), 


respondent no.| falls under the definition of ‘industry’ as defined under the Act. 


8. So far as argument of AR for respondent no.| that respondent no.! being instrument of state does not fall 
under the definition of ‘industry’. In this regard, Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Chief Conservator of Forest 
Versus Jagannath Maruti Kondhare (/99०6 (2) SCT 764), has held that work, which was not be regarded as a part of 
inalienable of inescapable function of the State and which work can be well undertaken by a private agency does not 
require an instrumentality of State, such functions of the State fall within the ambit of Industry. Thus, function of 
doing research and other allied works of selling of goods and earning from research cannot be said to be sovereign 
function of the State and thus for this purpose of industrial dispute, respondents would be termed as industry. 


9. Thus, from every angle, respondent no.! is an industry. Moreover, its employees are not governed by IHBT 
Rules or CCS Rules, thus it is an industry. In view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Banglore 
Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court_the case law Central Institute of 
Medicinal and Aromatic Plants and others (supra) decided by Hon'ble High Court at Allahabad cited by AR for 
respondent no.! is not attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 


20. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.|. Thus, he would also fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


2i. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 
and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element 
for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, as per Banglore Water Supply (supra), respondent no.2 would be 
termed as industry. 


22. Next question, which arises for consideration is whether there exists relationship of employer and employee 
between respondent no.| and present workman. In this regard, it is pointed out that admittedly in this case, union of 
workmen has filed ID _No.255 ० 20I3 titled 6४ The General Secretary, Institute_of Himalayan _Bio-Source 
Technology (CSIR) (supra), wherein name of the worker appeared at Sr. No.l9 of the list of enclosed by union as 
Annexure P-5. It is further pointed out that in order to prove relationship of employer and employee i.e. master and 
servant, the Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ७०.70266 dated 25.06, 20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


In this case, admittedly, as per statement of Sh. Om Parkash (MW2), wages were paid by respondent no.2, however, 
control was of the respondent no.l. This fact got proved in statement of MW2. Thus, under these circumstances, it is 
held that there exist relationship of master and servant between respondent no.! and workman. 


23. Further, in the present case, admittedly respondent no.| is entering into different contract agreements with 
respondent no.2 (-.२७४|/] colly and Ex.RW2/2 as detailed above) by retaining same workmen and thus contracts 
are sham in view of the observation of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in similar matter in Management of CPWD versus 


Anand Kumar Gautam and ors. (2024:DHC:2757) which is as under: 


“Contract labourers can be engaged for the work of contractor only and not for the work of any establishment. In the 
present case the work is of the establishment and not of the contractor. The term supply of labour by a contractor is 
against human dignity. No one can be a supplier of human labour to any establishment. It is the duty of State to give 


7384 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


employment to citizen and not of the contractors. Contractors cannot supply labour to any establishment. In view of 
the above discussion it becomes quite obvious that the contractors workmen in the instant case have been retained all 
along and contractors have been changed. So the contractor is only a label of a bottle. This label is changed from 
time to time but the contents of the bottle always remain the same. The contractors have been changed and the 
workmen have been retained. Such a system is in-human. The contractors are the direct employees of the 
respondent/management. 


From the foregoing it becomes quite obvious that these two workmen have been working regularly and even without 


artificial breaks since /995-96, The contract is camouflage. There is direct relation of master and servant between 
the respondent and the workmen.” 


24. Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Bhilwara Dugdh Utpadak Sahakari_S. Ltd. Versus Vinod Kumar 
Sharma dead by LRs and others (AIR 20/7/ Supreme Court 3546) has held as under:- 


4. In order to avoid their liability under various labour statutes employers are very often resorting to subterfuge by 
trying to show that their employees are in fact, the employees of a contractor. It is high time that this subterfuge must 
come to an end. 


5. Labour statutes were meant to protect the employees/workmen because it was realized that the employers and the 
employees are not on an equal bargaining position. Hence, protection of employees was required so that they may not 
be exploited. However, this new technique of subterfuge has been adopted by some employers in recent years in order 
to deny the rights of the workmen under various labour statutes by showing that the concerned workmen are not their 
employees but are the employees/workmen of a contractor, or that they are merely daily wage or short term or casual 
employees when in fact they are doing the work of regular employees. 


25. Thus, from the above observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is clear that respondent no.! has resorted to 
subterfuge by trying to show that workman was employee of respondent no.2. 


26. Moreover, respondent no.2 contractor while appearing in the witness box in his deposition has stated that in 
IHBT, there is practice that the contract for engagement of the employer/labour through contractors is for one year 
only and it changes on the basis of bid of the contractors every year. The contractor may change but the 
employees/labourers always remain same. The workman was already working with the management when the 
contract was tendered to the respondent no.2. Neither the workman was engaged by respondent no.2 nor the services 
of workman were terminated by respondent no.2. It is the respondent no.l who uses to select/engage and terminate 
the labour/workman and respondent no.2 has no role in the same. Thus, it shows that the contract was just an 
eyewash. It is further submitted that contract was allotted to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! on different years as 
per Ex.RWI/I (colly) and Ex.RW2/2 and sometime to other contractors, meaning thereby the respondent no.| is 
controlling authority of the workmen including their engagement, termination etc. and even the wages of workman 
were also decided by respondent no.l only and respondent no.2 has no role to play in the same. So, there exist 
relationship of employees/servant and employer/master between the workmen and respondent no.l. Thus, the 
judgment The _ Joint Secretary, Central_Board of Secondary education and another (supra) cited by AR for 
respondent no.! is not attracted to the present case as in this case, time and again, same workers were being engaged 
through contractor and in view of clear cut dictum of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Management of CPWD (supra), 
the aforementioned case law is not attracted. 


27. So far as Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (supra) relied upon by the AR for respondent 


no.| is concerned, facts and circumstances of this case are distinguishable. In the said Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. 
Ramcharan and others (supra), Court has held that that when there are no allegations or findings of sham and bogus 
contract then the contention of the reinstatement or the absorption of the workman cannot be sustained but the facts of 
the matter at hand is different from the facts of the case as in the instant case. In this case, workman was working 
since long and the work was of perennial nature. Thus, it tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


28. It is added here that admittedly in this case, workman was discharged by the respondent no.! & 2 and as per 
agreement Ex.RWI/2, contract was awarded to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! for a period of two years i.e. from 
9.2.202 to 9.2.20!4. However, workman was discharged prior to that on 28.!.20I4 as per Mark-2/A, wherein 
it is stated by respondent no.! as under :- 


The contract for the related forms and field work, as per this institute's letter dated 94-7/2-2042, is scheduled to expire 
on November 30, 2074., Therefore, you are hereby informed that you must submit the fully completed EPF payment 
documents for all the workers employed under these contracts to the concerned EPF department, along with a copy to 
the institute, by October 2074, so that your final bill can be processed on time. Furthermore, please ensure that there 
are no outstanding financial dues of any kind for any worker; otherwise, these dues may be recovered from your 
security deposit.

29. No prior permission was taken by respondent no.| & 2 before the discharging the services of workman. 
Section 33(2)(b) of the Act is very material and the same is reproduced below:- 


“(b) for any misconduct not connected with the dispute, or discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, 
that workman: 


Provided that no such workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one 
month and an application has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for 
approval of the action taken by the employer.” 


30. As per aforesaid provision, the workman can be discharged or dismissed after paying one month wages and 
after getting approval of the competent authority. In this case, no wages for one month was paid nor any permission 
from competent authority was taken before discharging the workman and consequently, it would be considered that 
workman was in regular services of the workman. A Full Constitutional Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case 
titled as Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. versus Ram Gopal Sharma and others (2002 SCC (L_& ७) 


279) has held that failure to make application for approval of the order of discharge or dismissal or withdrawal of 
such application after making it, held, renders the order of discharge or dismissal void and inoperative. 


3): The present application under Section 33A is well maintainable and purpose has also been defined by the 


Hon'ble Supreme Court in Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. (supra) case, which read as follows:- 


Section 33A is available to an employee and is intended to save his time and trouble in as much as he can straightway 
make a complaint before the very authority, where the industrial dispute is already pending between the parties, 
challenging the order of approval instead of making efforts to raise an industrial dispute, get a reference and thereafter 
adjudication. Section ३3] speaks of penalty in respect of the offences stated therein. This provision is not intended to 
give any remedy to an aggrieved employee. It is only to punish the offender. Merely because penal provision is 
available or a workman has a further remedy under Section 33A to challenge the approval granted, it canoe be said 
that the order of discharge or dismissal does not become inoperative or invalid unless set aside under Section 33A. 


32. In view of the above discussion, the termination of workman on 28.!].20I4 is bad in law and hence is set 
aside. In this case, both the respondents in connivance with each other has dispensed the services of the workman. 
Hence, both respondents are liable. The workman is entitled for reinstatement along with full back wages. It is 
ordered accordingly. The services of the workman would not be discharged/terminated during the pendency of the ID 
No.255 of 20i3, wherein, they have claimed various demands vide charter of demands dated 09.05.20l. However, in 
case workman has attained the age of retirement, then he would be entitled for full back wages along with other 
consequential benefits instead of reinstatement in service.

publication.

Submissions of workman:- 


0. While arguing the case, AR for workman contended that in this case, reference was pending before this
