Findings:- 
4. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by Sh. R P Rana (AR for workman), Sh. G S 
Sidhu (AR for respondent no.|) and Sh. K 8 Sharma (AR for respondent no.2). 


5. First question which arise for consideration is whether the applicant is workman as defined under Section 
2(s) of the Act. To my mind, the claimant is a workman within the definition of Section 2(s) of the Act. In this regard, 
reliance can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2077 
Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act 
which deals with the definition of "workman" has observed as under : 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 745 


"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of service, 
the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a 
workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in the plain 
language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person 
employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on 
fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observations that even if a person is engaged on temporary, part time or 
contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in that eventuality such a 
person would be covered by the definition of "workman" as provided in Section 2(s) of the Act. Thus, nature of 
appointment or source of appointment is not relevant to be a "workman" within the Act. Since, the workman was 
engaged on contract basis by respondent no.2 for the work of respondent no.|, thus it would be termed as workman 
under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


6. Next question which arises for consideration is whether respondent no.| is an industry. The Hon’ble Apex 
Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /9728(36) FLR 266 dealt at length 
with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test 
for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity 
(b) organised by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) 
for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is 
an “Industry” in that enterprise. Relevant part of judgment of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra) is 
reproduced as under-- 


“Does research involve collaboration between employer and employee? It does. The employer is the institution, the 
employees are the scientists, para-scientists and other personnel. Is scientific research service? Undoubtedly it is. Its 
discoveries are valuable contributions to the wealth of the nation. Such discoveries may be sold for a heavy price in 
the industrial or other markets. Technology has to be plate for and technological inventions and innovations may be 
patented and sold. In our scientific and technological age nothing has more cash value, as intangible goods and 
invaluable services, than discoveries. For instance, the discoveries of Thomas Alva Edison made him fabulously rich. 
It has been said that his brain had the highest cash value in history for he made the world vibrate with the miraculous 
discovery of recorded, sound. Unlike most inventors, he did not have to wait to get his reward in heaven; he received, 
it munificently on this gratified and grateful earth, thanks to conversion of his inventions into, money a plenty. 
Research benefits industry. Even though a research institute may be a separate entity disconnected from the many 
industries which funded the institute itself, it can be regarded as an Organisation, propelled by systematic activity, 
modeled on co-operation between employer and employee and calculated to throw up discoveries and inventions and 
useful solutions which benefit individual industries and the nation in terms of goods and services and wealth. It 
follows that research institutes, albeit run without profit-motive, are industries.” 


7. In the present case, respondent no.| is doing research work and as per RW Sh. Virender Lamba, black tea, 
rose water, stevia plant, harar, amla and other medicinal plants are sold in the institute. He has also admitted that vide 
Ex.WI to W7, various products of the institute have been sold to the customers. Thus, respondent no.lis engaged in 
systematic activity organized by cooperation between employer and employee (employees being workmen in the 
present case) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants. In this 
regard, it is carrying out research. In addition to this, from the research work, benefits are being driven by respondent 


no.l and as per observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), 


respondent no.| falls under the definition of ‘industry’ as defined under the Act. 


8. So far as argument of AR for respondent no.| that respondent no.! being instrument of state does not fall 
under the definition of ‘industry’. In this regard, Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Chief Conservator of Forest 
Versus Jagannath Maruti Kondhare (/9०9०6 (2) SCT 764), has held that work, which was not be regarded as a part of 
inalienable of inescapable function of the State and which work can be well undertaken by a private agency does not 
require an instrumentality of State, such functions of the State fall within the ambit of Industry. Thus, function of 
doing research and other allied works of selling of goods and earning from research cannot be said to be sovereign 
function of the State and thus for this purpose of industrial dispute, respondents would be termed as industry. 


9. Thus, from every angle, respondent no.| is an industry. Moreover, its employees are not governed by IHBT 
Rules or CCS Rules, thus it is an industry. In view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Banglore 


Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court, the case law Central Institute of 


Medicinal and Aromatic Plants and others (supra) decided by Hon'ble High Court at Allahabad cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 


20. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 


746 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


labour to the respondent no.|. Thus, he would also fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


2i. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 
and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element 
for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, as per Banglore Water Supply (supra), respondent no.2 would be 
termed as industry. 


22. Next question, which arises for consideration is whether there exists relationship of employer and employee 
between respondent no.| and present workman. In this regard, it is pointed out that admittedly in this case, union of 
workmen has filed ID No.255_of 20/3 titled_as The General Secretary, Institute _of Himalayan Bio-Source 
Technology (CSIR) (supra), wherein name of the worker appeared at Sr. No.5 of the list of enclosed by union as 
Annexure P-5. It is further pointed out that in order to prove relationship of employer and employee i.e. master and 
servant, the Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ७०. 70266 dated 25.06. 2074, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


In this case, admittedly, as per statement of Sh. Om Parkash (MW2), wages were paid by respondent no.2, however, 
control was of the respondent no.!. This fact got proved in statement of MW2. Thus, under these circumstances, it is 
held that there exist relationship of master and servant between respondent no.! and workman. 


23. Further, in the present case, admittedly respondent no.| is entering into different contract agreements with 
respondent no.2 (.२७४७॥/॥ Colly and Ex.RW2/2 as detailed above) by retaining same workmen and thus contracts 
are sham in view of the observation of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in similar matter in Management of CPWD versus 


Anand Kumar Gautam and ors. (2024:DHC:2757) which is as under: 


“Contract labourers can be engaged for the work of contractor only and not for the work of any establishment. In the 
present case the work is of the establishment and not of the contractor. The term supply of labour by a contractor is 
against human dignity. No one can be a supplier of human labour to any establishment. It is the duty of State to give 
employment to citizen and not of the contractors. Contractors cannot supply labour to any establishment. In view of 
the above discussion it becomes quite obvious that the contractors workmen in the instant case have been retained all 
along and contractors have been changed. So the contractor is only a label of a bottle. This label is changed from 
time to time but the contents of the bottle always remain the same. The contractors have been changed and the 
workmen have been retained. Such a system is in-human. The contractors are the direct employees of the 
respondent/management. 


From the foregoing it becomes quite obvious that these two workmen have been working regularly and even without 


artificial breaks since /995-96, The contract is camouflage. There is direct relation of master and servant between 
the respondent and the workmen.” 


24. Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Bhilwara Dugdh Utpadak Sahakari_S. Ltd. Versus Vinod Kumar 
Sharma dead by LRs and others (AIR 20I] Supreme Court 3546) has held as under:- 


4. In order to avoid their liability under various labour statutes employers are very often resorting to subterfuge by 
trying to show that their employees are in fact, the employees of a contractor. It is high time that this subterfuge must 
come to an end. 


5. Labour statutes were meant to protect the employees/workmen because it was realized that the employers and the 
employees are not on an equal bargaining position. Hence, protection of employees was required so that they may not 
be exploited. However, this new technique of subterfuge has been adopted by some employers in recent years in order 
to deny the rights of the workmen under various labour statutes by showing that the concerned workmen are not their 
employees but are the employees/workmen of a contractor, or that they are merely daily wage or short term or casual 
employees when in fact they are doing the work of regular employees. 


25. Thus, from the above observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is clear that respondent no.! has resorted to 
subterfuge by trying to show that workman was employee of respondent no.2. 


26. Moreover, respondent no.2 contractor while appearing in the witness box in his deposition has stated that in 
IHBT, there is practice that the contract for engagement of the employer/labour through contractors is for one year 
only and it changes on the basis of bid of the contractors every year. The contractor may change but the 
employees/labourers always remain same. The workman was already working with the management when the 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण L0, 948 TAl7 


contract was tendered to the respondent no.2. Neither the workman was engaged by respondent no.2 nor the services 
of workman were terminated by respondent no.2. It is the respondent no.l who uses to select/engage and terminate 
the labour/workman and respondent no.2 has no role in the same. Thus, it shows that the contract was just an 
eyewash. It is further submitted that contract was allotted to respondent no.2 by respondent no.| on different years as 
per Ex.RWI/I (colly) and Ex.RW2/2 and sometime to other contractors, meaning thereby the respondent no.| is 
controlling authority of the workmen including their engagement, termination etc. and even the wages of workman 
were also decided by respondent no.l only and respondent no.2 has no role to play in the same. So, there exist 
relationship of employees/servant and employer/master between the workmen and respondent no.l. Thus, the 
judgment The Joint Secretary, Central Board of Secondary education and another (supra) cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the present case as in this case, time and again, same workers were being engaged 
through contractor and in view of clear cut dictum of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Management of CPWD (supra), 
the aforementioned case law is not attracted. 


27. So far as Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (supra) relied upon by the AR for respondent 


no.| is concerned, facts and circumstances of this case are distinguishable. In the said Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. 
Ramcharan and others (supra), Court has held that that when there are no allegations or findings of sham and bogus 
contract then the contention of the reinstatement or the absorption of the workman cannot be sustained but the facts of 
the matter at hand is different from the facts of the case as in the instant case. In this case, workman was working 
since long and the work was of perennial nature. Thus, it tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


28. It is added here that admittedly in this case, workman was discharged by the respondent no.! & 2 and as per 
agreement Ex.RWI/2, contract was awarded to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! for a period of two years i.e. from 
9.2.202 to 9.2.204. However, workman was discharged prior to that on 28.!.20I4 as per Mark-2/A, wherein 
it is stated by respondent no.! as under :- 


The contract for the related forms and field work, as per this institute's letter dated 04-7/2-2072, is scheduled to expire 
on November 30, 2074., Therefore, you are hereby informed that you must submit the fully completed EPF payment 
documents for all the workers employed under these contracts to the concerned EPF department, along with a copy to 
the institute, by October 2074, so that your final bill can be processed on time. Furthermore, please ensure that there 
are no outstanding financial dues of any kind for any worker; otherwise, these dues may be recovered from your 
security deposit. 


29. No prior permission was taken by respondent no.| & 2 before the discharging the services of workman. 
Section 33(2)(b) of the Act is very material and the same is reproduced below:- 


“(b) for any misconduct not connected with the dispute, or discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, 
that workman: 


Provided that no such workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one 
month and an application has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for 
approval of the action taken by the employer.” 


30. As per aforesaid provision, the workman can be discharged or dismissed after paying one month wages and 
after getting approval of the competent authority. In this case, no wages for one month was paid nor any permission 
from competent authority was taken before discharging the workman and consequently, it would be considered that 
workman was in regular services of the workman. A Full Constitutional Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case 
titled as Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. versus Ram Gopal Sharma and others (2002 SCC (L_ & ७) 


279) has held that failure to make application for approval of the order of discharge or dismissal or withdrawal of 
such application after making it, held, renders the order of discharge or dismissal void and inoperative. 


3. The present application under Section 33A is well maintainable and purpose has also been defined by the 


Hon'ble Supreme Court in Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. (supra) case, which read as follows:- 


Section 33A is available to an employee and is intended to save his time and trouble in as much as he can straightway 
make a complaint before the very authority, where the industrial dispute is already pending between the parties, 
challenging the order of approval instead of making efforts to raise an industrial dispute, get a reference and 
thereafter adjudication. Section 347 speaks of penalty in respect of the offences stated therein. This provision is not 
intended to give any remedy to an aggrieved employee. It is only to punish the offender. Merely because penal 
provision is available or a workman has a further remedy under Section 33A to challenge the approval granted, it 
canoe be said that the order of discharge or dismissal does not become inoperative or invalid unless set aside under 
Section 33A. 


32. In view of the above discussion, the termination of workman on 28.].20I4 is bad in law and hence is set 
aside. In this case, both the respondents in connivance with each other have dispensed the services of the workman. 
Hence, both respondents are liable. The workman is entitled for reinstatement along with full back wages. It is 
ordered accordingly. The services of the workman would not be discharged/terminated during the pendency of the ID 
No.255 of 20I3, wherein, they have claimed various demands vide charter of demands dated 09.05.20I. However, in

case workman has attained the age of retirement, then he would be entitled for full back wages along with other 
consequential benefits instead of reinstatement in service.

publication.

Findings:- 
4. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by Sh. R P Rana (AR for workman), Sh. G $ 
Sidhu (AR for respondent no.l) and Sh. K 8 Sharma (AR for respondent no.2). 


5: First question which arise for consideration is whether the applicant is workman as defined under Section 
2(s) of the Act. To my mind, the claimant is a workman within the definition of Section 2(s) of the Act. In this regard, 
reliance can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2077 
Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act 
which deals with the definition of "workman" has observed as under : 


"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of service, 
the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a 
workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in the plain 
language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person 
employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on 
fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observations that even if a person is engaged on temporary, part time or 
contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in that eventuality such a 
person would be covered by the definition of "workman" as provided in Section 2(s) of the Act. Thus, nature of 
appointment or source of appointment is not relevant to be a "workman" within the Act. Since, the workman was 
engaged on contract basis by respondent no.2 for the work of respondent no.|, thus it would be termed as workman 
under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


6. Next question which arises for consideration is whether respondent no.| is an industry. The Hon’ble Apex 
Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /9728(36) FLR 266 dealt at length 
with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test 
for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity 
(b) organised by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) 
for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is 
an “Industry” in that enterprise. Relevant part of judgment of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra) is 
reproduced as under-- 


“Does research involve collaboration between employer and employee? It does. The employer is the institution, the 
employees are the scientists, para-scientists and other personnel. Is scientific research service? Undoubtedly it is. Its 
discoveries are valuable contributions to the wealth of the nation. Such discoveries may be sold for a heavy price in 
the industrial or other markets. Technology has to be plate for and technological inventions and innovations may be 
patented and sold. In our scientific and technological age nothing has more cash value, as intangible goods and 
invaluable services, than discoveries. For instance, the discoveries of Thomas Alva Edison made him fabulously rich. 
It has been said that his brain had the highest cash value in history for he made the world vibrate with the miraculous 
discovery of recorded, sound. Unlike most inventors, he did not have to wait to get his reward in heaven; he received, 
it munificently on this gratified and grateful earth, thanks to conversion of his inventions into, money a plenty. 
Research benefits industry. Even though a research institute may be a separate entity disconnected from the many 


7422 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SECc. 3(ii)] 


industries which funded the institute itself, it can be regarded as an Organisation, propelled by systematic activity, 
modeled on co-operation between employer and employee and calculated to throw up discoveries and inventions and 
useful solutions which benefit individual industries and the nation in terms of goods and services and wealth. It 
follows that research institutes, albeit run without profit-motive, are industries.” 


7. In the present case, respondent no.| is doing research work and as per RW Sh. Virender Lamba, black tea, 
rose water, stevia plant, harar, amla and other medicinal plants are sold in the institute. He has also admitted that vide 
Ex.WI to W7, various products of the institute have been sold to the customers. Thus, respondent no. lis engaged in 
systematic activity organized by cooperation between employer and employee (employees being workmen in the 
present case) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants. In this 
regard, it is carrying out research. In addition to this, from the research work, benefits are being driven by respondent 


no.| and as per observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), 


respondent no.| falls under the definition of ‘industry’ as defined under the Act. 


8. So far as argument of AR for respondent no.| that respondent no.! being instrument of state does not fall 
under the definition of ‘industry’. In this regard, Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Chief Conservator of Forest 
Versus Jagannath Maruti Kondhare (/99०6 (2) SCT 764), has held that work, which was not be regarded as a part of 
inalienable of inescapable function of the State and which work can be well undertaken by a private agency does not 
require an instrumentality of State, such functions of the State fall within the ambit of Industry. Thus, function of 
doing research and other allied works of selling of goods and earning from research cannot be said to be sovereign 
function of the State and thus for this purpose of industrial dispute, respondents would be termed as industry. 


9. Thus, from every angle, respondent no.! is an industry. Moreover, its employees are not governed by IHBT 
Rules or CCS Rules, thus it is an industry. In view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Banglore 
Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court, the case law Central Institute of 


Medicinal and Aromatic Plants and others (supra) decided by Hon'ble High Court at Allahabad cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 


20. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.|. Thus, he would also fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Act is reproduced as under: 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


27, The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.! at the asking of respondent no.2 
and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element 
for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, as per Banglore Water Supply (supra), respondent no.2 would be 
termed as industry. 


22. Next question, which arises for consideration is whether there exists relationship of employer and employee 
between respondent no.| and present workman. In this regard, it is pointed out that admittedly in this case, union of 
workmen has filed ID No.255_of 207/3 titled ०४ The General Secretary, Institute _of Himalayan Bio-Source 
Technology (CSIR) (supra), wherein name of the worker appeared at Sr. No.5 of the list of enclosed by union as 
Annexure P-5. It is further pointed out that in order to prove relationship of employer and employee i.e. master and 
servant, the Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ७०. 70266 dated 25.08.20I4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


In this case, admittedly, as per statement of Sh. Om Parkash (MW2), wages were paid by respondent no.2, however, 
control was of the respondent no.l. This fact got proved in statement of MW2. Thus, under these circumstances, it is 
held that there exist relationship of master and servant between respondent no.! and workman. 


23. Further, in the present case, admittedly respondent no.| is entering into different contract agreements with 
respondent no.2 (.२७४७॥/॥ Colly and Ex.RW2/2 as detailed above) by retaining same workmen and thus contracts 
are sham in view of the observation of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in similar matter in Management of CPWD versus 
Anand Kumar Gautam and ors. (2024:DHC:2757) which is as under: 


“Contract labourers can be engaged for the work of contractor only and not for the work of any establishment. In the 
present case the work is of the establishment and not of the contractor. The term supply of labour by a contractor is 
against human dignity. No one can be a supplier of human labour to any establishment. It is the duty of State to give 
employment to citizen and not of the contractors. Contractors cannot supply labour to any establishment. In view of 


[भाग [lave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7423 


the above discussion it becomes quite obvious that the contractors workmen in the instant case have been retained all 
along and contractors have been changed. So the contractor is only a label of a bottle. This label is changed from 
time to time but the contents of the bottle always remain the same. The contractors have been changed and the 
workmen have been retained. Such a system is in-human. The contractors are the direct employees of the 
respondent/management. 


From the foregoing it becomes quite obvious that these two workmen have been working regularly and even without 


artificial breaks since /995-96, The contract is camouflage. There is direct relation of master and servant between 
the respondent and the workmen.” 


24. Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Bhilwara Dugdh Utpadak Sahakari_S. Ltd. Versus Vinod Kumar 
Sharma dead by LRs and others (AIR 207// Supreme Court 3546) has held as under:- 


4. In order to avoid their liability under various labour statutes employers are very often resorting to subterfuge by 
trying to show that their employees are in fact, the employees of a contractor. It is high time that this subterfuge must 
come to an end. 


5. Labour statutes were meant to protect the employees/workmen because it was realized that the employers and the 
employees are not on an equal bargaining position. Hence, protection of employees was required so that they may not 
be exploited. However, this new technique of subterfuge has been adopted by some employers in recent years in order 
to deny the rights of the workmen under various labour statutes by showing that the concerned workmen are not their 
employees but are the employees/workmen of a contractor, or that they are merely daily wage or short term or casual 
employees when in fact they are doing the work of regular employees. 


25. Thus, from the above observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is clear that respondent no.! has resorted to 
subterfuge by trying to show that workman was employee of respondent no.2. 


26. Moreover, respondent no.2 contractor while appearing in the witness box in his deposition has stated that in 
IHBT, there is practice that the contract for engagement of the employer/labour through contractors is for one year 
only and it changes on the basis of bid of the contractors every year. The contractor may change but the 
employees/labourers always remain same. The workman was already working with the management when the 
contract was tendered to the respondent no.2. Neither the workman was engaged by respondent no.2 nor the services 
of workman were terminated by respondent no.2. It is the respondent no.l who uses to select/engage and terminate 
the labour/workman and respondent no.2 has no role in the same. Thus, it shows that the contract was just an 
eyewash. It is further submitted that contract was allotted to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! on different years as 
per Ex.RWI/I (colly) and Ex.RW2/2 and sometime to other contractors, meaning thereby the respondent no.! is 
controlling authority of the workmen including their engagement, termination etc. and even the wages of workman 
were also decided by respondent no.l only and respondent no.2 has no role to play in the same. So, there exist 
relationship of employees/servant and employer/master between the workmen and respondent no.l. Thus, the 
judgment The Joint Secretary, Central Board of Secondary education and another (supra) cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the present case as in this case, time and again, same workers were being engaged 
through contractor and in view of clear cut dictum of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Management of CPWD (supra), 
the aforementioned case law is not attracted. 


27. So far as Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (supra) relied upon by the AR for respondent 


no.| is concerned, facts and circumstances of this case are distinguishable. In the said Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. 
Ramcharan and others (supra), Court has held that that when there are no allegations or findings of sham and bogus 
contract then the contention of the reinstatement or the absorption of the workman cannot be sustained but the facts of 
the matter at hand is different from the facts of the case as in the instant case. In this case, workman was working 
since long and the work was of perennial nature. Thus, it tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


28. It is added here that admittedly in this case, workman was discharged by the respondent no.! & 2 and as per 
agreement एज.२५७४|/2, contract was awarded to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! for a period of two years i.e. from 
9.2.202 to 9.2.20l4. However, workman was discharged prior to that on 28.!.20I4 as per Mark-2/A, wherein 
it is stated by respondent no.! as under :- 


The contract for the related forms and field work, as per this institute's letter dated 04-/2-2072, is scheduled to expire 
on November 30, 2074., Therefore, you are hereby informed that you must submit the fully completed EPF payment 
documents for all the workers employed under these contracts to the concerned EPF department, along with a copy to 
the institute, by October 2074, so that your final bill can be processed on time. Furthermore, please ensure that there 
are no outstanding financial dues of any kind for any worker; otherwise, these dues may be recovered from your 
security deposit. 


29. No prior permission was taken by respondent no.| & 2 before the discharging the services of workman. 
Section 33(2)(b) of the Act is very material and the same is reproduced below:- 


7424 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


“(b) for any misconduct not connected with the dispute, or discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, 
that workman: 


Provided that no such workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one 
month and an application has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for 
approval of the action taken by the employer.” 


30. As per aforesaid provision, the workman can be discharged or dismissed after paying one month wages and 
after getting approval of the competent authority. In this case, no wages for one month was paid nor any permission 
from competent authority was taken before discharging the workman and consequently, it would be considered that 
workman was in regular services of the workman. A Full Constitutional Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case 
titled as Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. versus Ram Gopal Sharma and others (2002 SCC (L_ & S) 


279) has held that failure to make application for approval of the order of discharge or dismissal or withdrawal of 
such application after making it, held, renders the order of discharge or dismissal void and inoperative. 


3. The present application under Section 33A is well maintainable and purpose has also been defined by the 


Hon'ble Supreme Court in Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. (supra) case, which read as follows:- 


Section 33A is available to an employee and is intended to save his time and trouble in as much as he can straightway 
make a complaint before the very authority, where the industrial dispute is already pending between the parties, 
challenging the order of approval instead of making efforts to raise an industrial dispute, get a reference and 
thereafter adjudication. Section 347 speaks of penalty in respect of the offences stated therein. This provision is not 
intended to give any remedy to an aggrieved employee. It is only to punish the offender. Merely because penal 
provision is available or a workman has a further remedy under Section 33A to challenge the approval granted, it 
canoe be said that the order of discharge or dismissal does not become inoperative or invalid unless set aside under 
Section 33A. 


32. In view of the above discussion, the termination of workman on 28.!.204 is bad in law and hence is set 
aside. In this case, both the respondents in connivance with each other have dispensed the services of the workman. 
Hence, both respondents are liable. The workman is entitled for reinstatement along with full back wages. It is 
ordered accordingly. The services of the workman would not be discharged/terminated during the pendency of the ID 
No.255 of 20i3, wherein, they have claimed various demands vide charter of demands dated 09.05.20l. However, in 
case workman has attained the age of retirement, then he would be entitled for full back wages along with other 
consequential benefits instead of reinstatement in service.

Findings:- 
4. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by Sh. R P Rana (AR for workman), Sh. G $ 
Sidhu (AR for respondent no.l) and Sh. K B Sharma (AR for respondent no.2). 


5. First question which arise for consideration is whether the applicant is workman as defined under Section 
2(s) of the Act. To my mind, the claimant is a workman within the definition of Section 2(s) of the Act. In this regard, 
reliance can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2077 
Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act 
which deals with the definition of "workman" has observed as under : 


"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of service, 
the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a 


7428 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in the plain 
language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person 
employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on 
fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observations that even if a person is engaged on temporary, part time or 
contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in that eventuality such a 
person would be covered by the definition of "workman" as provided in Section 2(s) of the Act. Thus, nature of 
appointment or source of appointment is not relevant to be a "workman" within the Act. Since, the workman was 
engaged on contract basis by respondent no.2 for the work of respondent no.|, thus it would be termed as workman 
under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


6. Next question which arises for consideration is whether respondent no.| is an industry. The Hon’ble Apex 
Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length 
with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test 
for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity 
(b) organised by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) 
for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is 
an “Industry” in that enterprise. Relevant part of judgment of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra) is 
reproduced as under-- 


“Does research involve collaboration between employer and employee? It does. The employer is the institution, the 
employees are the scientists, para-scientists and other personnel. Is scientific research service? Undoubtedly it is. Its 
discoveries are valuable contributions to the wealth of the nation. Such discoveries may be sold for a heavy price in 
the industrial or other markets. Technology has to be plate for and technological inventions and innovations may be 
patented and sold. In our scientific and technological age nothing has more cash value, as intangible goods and 
invaluable services, than discoveries. For instance, the discoveries of Thomas Alva Edison made him fabulously rich. 
It has been said that his brain had the highest cash value in history for he made the world vibrate with the miraculous 
discovery of recorded, sound. Unlike most inventors, he did not have to wait to get his reward in heaven; he received, 
it munificently on this gratified and grateful earth, thanks to conversion of his inventions into, money a plenty. 
Research benefits industry. Even though a research institute may be a separate entity disconnected from the many 
industries which funded the institute itself, it can be regarded as an Organisation, propelled by systematic activity, 
modeled on co-operation between employer and employee and calculated to throw up discoveries and inventions and 
useful solutions which benefit individual industries and the nation in terms of goods and services and wealth. It 
follows that research institutes, albeit run without profit-motive, are industries.” 


7. In the present case, respondent no.| is doing research work and as per RW Sh. Virender Lamba, black tea, 
rose water, stevia plant, harar, amla and other medicinal plants are sold in the institute. He has also admitted that vide 
Ex.WI to W7, various products of the institute have been sold to the customers. Thus, respondent no. lis engaged in 
systematic activity organized by cooperation between employer and employee (employees being workmen in the 
present case) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants. In this 
regard, it is carrying out research. In addition to this, from the research work, benefits are being driven by respondent 


no.l and as per observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), 


respondent no.| falls under the definition of ‘industry’ as defined under the Act. 


8. So far as argument of AR for respondent no.| that respondent no.! being instrument of state does not fall 
under the definition of ‘industry’. In this regard, Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Chief Conservator of Forest 
Versus Jagannath Maruti Kondhare (/9०9०6 (2) SCT 764), has held that work, which was not be regarded as a part of 
inalienable of inescapable function of the State and which work can be well undertaken by a private agency does not 
require an instrumentality of State, such functions of the State fall within the ambit of Industry. Thus, function of 
doing research and other allied works of selling of goods and earning from research cannot be said to be sovereign 
function of the State and thus for this purpose of industrial dispute, respondents would be termed as industry. 


9. Thus, from every angle, respondent no.| is an industry. Moreover, its employees are not governed by IHBT 
Rules or CCS Rules, thus it is an industry. In view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Banglore 


Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court, the case law Central Institute of 


Medicinal and Aromatic Plants and others (supra) decided by Hon'ble High Court at Allahabad cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 


20. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.|. Thus, he would also fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Act is reproduced as under: 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7429 


“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


2i. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 
and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element 
for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, as per Banglore Water Supply (supra), respondent no.2 would be 
termed as industry. 


22. Next question, which arises for consideration is whether there exists relationship of employer and employee 
between respondent no.! and present workman. In this regard, it is pointed out that admittedly in this case, union of 
workmen has filed ID _No.255 ० 20I3 titled _as_The General Secretary, Institute_of Himalayan _Bio-Source 
Technology (CSIR) (supra), wherein name of the worker appeared at Sr. No.5 of the list of enclosed by union as 
Annexure P-5. It is further pointed out that in order to prove relationship of employer and employee i.e. master and 
servant, the Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal ५०.70266 dated 25.06, 20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 


3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


In this case, admittedly, as per statement of Sh. Om Parkash (MW2), wages were paid by respondent no.2, however, 
control was of the respondent no.l. This fact got proved in statement of MW2. Thus, under these circumstances, it is 
held that there exist relationship of master and servant between respondent no.! and workman. 


23. Further, in the present case, admittedly respondent no.| is entering into different contract agreements with 
respondent no.2 (.२७४७॥।/॥ Colly and Ex.RW2/2 as detailed above) by retaining same workmen and thus contracts 
are sham in view of the observation of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in similar matter in Management of CPWD versus 


Anand Kumar Gautam and ors. (2024:DHC:2757) which is as under: 


“Contract labourers can be engaged for the work of contractor only and not for the work of any establishment. In the 
present case the work is of the establishment and not of the contractor. The term supply of labour by a contractor is 
against human dignity. No one can be a supplier of human labour to any establishment. It is the duty of State to give 
employment to citizen and not of the contractors. Contractors cannot supply labour to any establishment. In view of 
the above discussion it becomes quite obvious that the contractors workmen in the instant case have been retained all 
along and contractors have been changed. So the contractor is only a label of a bottle. This label is changed from 
time to time but the contents of the bottle always remain the same. The contractors have been changed and the 
workmen have been retained. Such a system is in-human. The contractors are the direct employees of the 
respondent/management. 


From the foregoing it becomes quite obvious that these two workmen have been working regularly and even without 


artificial breaks since /995-96, The contract is camouflage. There is direct relation of master and servant between 
the respondent and the workmen.” 


24. Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Bhilwara Dugdh Utpadak Sahakari_S. Ltd. Versus Vinod Kumar 
Sharma dead by LRs and others (AIR 20// Supreme Court 3546) has held as under:- 


4. In order to avoid their liability under various labour statutes employers are very often resorting to subterfuge by 
trying to show that their employees are in fact, the employees of a contractor. It is high time that this subterfuge must 
come to an end. 


5. Labour statutes were meant to protect the employees/workmen because it was realized that the employers and the 
employees are not on an equal bargaining position. Hence, protection of employees was required so that they may not 
be exploited. However, this new technique of subterfuge has been adopted by some employers in recent years in order 
to deny the rights of the workmen under various labour statutes by showing that the concerned workmen are not their 
employees but are the employees/workmen of a contractor, or that they are merely daily wage or short term or casual 
employees when in fact they are doing the work of regular employees. 


25. Thus, from the above observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is clear that respondent no.! has resorted to 
subterfuge by trying to show that workman was employee of respondent no.2. 


26. Moreover, respondent no.2 contractor while appearing in the witness box in his deposition has stated that in 
IHBT, there is practice that the contract for engagement of the employer/labour through contractors is for one year 
only and it changes on the basis of bid of the contractors every year. The contractor may change but the 
employees/labourers always remain same. The workman was already working with the management when the 
contract was tendered to the respondent no.2. Neither the workman was engaged by respondent no.2 nor the services 
of workman were terminated by respondent no.2. It is the respondent no.l who uses to select/engage and terminate 


7430 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST |, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


the labour/workman and respondent no.2 has no role in the same. Thus, it shows that the contract was just an 
eyewash. It is further submitted that contract was allotted to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! on different years as 
per Ex.RWI/I (colly) and Ex.RW2/2 and sometime to other contractors, meaning thereby the respondent no.| is 
controlling authority of the workmen including their engagement, termination etc. and even the wages of workman 
were also decided by respondent no.! only and respondent no.2 has no role to play in the same. So, there exist 
relationship of employees/servant and employer/master between the workmen and respondent no.l. Thus, the 
judgment The Joint Secretary, Central Board of Secondary education and another (supra) cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the present case as in this case, time and again, same workers were being engaged 
through contractor and in view of clear cut dictum of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Management of CPWD (supra), 
the aforementioned case law is not attracted. 


27. So far as Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (supra) relied upon by the AR for respondent 


no.| is concerned, facts and circumstances of this case are distinguishable. In the said Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. 
Ramcharan and others (supra), Court has held that that when there are no allegations or findings of sham and bogus 
contract then the contention of the reinstatement or the absorption of the workman cannot be sustained but the facts of 
the matter at hand is different from the facts of the case as in the instant case. In this case, workman was working 
since long and the work was of perennial nature. Thus, it tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


28. It is added here that admittedly in this case, workman was discharged by the respondent no.|! & 2 and as per 
agreement 75.२५ |/2, contract was awarded to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! for a period of two years i.e. from 
9.2.202 to 9.2.20l4. However, workman was discharged prior to that on 28.!.204 as per Mark-2/A, wherein 
it is stated by respondent no.| as under :- 


The contract for the related forms and field work, as per this institute's letter dated 04-/2-2072, is scheduled to expire 
on November 30, 2074., Therefore, you are hereby informed that you must submit the fully completed EPF payment 
documents for all the workers employed under these contracts to the concerned EPF department, along with a copy to 
the institute, by October 2074, so that your final bill can be processed on time. Furthermore, please ensure that there 
are no outstanding financial dues of any kind for any worker; otherwise, these dues may be recovered from your 
security deposit. 


29. No prior permission was taken by respondent no.| & 2 before the discharging the services of workman. 
Section 33(2)(b) of the Act is very material and the same is reproduced below:- 


“(b) for any misconduct not connected with the dispute, or discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, 
that workman: 


Provided that no such workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one month and 
an application has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for approval 
of the action taken by the employer.” 


30. As per aforesaid provision, the workman can be discharged or dismissed after paying one month wages and 
after getting approval of the competent authority. In this case, no wages for one month was paid nor any permission 
from competent authority was taken before discharging the workman and consequently, it would be considered that 
workman was in regular services of the workman. A Full Constitutional Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case 
titled as Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. versus Ram Gopal Sharma and others (2002 SCC (L_ & S) 


279) has held that failure to make application for approval of the order of discharge or dismissal or withdrawal of 
such application after making it, held, renders the order of discharge or dismissal void and inoperative. 


3. The present application under Section 33A is well maintainable and purpose has also been defined by the 


Hon'ble Supreme Court in Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. (supra) case, which read as follows:- 


Section 33A is available to an employee and is intended to save his time and trouble in as much as he can straightway 
make a complaint before the very authority, where the industrial dispute is already pending between the parties, 
challenging the order of approval instead of making efforts to raise an industrial dispute, get a reference and 
thereafter adjudication. Section 347 speaks of penalty in respect of the offences stated therein. This provision is not 
intended to give any remedy to an aggrieved employee. It is only to punish the offender. Merely because penal 
provision is available or a workman has a further remedy under Section 33A to challenge the approval granted, it 
canoe be said that the order of discharge or dismissal does not become inoperative or invalid unless set aside under 
Section 33A. 


32. In view of the above discussion, the termination of workman on 28..204 is bad in law and hence is set 
aside. In this case, both the respondents in connivance with each other have dispensed the services of the workman. 
Hence, both respondents are liable. The workman is entitled for reinstatement along with full back wages. It is 
ordered accordingly. The services of the workman would not be discharged/terminated during the pendency of the ID 
No.255 of 20i3, wherein, they have claimed various demands vide charter of demands dated 09.05.20I. However, in 
case workman has attained the age of retirement, then he would be entitled for full back wages along with other 
consequential benefits instead of reinstatement in service.

Findings:- 


4. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by Sh. R P Rana (AR for workman), Sh. G S 
Sidhu (AR for respondent no.|) and Sh. K B Sharma (AR for respondent no.2). 
85 First question which arise for consideration is whether the applicant is workman as defined under Section 


2(s) of the Act. To my mind, the claimant is a workman within the definition of Section 2(s) of the Act. In this regard, 
reliance can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2077 
Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act 
which deals with the definition of "workman" has observed as under : 

"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of service, 
the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a 
workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in the plain 
language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person 
employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on 
fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman.” 

It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observations that even if a person is engaged on temporary, part time or 
contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in that eventuality such a 
person would be covered by the definition of "workman" as provided in Section 2(s) of the Act. Thus, nature of 
appointment or source of appointment is not relevant to be a "workman" within the Act. Since, the workman was 
engaged on contract basis by respondent no.2 for the work of respondent no.|, thus it would be termed as workman 
under Section 2(s) of the Act. 

6. Next question which arises for consideration is whether respondent no.| is an industry. The Hon’ble Apex 
Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length 
with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test 
for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity 
(b) organised by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) 
for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is 
an “Industry” in that enterprise. Relevant part of judgment of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra) is 
reproduced as under-- 

“Does research involve collaboration between employer and employee? It does. The employer is the institution, the 
employees are the scientists, para-scientists and other personnel. Is scientific research service? Undoubtedly it is. Its 
discoveries are valuable contributions to the wealth of the nation. Such discoveries may be sold for a heavy price in 
the industrial or other markets. Technology has to be plate for and technological inventions and innovations may be 
patented and sold. In our scientific and technological age nothing has more cash value, as intangible goods and 
invaluable services, than discoveries. For instance, the discoveries of Thomas Alva Edison made him fabulously rich. 
It has been said that his brain had the highest cash value in history for he made the world vibrate with the miraculous 
discovery of recorded, sound. Unlike most inventors, he did not have to wait to get his reward in heaven; he received, 
it munificently on this gratified and grateful earth, thanks to conversion of his inventions into, money a plenty. 
Research benefits industry. Even though a research institute may be a separate entity disconnected from the many 
industries which funded the institute itself, it can be regarded as an Organisation, propelled by systematic activity, 
modeled on co-operation between employer and employee and calculated to throw up discoveries and inventions and 
useful solutions which benefit individual industries and the nation in terms of goods and services and wealth. It 
follows that research institutes, albeit run without profit-motive, are industries.” 

7. In the present case, respondent no.| is doing research work and as per RW Sh. Virender Lamba, black tea, 
rose water, stevia plant, harar, amla and other medicinal plants are sold in the institute. He has also admitted that vide 
Ex.WI to W7, various products of the institute have been sold to the customers. Thus, respondent no.lis engaged in 
systematic activity organized by cooperation between employer and employee (employees being workmen in the 
present case) for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants. In this 
regard, it is carrying out research. In addition to this, from the research work, benefits are being driven by respondent 
no.| and as per observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), 
respondent no.| falls under the definition of ‘industry’ as defined under the Act. 

8. So far as argument of AR for respondent no.| that respondent no.! being instrument of state does not fall 
under the definition of ‘industry’. In this regard, Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Chief Conservator of Forest 
Versus Jagannath Maruti Kondhare (/99०6 (2) SCT 764), has held that work, which was not be regarded as a part of 
inalienable of inescapable function of the State and which work can be well undertaken by a private agency does not 
require an instrumentality of State, such functions of the State fall within the ambit of Industry. Thus, function of 
doing research and other allied works of selling of goods and earning from research cannot be said to be sovereign 
function of the State and thus for this purpose of industrial dispute, respondents would be termed as industry. 

9. Thus, from every angle, respondent no.! is an industry. Moreover, its employees are not governed by IHBT 
Rules or CCS Rules, thus it is an industry. In view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court titled as Banglore 


[भाग [lave 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7435 


Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court, the case law Central Institute of 


Medicinal and Aromatic Plants and others (supra) decided by Hon'ble High Court at Allahabad cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the facts and circumstances of the present case. 


20. It is also added here that as per definition of contractor as given in the Section 2(c) of the Contract Labour 
(Regulation and Abolition) Act, 970 (hereinafter called as Contract Act), respondent no.2 was supplying contract 
labour to the respondent no.|l. Thus, he would also fall under the definition of contractor. Section 2(c) of the Contract 
Act is reproduced as under: 

“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a given result for the 
establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of manufacture to such establishment, through contract 
labour or who supplies contract labour for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 

2i. The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.| at the asking of respondent no.2 
and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve substantial commercial element 
for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, as per Banglore Water Supply (supra), respondent no.2 would be 
termed as industry. 

22. Next question, which arises for consideration is whether there exists relationship of employer and employee 
between respondent no.| and present workman. In this regard, it is pointed out that admittedly in this case, union of 
workmen has filed ID _No.255_of 20I3 titled 6४ The General Secretary, Institute_of Himalayan _Bio-Source 
Technology (CSIR) (supra), wherein name of the worker appeared at Sr. No.5 of the list of enclosed by union as 
Annexure P-5. It is further pointed out that in order to prove relationship of employer and employee i.e. master and 
servant, the Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air 
India Limited in Civil Appeal /५०.70266 dated 25.06, 20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours 
are the contract employees of the principal employer are:- 

3) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 

2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


In this case, admittedly, as per statement of Sh. Om Parkash (MW2), wages were paid by respondent no.2, however, 
control was of the respondent no.l. This fact got proved in statement of MW2. Thus, under these circumstances, it is 
held that there exist relationship of master and servant between respondent no.! and workman. 

23. Further, in the present case, admittedly respondent no.| is entering into different contract agreements with 
respondent no.2 (.२७४॥/॥ Colly and Ex.RW2/2 as detailed above) by retaining same workmen and thus contracts 
are sham in view of the observation of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in similar matter in Management of CPWD versus 
Anand Kumar Gautam and ors. (2024:DHC:2757) which is as under: 

“Contract labourers can be engaged for the work of contractor only and not for the work of any establishment. In the 
present case the work is of the establishment and not of the contractor. The term supply of labour by a contractor is 
against human dignity. No one can be a supplier of human labour to any establishment. It is the duty of State to give 
employment to citizen and not of the contractors. Contractors cannot supply labour to any establishment. In view of 
the above discussion it becomes quite obvious that the contractors workmen in the instant case have been retained all 
along and contractors have been changed. So the contractor is only a label of a bottle. This label is changed from 
time to time but the contents of the bottle always remain the same. The contractors have been changed and the 
workmen have been retained. Such a system is in-human. The contractors are the direct employees of the 
respondent/management. 

From the foregoing it becomes quite obvious that these two workmen have been working regularly and even without 


artificial breaks since /995-96, The contract is camouflage. There is direct relation of master and servant between 
the respondent and the workmen.” 

24. Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Bhilwara Dugdh Utpadak Sahakari_S. Ltd. Versus Vinod Kumar 
Sharma dead by LRs and others (AIR 20/7 Supreme Court 3546) has held as under:- 

4. In order to avoid their liability under various labour statutes employers are very often resorting to subterfuge by 
trying to show that their employees are in fact, the employees of a contractor. It is high time that this subterfuge must 
come to an end. 

5. Labour statutes were meant to protect the employees/workmen because it was realized that the employers and the 
employees are not on an equal bargaining position. Hence, protection of employees was required so that they may not 
be exploited. However, this new technique of subterfuge has been adopted by some employers in recent years in order 
to deny the rights of the workmen under various labour statutes by showing that the concerned workmen are not their 
employees but are the employees/workmen of a contractor, or that they are merely daily wage or short term or casual 
employees when in fact they are doing the work of regular employees. 


25. Thus, from the above observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is clear that respondent no.! has resorted to 
subterfuge by trying to show that workman was employee of respondent no.2. 
26. Moreover, respondent no.2 contractor while appearing in the witness box in his deposition has stated that in 


IHBT, there is practice that the contract for engagement of the employer/labour through contractors is for one year 
only and it changes on the basis of bid of the contractors every year. The contractor may change but the 
employees/labourers always remains same. The workman was already working with the management when the 
contract was tendered to the respondent no.2. Neither the workman was engaged by respondent no.2 nor the services 


7436 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST I, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEc. 3(ii)] 


of workman were terminated by respondent no.2. It is the respondent no.l who uses to select/engage and terminate 
the labour/workman and respondent no.2 has no role in the same. Thus, it shows that the contract was just an 
eyewash. It is further submitted that contract was allotted to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! on different years as 
per Ex.RWI/I (colly) and Ex.RW2/2 and sometime to other contractors, meaning thereby the respondent no.! is 
controlling authority of the workmen including their engagement, termination etc. and even the wages of workman 
were also decided by respondent no.! only and respondent no.2 has no role to play in the same. So, there exist 
relationship of employees/servant and employer/master between the workmen and respondent no.l. Thus, the 
judgment The Joint Secretary, Central Board of Secondary education and another (supra) cited by AR for 
respondent no.| is not attracted to the present case as in this case, time and again, same workers were being engaged 
through contractor and in view of clear cut dictum of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Management of CPWD (supra), 
the aforementioned case law is not attracted. 

27. So far as Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (supra) relied upon by the AR for respondent 
no.| is concerned, facts and circumstances of this case are distinguishable. In the said Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. 
Ramcharan and others (supra), Court has held that that when there are no allegations or findings of sham and bogus 
contract then the contention of the reinstatement or the absorption of the workman cannot be sustained but the facts of 
the matter at hand is different from the facts of the case as in the instant case. In this case, workman was working 
since long and the work was of perennial nature. Thus, it tantamount to unfair labour practice. 

28. It is added here that admittedly in this case, workman was discharged by the respondent no.! & 2 and as per 
agreement Ex.RWI/2, contract was awarded to respondent no.2 by respondent no.| for a period of two years i.e. from 
9.2.202 to 9.2.20l4. However, workman was discharged prior to that on 28.!.20I4 as per Mark-2/A, wherein 
it is stated by respondent no.| as under :- 

The contract for the related forms and field work, as per this institute's letter dated 94-/2-2072, is scheduled to expire 
on November 30, 2074., Therefore, you are hereby informed that you must submit the fully completed EPF payment 
documents for all the workers employed under these contracts to the concerned EPF department, along with a copy to 
the institute, by October 2074, so that your final bill can be processed on time. Furthermore, please ensure that there 
are no outstanding financial dues of any kind for any worker; otherwise, these dues may be recovered from your 
security deposit. 

29. No prior permission was taken by respondent no.| & 2 before the discharging the services of workman. 
Section 33(2)(b) of the Act is very material and the same is reproduced below:- 

“(b) for any misconduct not connected with the dispute, or discharge or punish, whether by dismissal or otherwise, 
that workman: 

Provided that no such workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been paid wages for one 
month and an application has been made by the employer to the authority before which the proceeding is pending for 
approval of the action taken by the employer.”’ 

30. As per aforesaid provision, the workman can be discharged or dismissed after paying one month wages and 
after getting approval of the competent authority. In this case, no wages for one month was paid nor any permission 
from competent authority was taken before discharging the workman and consequently, it would be considered that 


workman was in regular services of the workman. A Full Constitutional Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case 
titled as Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. versus Ram Gopal Sharma and others (2002 SCC (L_ & S) 


279) has held that failure to make application for approval of the order of discharge or dismissal or withdrawal of 
such application after making it, held, renders the order of discharge or dismissal void and inoperative. 
3. The present application under Section 33A is well maintainable and purpose has also been defined by the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court in Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. (supra) case, which read as follows:- 
Section 33A is available to an employee and is intended to save his time and trouble in as much as he can straightway 
make a complaint before the very authority, where the industrial dispute is already pending between the parties, 
challenging the order of approval instead of making efforts to raise an industrial dispute, get a reference and 
thereafter adjudication. Section 37 speaks of penalty in respect of the offences stated therein. This provision is not 
intended to give any remedy to an aggrieved employee. It is only to punish the offender. Merely because penal 
provision is available or a workman has a further remedy under Section 33A to challenge the approval granted, it 
canoe be said that the order of discharge or dismissal does not become inoperative or invalid unless set aside under 
Section 33A. 
32. In view of the above discussion, the termination of workman on 28..204 is bad in law and hence is set 
aside. In this case, both the respondents in connivance with each other have dispensed the services of the workman. 
Hence, both respondents are liable. The workman is entitled for reinstatement along with full back wages. It is 
ordered accordingly. The services of the workman would not be discharged/terminated during the pendency of the ID 
No.255 of 203, wherein, they have claimed various demands vide charter of demands dated 09.05.20l. However, in 
case workman has attained the age of retirement, then he would be entitled for full back wages along with other 
consequential benefits instead of reinstatement in service.

publication.

Findings:- 

4. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by Sh. R P Rana (AR for workman), Sh. G S 
Sidhu (AR for respondent no.|) and Sh. K B Sharma (AR for respondent no.2). 


5. First question which arise for consideration is whether the applicant is workman as defined under Section 
2(s) of the Act. To my mind, the claimant is a workman within the definition of Section 2(s) of the Act. In this regard, 
reliance can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal Council, Sanaur, AIR 2077 
Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act 


which deals with the definition of "workman" has observed as under : 


"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of employment/ contract of service, 
the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a 
workman within the meaning of Section 2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any distinction 
between full time and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in the plain 
language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular basis or a person 
employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on temporary, part time or contract basis on 


fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing duty for fixed hours is not a workman.” 


It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observations that even if a person is engaged on temporary, part time or 
contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in that eventuality such a 
person would be covered by the definition of "workman" as provided in Section 2(s) of the Act. Thus, nature of 
appointment or source of appointment is not relevant to be a "workman" within the Act. Since, the workman was 
engaged on contract basis by respondent no.2 for the work of respondent no.|, thus it would be termed as workman 


under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


6. Next question which arises for consideration is whether respondent no.| is an industry. The Hon’ble Apex 
Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa /978(36) FLR 266 dealt at length 
with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the Act, and has laid down triple test 
for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The triple test is where (a) systematic activity 
(b) organised by cooperation between employer and employee (the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) 
for the production or distribution of goods and services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is 
an “Industry” in that enterprise. Relevant part of judgment of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra) is 


reproduced as under-- 


“Does research involve collaboration between employer and employee? It does. The employer is the institution, the 


employees are the scientists, para-scientists and other personnel. Is scientific research service? Undoubtedly it is. Its
