Findings:- 
4. I have given due consideration to the arguments advanced by Sh. R P Rana (AR for workman), Sh. 
G S Sidhu (AR for respondent no.l) and Sh. K B Sharma (AR for respondent no.2). 


5. First question which arise for consideration is whether the applicant is workman as defined under 
Section 2(s) of the Act. To my mind, the claimant is a workman within the definition of Section 2(s) of the 
Act. In this regard, reliance can be made to the decision in the case of Devinder Singh Vs. Municipal 
Council, Sanaur, AIR 202] Supreme Court 2532, wherein the Hon'ble Apex Court while interpreting the 
provisions of Section 2(s) of the Act which deals with the definition of "workman" has observed as under : 


"The source of employment, the quantum of recruitment, the terms & conditions of 
employment/ contract of service, the quantum of wages/ pay and mode of payment are not at 
all relevant for deciding whether or not a person is a workman within the meaning of Section 
2(s) of the Act. The definition of workman also does not make any distinction between full time 
and part time employee or a person appointed on contract basis. There is nothing in the plain 
language of Section 2(s) from which it can be inferred that only person employed on regular 
basis or a person employed for doing whole time job is a workman and the one employed on 
temporary, part time or contract basis on fixed wages or as a casual employee or for doing 


I 


duty for fixed hours is not a workman.’ 


It is clear from the perusal of aforesaid observations that even if a person is engaged on temporary, 
part time or contract basis or for doing any other kind of work and is duly paid wages for the said work, in 
that eventuality such a person would be covered by the definition of "workman" as provided in Section 2(s) 
of the Act. Thus, nature of appointment or source of appointment is not relevant to be a "workman" within 
the Act. Since, the workman was engaged on contract basis by respondent no.2 for the work of respondent 


no.l, thus it would be termed as workman under Section 2(s) of the Act. 


6. Next question which arises for consideration is whether respondent no.l is an industry. The 
Hon’ble Apex Court in the case of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board Vs. A. Rajappa 7/9728(36) 
FLR 266 dealt at length with the ambit and scope of expression “industry” as defined in Section 2(j) of the 
Act, and has laid down triple test for determining whether a particular establishment is industry or not. The 
triple test is where (a) systematic activity (b) organized by cooperation between employer and employee 


(the direct and substantial element is commercial (c) for the production or distribution of goods and 


7686 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


services to calculated to satisfy human wants and wishes prima facie is an “Industry” in that enterprise. 


Relevant part of judgment of Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra) is reproduced as under: - 


“Does research involve collaboration between employer and employee? It does. The employer 
is the institution, the employees are the scientists, para-scientists and other personnel. Is 
scientific research service? Undoubtedly it is. Its discoveries are valuable contributions to the 
wealth of the nation. Such discoveries may be sold for a heavy price in the industrial or other 
markets. Technology has to be plate for and technological inventions and innovations may be 
patented and sold. In our scientific and technological age nothing has more cash value, as 
intangible goods and invaluable services, than discoveries. For instance, the discoveries of 
Thomas Alva Edison made him fabulously rich. It has been said that his brain had the highest 
cash value in history for he made the world vibrate with the miraculous discovery of recorded, 
sound. Unlike most inventors, he did not have to wait to get his reward in heaven; he received, 
it munificently on this gratified and grateful earth, thanks to conversion of his inventions into, 
money a plenty. Research benefits industry. Even though a research institute may be a 
separate entity disconnected from the many industries which funded the institute itself, it can 
be regarded as an Organisation, propelled by systematic activity, modeled on co-operation 
between employer and employee and calculated to throw up discoveries and inventions and 
useful solutions which benefit individual industries and the nation in terms of goods and 
services and wealth. It follows that research institutes, albeit run without profit-motive, are 


d 


industries. ’ 


। In the present case, respondent no.| is doing research work and as एथ' 7२७४] Sh. Virender Lamba, 
black tea, rose water, stevia plant, harar, amla and other medicinal plants are sold in the institute. He has 
also admitted that vide #ऋ.४७] to W7, various products of the institute have been sold to the customers. 
Thus, respondent no.lis engaged in systematic activity organized by cooperation between employer and 
employee (employee being workman in the present case) for the production or distribution of goods and 
services to calculated to satisfy human wants. In this regard, it is carrying out research. In addition to this, 
from the research work, benefits are being driven by respondent no.| and as per observation of Hon'ble 


Supreme Court in Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), respondent no.| falls under the 


definition of ‘industry’ as defined under the Act. 


8. So far as argument of AR for respondent no.| that respondent no.] being instrumentality of state 
does not fall under the definition of ‘industry’. In this regard, Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Chief 
Conservator of Forest Versus Jagannath Maruti Kondhare (7/०9०6 (2) SCT 464), has held that work, 
which was not be regarded as a part of inalienable of inescapable function of the State and which work can 
be well undertaken by a private agency does not require an instrumentality of State, such functions of the 
State fall within the ambit of Industry. Thus, function of doing research and other allied works of selling of 
goods and earning from research cannot be said to be sovereign function of the State and thus for this 


purpose of industrial dispute, respondents would be termed as industry. 


9. Thus, from every angle, respondent no.| is an industry. Moreover, its employees are not governed 


by IHBT Rules or CCS Rules, thus it is an industry. In view of the judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court 


titled as Banglore Water Supply & Sewerage Board (supra), decided by Hon'ble Supreme Court, the case 
law Central Institute of Medicinal and Aromatic Plants and others (supra) decided by Hon'ble High 


Court at Allahabad cited by AR for respondent no.I is not attracted to the facts and circumstances of the 


present case. 


[भाग त--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7687

“Contractor”, in relation to an establishment, means a person who undertakes to produce a 
given result for the establishment, other than a mere supply of goods or articles of 
manufacture to such establishment, through contract labour or who supplies contract labour 


for any work of the establishment and includes a sub-contractor; 


22 The workman was doing work i.e. systematic activity for respondent no.l at the asking of 
respondent no.2 and there was cooperation between the workman and respondent no.2, which involve 
substantial commercial element for rendering service to satisfy human wants. Thus, as per Banglore Water

employer and employee i.e. master and servant, the Hon’ble Supreme Court after analyzing the catena of 
cases has laid down in Balwant Raj Saluja Vs. Air India Limited _in Civil Appeal ४०.70266 dated 
235.06.20/4, two well recognized tests to find out whether the labours are the contract employees of the 


principal employer are:- 
(2) Whether the principal employer pays the salary instead of contractor and 
(2) Whether the principal employer controls and supervise the work of the employees? 


In this case, admittedly, as per statement of Sh. Rajeev Sood (MW2), wages were paid by 
respondent no.2, however, control was of the respondent no.l. This fact got proved in statement of MW2. 
Thus, under these circumstances, it is held that there exist relationship of master and servant between 


respondent no.l and workman. 


23. Further, in the present case, admittedly respondent no.l is entering into different contract 
agreements with respondent no.2(Ex.RWI/l Colly and Ex.RW2/2 as detailed above) by retaining same 
workmen and thus contracts are sham in view of the observation of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in similar 


matter in Management of CPWD versus Anand Kumar Gautam and ors. (2024:DHC:2757)which is as 


under: 


“Contract labourers can be engaged for the work of contractor only and not for the work of 
any establishment. In the present case the work is of the establishment and not of the 
contractor. The term supply of labour by a contractor is against human dignity. No one can be 
a supplier of human labour to any establishment. It is the duty of State to give employment to 
citizen and not of the contractors. Contractors cannot supply labour to any establishment. In 
view of the above discussion it becomes quite obvious that the contractors workmen in the 
instant case have been retained all along and contractors have been changed. So the 
contractor is only a label of a bottle. This label is changed from time to time but the contents 


of the bottle always remain the same. The contractors have been changed and the workmen 


7688 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST , 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


have been retained. Such a system is in-human. The contractors are the direct employees of 


the respondent/management. 


From the foregoing it becomes quite obvious that these two workmen have been working 
regularly and even without artificial breaks since /995-96, The contract is camouflage. 
There is direct relation of master and servant between the respondent and the workmen.” 


24. Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Bhilwara Dugdh Utpadak Sahakari S. Ltd. Versus Vinod 
Kumar Sharma dead by LRs and others (AIR 20/7 Supreme Court 3546) has held as under:- 


4. In order to avoid their liability under various labour statutes employers are very often 
resorting to subterfuge by trying to show that their employees are in fact, the employees of a 


contractor. It is high time that this subterfuge must come to an end. 


5. Labour statutes were meant to protect the employees/workmen because it was realized that 
the employers and the employees are not on an equal bargaining position. Hence, protection 
of employees was required so that they may not be exploited. However, this new technique of 
subterfuge has been adopted by some employers in recent years in order to deny the rights of 
the workmen under various labour statutes by showing that the concerned workmen are not 
their employees but are the employees/workmen of a contractor, or that they are merely daily 
wage or short term or casual employees when in fact they are doing the work of regular 


employees. 


25. Thus, from the above observation of Hon'ble Supreme Court, it is clear that respondent no.| has 


resorted to subterfuge by trying to show that workman was employee of respondent no.2. 


26. Moreover, respondent no.2 contractor while appearing in the witness box in his deposition has 
stated that in IHBT, there is practice that the contract for engagement of the employer/labour through 
contractors is for one year only and it changes on the basis of bid of the contractors every year. The 
contractor may change but the employees/labourers always remain same. The workman was already 
working with the management when the contract was tendered to the respondent no.2. Neither the 
workman was engaged by respondent no.2 nor the services of workman were terminated by respondent 
no.2. It is the respondent no.l who uses to select/engage and terminate the labour/workman and respondent 
no.2 has no role in the same. Thus, it shows that the contract was just an eyewash. It is further submitted 
that contract was allotted to respondent no.2 by respondent no.! on different years as per 75 .२४७४ |/| (colly) 
and Ex.RW2/2 and sometime to other contractors, meaning thereby the respondent no.! is controlling 
authority of the workmen including their engagement, termination etc. and even the wages of workman 
were also decided by respondent no.| only and respondent no.2 has no role to play in the same. So, there 
exist relationship of employees/servant and employer/master between the workmen and respondent no.|. 
Thus, the judgment Zhe Joint Secretary, Central Board of Secondary education and another (supra) 
cited by AR for respondent no.] is not attracted to the present case as in this case, time and again, same 
workers were being engaged through contractor and in view of clear cut dictum of Hon'ble Delhi High 
Court in Management of CPWD (supra), the aforementioned case law is not attracted. 


27. So far as Kirlosker Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (supra) relied upon by the AR for 


respondent no.| is concerned, facts and circumstances of this case are distinguishable. In the said Kirlosker 


Brothers Ltd. Vs. Ramcharan and others (supra), Court has held that that when there are no allegations or 


findings of sham and bogus contract then the contention of the reinstatement or the absorption of the 


workman cannot be sustained but the facts of the matter at hand is different from the facts of the case as in 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7689 


the instant case. In this case, workman was working since long and the work was of perennial nature. Thus, 


it tantamount to unfair labour practice. 


28. It is added here that admittedly in this case, workman was discharged by the respondent no.l & 2 
and as per agreement Ex.RWI/2, contract was awarded to respondent no.2 by respondent no.| for a period 
of two years i.e. from 9.2.20I2 to 8.2.20l4. However, workman was discharged prior to that on 
28..204 as per Ex.MW2/2, wherein it is stated by respondent no.| as under :- 


The contract for the related forms and field work, as per this institute's letter dated 04-]2- 
2072, is scheduled to expire on November 30, 20l4. Therefore, you are hereby informed that 
you must submit the fully completed EPF payment documents for all the workers employed 
under these contracts to the concerned EPF department, along with a copy to the institute, by 
October 2074, so that your final bill can be processed on time. Furthermore, please ensure 
that there are no outstanding financial dues of any kind for any worker; otherwise, these dues 


may be recovered from your security deposit. 


29. No prior permission was taken by respondent no.] & 2 before the discharging the services of 


workman. Section 33(2)(b) of the Act is very material and the same is reproduced below:- 


“(b) for any misconduct not connected with the dispute, or discharge or punish, whether by 


dismissal or otherwise, that workman: 


Provided that no such workman shall be discharged or dismissed, unless he has been 
paid wages for one month and an application has been made by the employer to the authority 


before which the proceeding is pending for approval of the action taken by the employer.” 


30. As per aforesaid provision, the workman can be discharged or dismissed after paying one month 
wages and after getting approval of the competent authority. In this case, no wages for one month was paid 
nor any permission from competent authority was taken before discharging the workman and consequently, 


it would be considered that workman was in regular services of the workman. A Full Constitutional 


Bench of Hon'ble Supreme Court in case titled as Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. versus 
Ram Gopal Sharma and others (2002 SCC (L_ & S) 279) has held that failure to make application for 


approval of the order of discharge or dismissal or withdrawal of such application after making it, held, 


renders the order of discharge or dismissal void and inoperative. 


3. The present application under Section 33A is well maintainable and purpose has also been defined 


by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Jaipur Zila Sahakari Bhoomi Vikas Bank Ltd. (supra) case, which read 


as follows:- 


Section 33A is available to an employee and is intended to save his time and trouble in as 
much as he can straightway make a complaint before the very authority, where the industrial 
dispute is already pending between the parties, challenging the order of approval instead of 
making efforts to raise an industrial dispute, get a reference and thereafter adjudication. 
Section उा speaks of penalty in respect of the offences stated therein. This provision is not 
intended to give any remedy to an aggrieved employee. It is only to punish the offender. 
Merely because penal provision is available or a workman has a further remedy under 
Section 33A to challenge the approval granted, it cannot be said that the order of discharge or 


dismissal does not become inoperative or invalid unless set aside under Section 33A.

32. In view of the above discussion, the termination of workman on 28..20I4 is bad in law and 
hence is set aside. In this case, both the respondents in connivance with each other have dispensed the 
services of the workman. Hence, both respondents are liable. The workman is entitled for reinstatement 
along with full back wages. It is ordered accordingly. The services of the workman would not be 
discharged/terminated during the pendency of the ID No.255 of 203, wherein, they have claimed various 
demands vide charter of demands dated 09.05.20ll. However, in case workman has attained the age of 
retirement, then he would be entitled for full back wages along with other consequential benefits instead of 


reinstatement in service.

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour & Employment, New Delhi vide its order No. L- 
202/63/207-IR(B-ID dated 25.0.207 has referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for 


adjudication:- 


“Whether the action of the management of Vijaya Bank in awarding the punishment of 
dismissal from service to Shri M.K.Mani @ V.S. Manibharathi is justified? If not, to what 


relief the workman is entitled to?” 


2, As एशा' claim statement, the Petitioner joined the service of the Respondent Bank on 06.2.989 
and discharged his duties in a sincere and diligent manner. Vide its order dated 06..2003, the Petitioner 
was placed under suspension. Thereafter, the Respondent Bank issued charge sheet dated 30.2.2003 
alleging that by misusing single window operator’s powers had fraudulently withdrawn the amount of 
Rs.45,500/- from SB account No.487 of a customer of Erode branch namely Shri A.R.Palanisamy by 
withdrawal slips which were in the custody of the Petitioner by forging the signature of the said 
accountholder. In respect of the charge sheet, domestic enquiry was initiated and Shri K.Ravi Raj Hedge, 
Senior Manager was appointed as Enquiry Officer. It is furhter submitted that enquiry was conducted and 
closed on the same day i.e.,2.04.2004 without providing any reasonable opportunity either to cross- 
examine the management witnesses or to produce defense evidence on his side. The Enquiry Officer 
denied assistance of lawyer during the enquiry and has not provided any reasonable time to cross examine 
the management witnesses and the Petitioner was insisted to cross examine the witnesses on the very 
same day. The Petitioner has studied upto tenth standard through Tamil medium and did not have 
sufficient knowledge to read/write and understand the documents in English, which categorically 
disallowed the Petitioner to put forth his defense effectively. The Enquiry Officer has not appreciated 


7700 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST , 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SECc. 3(ii)] 


material evidence and had come to the conclusion that charges made against the Petitioner are proved, 
while there was no evidence against the Petitioner. Thus, the dismissal order passed by the Respondent 
Bank is unjustified and the same is liable to be set aside and the Respondent Bank may be directed to 


reinstate the Petitioner into service with full back wages. 


3. On receipt of reference, notices were issued to parties, but the Respondent/Management failed to 
appear and no counter statement has been filed on their behalf. Hence, the case was heard ex-parte. The 
Petitioner has filed proof of affidavit and adduced oral evidence in Chief as 7ै/५४] and marked documents 
as Ex.W] to W7.

4. Heard the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant and perused the records. 


5: The point that arises for my determination is whether the domestic enquiry conducted by the 
Respondent/Management against the Petitioner is fair, proper and based on the principles of natural 


justice? 


6. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant has argued that enquiry was conducted 
and closed on the same day i.e., 2.04.2004 and the Petitioner was not provided with any legal assistance 
and neither an opportunity to cross-examine the management witnesses or permitted to produce evidence 
on his side. The Petitioner was compelled to cross examine the witnesses on the same day and was not 


granted any opportunity to produce defense evidence. 


7. On perusal of documents submitted by the Petitioner, the same are not rebutted by the 
Respondent/Management. It appears that the charge sheet was issued to the Petitioner on 30.2.2003 i.e. 
available at page | & 2 of the paper book and marked as Ex.W]. the substance of the charge sheet is while 
working in single window counter at Erode branch, the Petitioner by misusing single window powers has 


fraudulently withdrawn an amount of Rs.45,500/- from SB account No.487 of Shri R.Palanisamy, a

customer of the branch. It is stated that from 0.04.2003 to 09.05.2003, the charge sheet describes the 


amount withdrawn by the Petitioner as under:-

0.04.2003 990808 20,000 
7.04.2003 990829 0,000 
26.04.2003 990868 7,000 
07.05.2003 99094 6,000

TOTAL Rs. 45,500 
8. The charge sheet further stated that the single window operators are empowered to pass/pay cash 


instruments to the extent of Rs.25,000/- independently without authorization by the officer/supervisor. So, 
the Petitioner has misused the aforesaid powers and had fraudulently withdrawn the amounts mentioned 
above. The charge sheet further stated that the Petitioner had forged the signature of the accountholder in 
the withdrawal slips which were under the custody of the Petitioner, and was misused by the Petitioner for 
fraudulently withdrawing the amount from the said SB account No.487. As per the order passed by the 
Disciplinary Authority, it appears that copy of enquiry report was provided to the Petitioner, but the same 
has not been produced before this Tribunal by the Petitioner. The minutes of personal hearing granted to 
the Petitioner is available on record. On perusal of this report, it appears that a copy of the enquiry report 
dated .05.2004 was forwarded to the Petitioner, for his representation with regard to the findings of the 
Enquiry Officer and he had submitted his representation dated 08.06.2004. This document further 
reveals that Disciplinary Authority has accepted the findings of the Enquiry Officer and found the charge 
sheeted employee guilty of charges constituting the acts of gross misconduct under sub-section (j) रण 
Clause 5 of Memorandum of Settlement on Disciplinary Action Procedure for Workman dated 
0.04.2002. Accordingly, the Disciplinary Authority had proposed to impose punishment of dismissal 
from service. The document further reveals that the Petitioner filed his representation dated 07.08.2004 
had requested for personal hearing to him with regard to the punishment proposed to be imposed on him. 
On perusal of answers given by the Petitioner to the Disciplinary Authority, he had repaid the money 
although denied to withdraw the money. He denied signature on the withdrawal slips. He is also admitted 
by the Petitioner that he had filled up the withdrawal slips but denied the signatures. He also denied 
custody of the withdrawal slips. He was asked to explain the circumstances under which he has filled 
withdrawal slip. The Petitioner submitted that generally the customers used to ask to fill up the withdrawal 
slips and this case also the Petitioner was asked to fill up the withdrawal slips. The Petitioner admitted that 
he had _ paid Rs.9500/- on 2.0.2003 and requested one week time to repay the total amount and pay 
balance money after Deepavali. Regarding the payment of money, the Petitioner has stated that Assistant 


General Manager told him to pay the amount, so he paid the amount. 


9. After affording personal hearing, the Disciplinary Authority passed an order of dismissal from 
service i.e, available at pages 3 to 2 of the paper book. The Disciplinary Authority mentioned in his 


order that enquiry was conducted by the Enquiry Officer at Erode branch on 2.04.2004 and concluded on 


7702 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST I, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


the same day and the Petitioner was denied legal assistance. Although the Petitioner was represented by 
Shri S.D.Srinivasan, Regional Secretary, Vijaya Bank Workers Organization , Tamil Nadu Region, the 
Presenting Officer produced 2l documents in support of the charge and it was stated that the defense 
neither produced any documents nor examined any witness in defense. However, the defense 
representative has cross examined the management witnesses. Thus, the statement of Petitioner is proved 
that proper time to submit his defense evidence was not provided by the Enquiry Officer. It is the 
principles of natural justice that in domestic enquiry reasonable opportunity and sufficient time to the 
employee for his defense is an essential requirement. Although, an opportunity to cross examine 
witness was provided, but no opportunity was provided to represent the evidence or defense 


representative to the Petitioner. The Petitioner was refused to visit Erode branch to verify the documents. 


0. The nature of charge is forged signature of the accountholder made by the Petitioner himself, 
while the withdrawal slips were in his custody. But, on perusal of dismissal order passed by the 
Disciplinary Authority, it appears that there was no perfect and cogent reasons/evidence about the 
signature of the Petitioner on the withdrawal slips. It also reveals that the preliminary investigation report 
was submitted by Shri M .Dineshan on 20.0.2003 and he did not point out any person who has been 


involved in the unauthorized withdrawal. 


ll. It is true that the Petitioner remitted the amount which was alleged to have been withdrawn by 
him but it was remitted under threat or duress given by the Senior Officers that a criminal complaint 
may be lodged, if the Petitioner fails to remit the amount. The remittance of amount is not a proof of 


withdrawal made by the Petitioner by forging the signature of the accountholder of the withdrawal slips. 


2. On perusal of order passed by the Disciplinary Authority, it appears that handwriting in 
withdrawal slip and the signature in the withdrawal slip was verified by the Enquiry Officer. The 
Petitioner admitted writing on the withdrawal slip, but denied forged signature on the withdrawal slip. In 
these circumstances, it is essential to seek handwriting expert report as evidence to establish that forged 


signature was made by the Petitioner. 


3. It was the duty of the Enquiry Officer to provide proper time to submit evidence of the charge 
sheeted employee and there was no occasion to close the enquiry on the same date. It is essential to 
provide a reasonable opportunity to defend the case of the Petitioner. But, in this case, this opportunity was 
denied by the Enquiry Officer, hence, the enquiry conducted by the Respondent Bank against the 


Petitioner is not fair, proper, reasonable and not based on principles of natural justice. 


4. Roll of Enquiry Officer: 


In the case of Prathama Bank (Chairman) Vs. Vijaya kumar Goel & Another AIR 989 SC 977, it was 
held that Enquiry Officer should give adequate opportunity to the delinquent employee to peruse relevant 


documents to enable him to prepare his reply. 


5. In the present case on hand, Enquiry Officer denied perusal of records of the concerned branch 
and not provided proper time to file defense evidence to the delinquent employee, although there is no 
right for the workmen to bring outsider or advocate to assist him in the enquiry. But it was essential to 
provide sufficient time for defense evidence on the cost of repetition. It is again worth to mention that 


remittance of the amount is not admission of guilt. 


[भाग I—a€ve 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण 0, 948 7703 


6. Thus, as per discussion above, it is clear that Petitioner was denied to visit concerned branch for 
the purpose of verification of documents. The Petitioner was not provided proper time to submit his 
defense evidence and there is no cogent reasons to conclude that forged signature was executed by the 
Petitioner on the withdrawal slips. The Respondent/Management failed to deny / rebut the allegations 
made by the Petitioner in the claim statement. Hence the enquiry conducted by the 
Respondent/Management against the Petitioner cannot be said as fair, proper and in accordance with law. 


Accordingly, the enquiry in the present case is set aside. 


7. Since the enquiry conducted by the Respondent bank is not fair, there is no need to discuss the 
proportionality of the punishment . The punishment imposed by the Respondent bank is based on unfair 


enquiry and thus, is liable to be set aside. 
AWARD 


The claim petition raised by the Petitioner is allowed. The enquiry conducted by the Enquiry 
Officer is set aside. Consequently, the order of punishment imposed by the Respondent bank on the 
Petitioner is also set aside. Therefore, the Petitioner workman is entitled to get relief of notional 
reinstatement with consequential benefits. The Respondent/Management is directed to give the relief of 
notional reinstatement to the Petitioner within a period of two months, after publication of this Award 


along with 50% of back wages. 


It is made clear that the Respondent is at liberty to conduct a fresh enquiry in accordance with law, 
if so advised, by providing sufficient time to the Petitioner to file his defense evidence on verification of 


documents at Erode branch. Ordered accordingly. 

The reference is answered accordingly.

The following points arise for adjudication:- 


The first point that arises for consideration is whether the Petitioner is a workman as defined 
u/s.2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947? 


The essential conditions provided u/s 2(s) of the Act are as under:- 


The person must be employed in any industry. 


He must do / perform any of the following kinds of work: 


Manual work; 
Skilled work 
Unskilled work 
Technical work 
Operational work 
Clerical work & 


Supervisory work 


9. As per definition of section 2(s) the following persons are not considered as a workman: 


(a) Managerial or administrative capacity, 


(b) supervisory capacity drawing wages above the statutory limit and performing managerial functions. 


0. It is argued by the 


Petitioner that the Respondent attempts to exclude the Petitioner from the 


definition of workman solely on the basis of his designation as Senior Executive and his salary. While, the 


real test is dominant nature of duties test. The Petitioner in his proof of affidavit has stated that the work 


involved was co-ordination of vessel and gate operations during loading and unloading of containers. He 


further stated that the nature of work is clerical/ operational and clearly falls under the purview of section 
2(s) of the Act. 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण L0, 948 7707 


l]. It is argued on behalf of the Respondent that Petitioner himself has admitted in his cross 
examination that he was vested with the powers of approving leave application of his subordinates. He 
admitted that he has sanctioned the leave of one Nithya.M. It is also admitted that he has approved leave 
of another workman namely S.Saravanan. Thus, the person who has vested with the powers of granting 


approval of leave cannot be considered as clerical cadre. 
2. Now, the Tribunal has to ascertain the following points:- 


a. Whether the workman was authorized to sanction leave and performed his duties during his 


employment? 


b. Whether he had control over the staff? 


८. Whether he has enjoyed the powers of independent decision making authority? 

d. What was the nature of related duties? 

e. Whether the work of the Petitioner was supervisory / clerical / technical? 

3. The Petitioner in his cross examination admitted that his qualification is B.Com and MBA and he 


is having experience of l4 years in handling of operation in capacity of supervision. He further stated that 
he was supervising the work of loading and unloading in the vessel and attend the work of gate entry & 
exist. He further submitted that approximately 25 persons were working under his control. Regarding the 


sanction of leave applications of workmen, he stated as under:- 
“T have approved leave application of Nithya .M, which is marked as Ex.M3.” 


With regard to making contact with other persons on behalf of Respondent he replied as 


under:- 
“T have sent a mail to one Mr.Maheshwaran and Others” 


4. He also admitted that he has approved leave to other employees. He contacted other parties and 
sent e-mail to maheswaran@srs.co.in, who is the vessel agent. Although, he stated that on behalf of the 
management only, the sent the e-mail, which is marked as ExM0. He further stated that Ex.M5 document 
was sent by him on behalf of his senior. He further stated that EX.M7 was sent by him to Southern 
Trading company to furnish copy of CHA license.(Custom House Agent). Copy of Ex.M8 was sent by 
him to M/s.MBK Logistics intimating that vessel arrived at their terminal. Copy of Ex.9 was sent by him 
to a vessel operator on behalf of the Respondent with regard to delay in unloading the container due to 
some technical problem. He further admitted that Ex.M9 was sent by him in the capacity of Senior 
Executive (Operations). He admitted that at the time of appointment, he received salary of Rs.45,000/- 
and at the time of termination, it was Rs.48,000/-. Thus, workman himself admitted that he was working in 
a supervisory capacity and was drawing Rs.48,000/- . He admitted that he approved leave applications of 
another workmen / employee, he contacted another parties and sent e-mail on behalf of Respondent. 
Although he admitted that he sent e-mail on behalf of the Respondent it is true that he sent e-mail on 
behalf of the Respondent But only the person who is holding managerial capacity can only send e-mail. 
Every employee perform the work on behalf of the Respondent. It is not a fact that originally wage ceiling 
was ५.।6,000/- per month and by one month or present the wage is Rs.l0,000/- per month. Thus, a 


supervisor who is drawing wags exceeding Rs.l0,000 per month may be excluded from the definition of 


7708 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST I, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


workman. It is true that salary is not decisive to decide the nature of work. This Tribunal has to decide 


the dominant nature of duties. 


5. As I discussed above, the Petitioner has approved the leave application of another employee and 


sent e-mail to third parties on behalf of Respondent. 


6. Inthe case of Bennett Colemann & Company Ltd, Vs, Yadeshwar Kumar 2007 (l) LLN 535, the 
Hon'ble High Court of Delhi held that if the employee was working in supervisory capacity and was 
responsible for sanction of leave for the persons working under him, and drawing salary above the 
prescribed limit, then such person cannot be considered to be a workman. This case law relied on by the 
learned counsel for the Respondent is squarely applicable to the facts of the present case on hand. At 
least 25 workmen were working under the Petitioner, who sanctioned their leave and contacted the third 


parties and has sent and received e-mails from third parties. 


7. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant relied on the judgement of the Hon'ble 
Supreme Court in Arkal Govind Raj Rao Vs CIBA Ceigy of India Ltd. (985) 3 SCC 37]. In this case, 
section 2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, !947 was interpreted and held that if a person is mainly 
performing clerical work and incidentally performing supervisory work is a workman. The Hon’ble 
Court further held that it was a primary, basic or dominant nature of duties for which a person whose 
status is under enquiry to be settled by the Court. In this case, the Hon’ble Court further held that the 
work distribution of clerical nature would not seize to be clerical work and further held that work of 


preparation of bank reconciliation cannot be said to be supervisory in nature. 


8. The Petitioner in the present case on hand, during cross examination has admitted that he has 
sanctioned leave of employees, who worked under him approximately 25 numbers of workmen and 
further on behalf of the Respondent/Management he contacted outside agencies / companies and sent e- 


mail in connection with official work of the Respondent. 


9. As per discussion above, this fact is established that the Petitioner does not fall under the 
definition of workman as defined u/s.2(s) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. The Petitioner was 
working in supervisory category and getting salary of Rs.48,000/- per month is more than the statutory 


ceiling limit . Therefore, the point is decided against the Petitioner. 


20. Since the Petitioner in this case is not a workman, this Industrial Dispute raised by the Petitioner is 
not maintainable and therefore, there is no need to discuss the case on merits. 
AWARD 


The Industrial Dispute raised by the Petitioner is dismissed as not maintainable for the reasons 


indicated above. 
The reference is answered accordingly.

II. On perusal of records submitted by the Respondent Authority the following facts prior to the 


impugned order of dismissal are established — 


a) As per domestic enquiry, the Respondent issued warning letter to the Petitioner for his habitual 


absence. 


b) As per the domestic enquiry, again a warning letter was issued by the Respondent/Management for 


the Petitioner’s habitual absence. 


c) As per the domestic enquiry dated 4.2.20l8 for 42 days absence a fresh charge sheet was issued 


and after enquiry, order of dismissal was issued by the Respondent/Management. 


2. The above mentioned facts clearly establish that the Petitioner remained unauthorized absence for 
more than three occasions ina year. The Petitioner submitted explanation on the ground of illness, but 
there is no document which may suggest any prescription / treatment provided by the Doctor. Only 
fitness and illness certificate were filed by the Petitioner. But in the said documents nowhere it is 
explained what kind of treatment was provided to the Petitioner. There is no document available on 
record that may prove prior permission of the Respondent Authority for the medical treatment of the 
Petitioner. There is no document on record which may show the Petitioner had informed the authority 


with reference to his illness and treatment. 


3. As per Annexure |, the Respondent issued show cause notice on .08.2005 to the Petitioner 
and issued warning letter dated 2.09.2005. The Respondent/Management again issued a warning letter 
dated 20.03.2006 for the unauthorized absence. Again the Respondent issued warning letter dated 
07.06.2006 for unauthorized absence of the Petitioner. The Respondent /Management again issued 
charge sheet dated 22.2.207 for his unauthorized absence and issued a warning letter based on written 
assurance and representation made by the Petitioner dated 0.02.208. But, the Petitioner had maintained 
the habit of unauthorized absence . Therefore, the Respondent issued one more charge sheet dated 
7.04.208 and again issued show cause notice dated 04.06.20l8 based on written assurance and 
explanation made by the Petitioner, stern warning letter was issued on 9.06.20l8. But, the Petitioner 
failed to maintain punctuality in working and remained unauthorized absence for which charge sheet 
dated 0.07.20I8 was issued. Based on the written request of the Petitioner, no further action was taken 
by the Respondent/Management. The Petitioner repeated the unauthorized absence and charge sheet dated 
4.2.208 was issued against the Petitioner and enquiry was conducted. After completion of enquiry, 
enquiry report was provided to the Petitioner and after considering the explanation of the Petitioner, the 


impugned order was passed. 


4. From the above facts, it emerges and establishes the conduct of the Petitioner, who remained 
habitual absence for duty; failed to establish that he suffered from illness; never informed the 
Respondent/Management regarding medical treatment and remained absent without prior approval of the 


Respondent/Management. 


5: The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Petitioner relied on the case law in UOI vs. Giriraj 
Sharma (MANU/S/0058/994) . In that case, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that punishment of 
dismissal for overstaying the period of l2 days was harsh and further held that it is open to the 


department to impose minor punishment to the Respondent. 


6. On perusal of the above judgement, it appears that the workman has explained the circumstances 


in which it was inevitable for him to continue on leave as he was forced to do so on account of unexpected 


77\6 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST I, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


circumstances . But, in the present case on hand, the Petitioner failed to establish the unexpected 
circumstances which was faced by him. He failed to submit any medical prescription or treatment 


provided to him by the Doctor. 


7. The Petitioner relied on the another judgement delivered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Shri 
Ashok Kumar Vs UOI and Another (MANU/SC 0785/988). In that case, the Petitioner absented himself 
from duty for three days without leave. Therefore, the Hon'ble Supreme Court considering the punishment 
of termination from service in excess, punishment was set aside and new punishment of censure was 


imposed. 


8. In the present case on hand, the Petitioner absented himself repeatedly and not only for 3 days, 
but he had absented during the whole period of enquiry from the date of suspension till the date of 
punishment order (3 days). The Respondent/Management initiated disciplinary proceedings against the 


Petitioner on so many occasions. As I discussed above, this case law is not helpful to the Petitioner. 


9. The Respondent/Management relied on a case law in LIC of India Vs. R.Dhandapani 2006 (43) 
SCC 63. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in that case held that power १/$. 0 (of the Industrial Disputes 
Act, 947) is to be exercised only when the punishment is found to be shockingly disproportionate to the 
degree of guilt of the workman and the Industrial Tribunal / Labour Court has to give reasons in support of 
its decision. It is also held that mere use of words “disproportionate” or “grossly disproportionate” by 
itself will not be sufficient. In that case, the Petitioner continuously remained absent after his transfer 
order from one branch to another branch of LIC. The Hon'ble Supreme Court held that punishment of 


dismissal was justified. 


20. In the present case on hand, the Petitioner remained absent for so many occasions. This fact is 
established that he was habitually absent without informing the Respondent/Management which creates 
hurdle in performance of the work of the Respondent/Management. This case law is squarely applicable 


to the facts of the present case. 


2l. It is argued on behalf of the Petitioner that he was provided with appreciation letter for the good 
work by the Respondent/Management. The appreciation letters are available on record at page Nos. 5 to 7 
of the paper book. But, the appreciation letters do not justify the conduct of repeated absence of the 


Petitioner from duty. 


22. In view of the above discussion, in my view, the impugned order passed by the

0. Heard the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant and perused the records. 


II. The first question that arises for determination is whether the Disciplinary Authority is entitled to 


conduct enquiry himself instead of appointing a separate Enquiry Officer? 


2. The answer to this question depends on interpretation of service rules and standing orders. If the 
rule specifically prohibits it, then the Disciplinary Authority is not entitled to conduct enquiry. But, if the 
rules permits, the Disciplinary Authority can conduct enquiry, the Disciplinary Authority may enquire 
into the charges. But, since the charges against the workmen were grave and he was dismissed on the 
basis of proven charges, it was not logical to conduct enquiry by the Disciplinary Authority himself. 
Further, if the Disciplinary Authority conducts enquiry himself, it may cause apprehension of bias in the 


mind of the workman. 


3. The Respondent Bank in its reply stated that as per settlement entered into between the 
Respondent and employees union, it is permissible to conduct enquiry by the Disciplinary Authority 
himself. The Respondent Bank filed 2 documents before this Tribunal. But, none of these documents 
relate to agreement/settlement entered between the parties which may suggest that Disciplinary Authority 
is empowered to conduct enquiry against the workman. Therefore, enquiry conducted by the Disciplinary 


Authority against the Petitioner itself is illegal. 


4. The second point that arises for determination is whether charges levelled against the Petitioner 


are proved on the basis of evidence collected by the Enquiry Officer? 


5. The first charge against the Petitioner is that he had demanded and received bribe of Rs.5,000/- 
from a customer of the bank branch Mr. I.Krishnan, a borrower of the educational loan from the bank. Mr. 
I.Krishnan was examined and recorded as ७४] before the Enquiry Officer that he submitted the 
complaint letter dated 03.07.203 and he stand by the contents of the letter. He further stated that he has 
withdrawn the letter dated 03.07.203 and examination in chief was over with this statement. Although, 
withdrawal of complaint by the customer does not automatically drop disciplinary proceedings against 
the bank employee. Since, it is not a private dispute between the customer and employee of the bank, it is 


the right of the bank to continue with departmental enquiry. 


6. Now, I have to consider the value of evidence of ५७]. The case of the Respondent is based 
only on customer’s complaint and there is no other independent evidence. There is no other documentary 
evidence, accounts records or CC TV footage, added finding or any other witness which might have 
suggested that bribe of Rs.l5,000/- was asked or received by the delinquent employee. If the 
complainant withdraws the complaint, then it was the duty of the Enquiry Officer to ascertain the fact 
that whether the complaint was withdrawn under pressure, or settlement or compromise. On perusal of 
the enquiry report, it appears that the Enquiry Officer failed to put any question to the complainant 
Mr.I. Krishnan under what circumstances he has withdrawn the complaint letter dated 03.07.203. 


7. On perusal of enquiry report, it appears that the Petitioner was not given due opportunity to 
cross examine the management witness ७७] and the Presenting Officer introduced Shri K.Sornam, 
Manager of Melur Branch as MW2. At that time, charge sheeted employee was not present. Although, it 
was kept for cross examination of ५] and MW2, it was decided to hold ex-parte enquiry without 
reference of either parties. On 28.03.204, the delinquent employee was present. On this date itself another 
witness Mr. G.R.Nagarajan, Sr.Manager, Regional Office, Madurai was introduced as management 
witness No.3. He has approved the investigation report on 09.0.20l3. This witness further stated that 


charge sheeted employee initially refused to accept the bribe but subsequently he agreed and confessed 


7726 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST , 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


that he had received the bribery of Rs.l5,000/- towards educational loan sanctioned to children of Mr.I 
Krishnan and Mr.Krishnan never deposed before the Enquiry Officer that he had paid Rs.l5,000/- to the 
delinquent employee. Therefore, this statement had lost its value, since the main complainant withdrew the 
complaint and failed to submit any details of bribery money paid to the delinquent employee. MW3 in his 
cross examination admitted that investigation was based on the oral complaint received from the Regional 
Office. The extract of oral complaint was not provided to the delinquent employee. The evidence of MW2 
and MW3 was based on the discussion held with main complainant who withdrew the complaint against 
the delinquent employee. Therefore , there is no evidence available on record against the Petitioner 


workman which may establish the fact of asking or receiving the bribe of Rs.5,000/-. 


8. The next charge against the Petitioner relates to that he was instigating education loan borrowers 


not to repay the loan as the Government would grant waiver of the loans. 


9. As per the Respondent/Management Shri P.Sampath Kumar, Assistant Manager of the branch 
informed misconduct of the employee vide his letter dated 2.08.203. The second letter was written by 
Mr.Sornam, Manager of the Branch vide letter dated 04.09.203 and third information was given by the 
Regional Office vide its letter dated 07.09.20I3 and the Investigating Officer Mr.G.R.Nagarajan vide his 
enquiry report dated 06.09.20l3. But, there is no evidence of any borrower of education loan who 
mentioned in his statement that he was misguided by the Petitioner that there is no need to repay their 


educational loans. 


20. The Enquiry Officer or the Investigating Officer nowhere reported any evidence of even a single 
person who may have stated before the Enquiry Officer or the Investigating Officer that the Petitioner was 
asking them not to repay their educational loans. Therefore, this charge levelled against the Petitioner was 


also not proved by the Respondent/Management with sufficient evidence. 


2l. Another charge levelled against the Petitioner was that he instigated and threatened the bank officials 
through a borrower while the officer was on official duty. The charge of Respondent/Management against 
the Petitioner is that Mr. P.Sampath Kumar, Assistant Manager of the branch was threatened by one 
person who was working at Gowri Hotel, Arasaradi on the influence of the Petitioner. Even, this person 
was not enquired into by the Enquiry Officer. He was not called for to produce evidence. It is further 
alleged that delinquent employee instigated one borrower Mr.Thangavel to send anonymous letter 


against the member, but Mr.Thangavel was not examined by the EO. 


22, The another charge against the Petitioner is that he demanded money from the borrower towards 
waiver of loans which was granted under Debt Waiver Scheme and the Petitioner demanded Rs.45,000/- 
from Shri S.R Kannappan. But, this person was also not examined by the Enquiry Officer. There is no 
evidence on record to show that how the petitioner/delinquent employee has demanded money from the 


customer / education loan borrower as bribe. No such person was examined by the Enquiry Officer. 


23. The Respondent bank in its reply mentioned the case law IN Municipal Committee, 
Bahadurgarh v. Krishnan Behari and others, (996) 2 LLN 88],wherein it was observed by the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court that act of misappropriation is relevant and the amount of misappropriation may 
be small or large, but, as I discussed above, there is no direct or indirect evidence to show that Petitioner 
has received/accepted bribe from loan borrowers of the bank or misappropriated bank money. Therefore, 


this case law has no relevance to the present case on hand. 


24. The Respondent/Management cited another case law in State Bank of India v. Ram Lal Bhaskar 
& Anr (20i2) I LLN 56. In that case, the Hon'ble Supreme Court observed that as long as there is some 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण L0, 948 7727 


evidence, which the authority entrusted with the duty to hold the enquiry has accepted and which evidence 
may reasonably support the conclusion that the delinquent officer is guilty of the charge, it is not the 
function of the High Court in a petition for a writ to review the evidence and to arrive at an independent 


finding on the evidence. 


25. On perusal of this case law, it appears that the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that there must be some 
evidence which may reasonably support the conclusion that delinquent employee is guilty of charge. But 
in the present case on hand, there is no evidence at all to support the conclusion that delinquent employee 


is guilty of charges. 


26. The Respondent/Management relied on another case law in Ramana Vs. APSRT Corporation & 
Others (2005) III LLJ 725. In this case, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that the court should not 
interfere with the administrator’s decision unless it was illogical and suffers from procedural 
impropriety or was shocking the conscience of the court . In the present case on hand, enquiry was 
conducted by the person who was Disciplinary Authority himself and conclusion arrived on the basis of 
no evidence case. Moreover, the complainant withdrew his complaint and he was not questioned about 
the withdrawal of the complaint by the Enquiry Officer. Therefore, this case law relied on by the 


Respondent/Management is not applicable to the facts of the present case. 


27. The Respondent/Management has relied on another case law in State Bank of India Vs. Ramesh 
Dinkar Punde (2006) 4 LLN 79, whereby the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that loss of confidence is 
primary factor and not the amount of money misappropriated. As I discussed above, there is no evidence 
on record to show that Petitioner has asked or received any bribe from the borrower of loan / customer 
and there is no evidence which proves that he instigated the borrowers not to repay borrowed money as 
the Govt will waive all loan amounts. Further, there is no evidence to show some persons were 


threatening the officials of the bank / management on the instigation of the Petitioner. 


28. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant relied on a case law in Roop Singh 
Negi Vs. Punjab National Bank & Others CDJ 2008 SC 247. In this case , the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
held that confession should have been proved and some evidence should have been brought on record to 
show that he had indulged in stealing bank draft book. There was no direct or indirect evidence that 
tenor of the report demonstrates that Enquiry Officer had made up his mind to find him guilty of charge. 
The Hon’ble Court held that reasons should have been assigned and the guilt is required to be proved. A 
decision must be arrived at on some evidence which is legally admissible. The Hon’ble Court further 
held that provisions of Evidence Act may not applicable to departmental proceedings but principles of 


natural justice are applicable. 


29. In the present case, conclusion of the Enquiry Officer is based on surmises and conjectures. 
There was no evidence at all regarding charges / allegations framed against the Petitioner employee. The 
above case law relied on by the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Appellant is squarely 


applicable to the facts of the present case on hand. 


30. Therefore, in the light of the above case law of the Hon'ble Supreme Court it can be concluded that 
the Enquiry Officer has given his findings purely on assumption, surmises and conjectures and there was 


no concrete evidence against the Petitioner which might have proved the charges.

period of two months from the date of publication of this Award.

The Central Government, Ministry of Labour & Employment, O/o. Dy,Chief Labour 
Commissioner (Central) Chennai vide its order No. 7/7/209/30007944/PDY/ADJ/AI dated 20.05.204 


has referred the following Industrial Dispute to this Tribunal for adjudication: - 


“Whether the management of Central Bank of Bank is justified in not considering the claim of legal heir 
Smt.N.Baby Saroja of the deceased employee i.e., Ms.N.Bama for payment of ex-gratia in lieu of 
compassionate employment as per the Scheme of the management bank vide circular 
No.CO:HRD:R&P:2006-07:57 dated 76.06.20962 If not to what relief the legal heir Smt.N.Baby Saroja 
of the deceased employee i.e., Ms.N. Bama is entitled to?” 


2. This claim petition is filed by the mother of deceased N.Bama, admittedly an employee of the 
Respondent Bank, who died on 30.0.204, after putting in service of only 3 years | month and ] days. 
The Petitioner claims that being legal heir of the deceased employee, she is entitled to get ex-gratia under 
the Respondent Bank circular CO: HRD;R&P:2006-07:57 dated 6.06.2006 was in force on 30.0.204. 


3. The Respondent Bank in its reply stated that Petitioner has relied on circular dated 6.06.2006 
which has no application. The relevant circular is dated 08.04.20I5. As per the said circular dependent 
family members are given as under:- 


(a) Spouse; 


(b) Wholly dependent son (including legally adopted son); 
(c) Wholly dependent daughter (including legally adopted daughter); 


7730 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST I, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


(d) Wholly dependent brother or sister in the case of unmarried employee. 
This circular does not include Mother as legal heir of the dependent employee. 


4. It is further stated that the matter is referred to Government of India and therefore, it comes u/s.2K 
of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947, which is not maintainable, since the workman or his dependent cannot 


raise any dispute u/s.2K of the Act. Therefore, the petition must be rejected by this Tribunal. 


Witnesses Examined :- 


On behalf the Petitioner : None 

On behalf of the Respondent : None 

Documents marked on either side : NIL 

मे Heard the learned counsel appearing on either side and perused the material available on record. 


6. The first question that arises for determination is whether the reference made by the Government 
of India u/s.l0 (2A) is maintainable or not? 


7. The Respondent/Management raised the issue of maintainability of this industrial dispute as per 
provisions of section 2A of the Act, which deals with dismissal, retrenchment or otherwise termination of 
service of the individual workman. While section 40 of the Act empowers the Central Govt. to refer 
industrial dispute to the Industrial Tribunal, it is further provided that where the dispute relates to any 
matter specified in Third Schedule and is not likely to affect more than one hundred workmen, the 


appropriate Government may, if it so thinks fit, make the reference to a Labour Court under clause (c). 


8. In the present case on hand, the employee died while she was in the service of the Respondent 
Bank. The dispute purely relates to ex-gratia may be considered not an industrial dispute on the following 


conditions:- 
(a) Payment of ex-gratia in this case is discretionary; 


(b) Is payable as compassionate not raising from settlement, award, service rules or statutory 


rules. 


But if the ex-gratia is part of service conditions or any scheme applicable to employee, then it becomes 
payable as a matter of right. Then, such dispute maybe considered as an industrial dispute and the Govt. 
may be referred the matter to the Industrial Tribunal and the Industrial Tribunal is also empowered to 


decide such disputes. 


9. Now, I have to consider whether the payment of ex-gratia was part of service conditions? If yes, 
then industrial dispute filed by the Mother of the deceased bank employee is maintainable. If not, then the 


industrial dispute is not maintainable. 


0. The Respondent Bank issued a circular dated 6.06.2006 with a heading Scheme for payment of 
ex-gratia lump sum amount in lieu of appointment on compassionate grounds. Para 2 to 4 of the said 


Scheme runs as under:- 


“2. In this connection, we inform you that in supersession to all our previous 
circulars/letters/guidelines on appointment on compassionate grounds, we have now 


introduced a new scheme in the bank viz. payment of ex-gratia lump sum amount in lieu 


[भाग ]--खण्ड 3(ii)] भारत का राजपत्र : अगस्त , 2026/श्रावण L0, 948 773i 


of appointment on compassionate grounds to the dependents of deceased 
employees/physically incapacitated employees in terms of Government/IBA guidelines 
and as such the scheme for providing appointment on compassionate grounds stands 


dispensed with. The new scheme comes into effect from 4.2.2005. 


3. Based on Model Scheme of Indian Banks Association for payment of ex-gratia lump 
sum amount in lieu of appointment on compassionate grounds, details of the scheme 
formulated by the Bank for the purpose and adopted by the Board are enclosed as per 
Annexure I along with format of application to be submitted by the family members of 


the deceased employees/ physically incapacitated employees. 


4. All pending cases as of 4.2.2005 and cases received to be received thereafter will 
be processed as per the new scheme for payment of ex-gratia lump sum amount, if 


eligible.” 


ll. The provisions of this Circular creates enforcement right and not purely discretionary, because it 
provides alternative remedy to the legal heir of the deceased person in place of compassionate 
appointment. There is no chance for interpretation that this circular is discretionary. It never describes that 
Respondent Bank may grant ex-gratia. This circular specifically describes that “we have introduced a 
new scheme in the bank viz., payment of ex-gratia lump sum amount in lieu of appointment on 


compassionate grounds to the dependent of the deceased employee.’ 


2. I will discuss entitlement of the Mother in later part of this Award. But, considering that Mother 
of the deceased employee is a legal heir can make claim as she acquired entitlement after the death of her 
daughter and this dispute is connected with the service conditions along with monetary benefits arising out 


of employment after her death. Thus, the Industrial Dispute is maintainable. 


3. The Respondent relied on the judgement of the Hon'ble High Court of Madras in the case of 
Madura Coats Ltd & Others Vs. Jayaraman & another reported in 2005 (2) LLN 944. In that case, the 
Hon’ble Court held that section 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 is applicable on the following 


conditions:- 
“Discharge/Dismissal/Retrenchment or termination” 


Any dispute not falling within the meaning of section 2A would be industrial dispute only if union or body 


of workmen supports the cause of individual workman. 


4. As per the facts of that case, the industrial dispute was filed by the |7 Respondent for declaration 
that order of demotion is not valid and a direction to the Petitioner to restore him in the same post as 
before. In the said case, matter was not referred by Govt. of India u/s. 0 of the Act. The present case is 
referred by the appropriate Government u/s.l0 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947, hence it is 


maintainable before the Industrial Tribunal. Therefore, the first point is decided in favour of the Petitioner. 


5. The second point that arises for determination is whether circular dated 6.06.2006 is applicable 
or 08.04.205 is applicable? 


6. The difference between these two circulars is that vide circular dated 6.06.2006, the Mother of the 
deceased employee of the Respondent Bank was legal heir, while as per circular dated 08.04.20I5, the 
Mother of the deceased employee of the Respondent Bank is not a legal heir. 


7732 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST , 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SECc. 3(ii)] 


7. Admittedly, the deceased employee had died on 30.0.20I4. On this date, circular dated 
08.04.20I5 was not in existence and circular dated 6.06.2006 was in existence. The Respondent Bank 
also relied on the judgement rendered by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in MGB Gramin Bank Vs. 
Chakrawarti Singh 204 ((3) SCC 583. As per facts of that case, the Respondent was entitled to be 
appointed under the scheme for compassionate appointment. The father of the Respondent was working as 
Class वा employee with the Appellant bank died on 9.04.2006. The Respondent applied for 
compassionate appointment on 2.05.2006. During the pendency of application filed by the Respondent, a 
new scheme dated 2.06.2006 came into force w.e.f. 06.0.2006. Clause 4 of the scheme provides that 
all applications pending on the date of commencement of the scheme shall be considered for grant of ex- 
gratia to the family instead of compassionate appointment. In view of the new Scheme, the Hon’ble Court 
held that respondent may apply for consideration of his case under new scheme and the Appellant shall 
consider his case strictly in accordance with clause 4 of the said new Scheme within a period of three 


months. 


8. In the present case on hand, two circulars had two different concept. The earlier circular had provided 
compassionate appointment while the latter provided ex-gratia scheme in lieu of compassionate 
appointment and it was made mandatory to consider pending cases under the new scheme. The facts of the 
case referred in MGB Gramin Bank cited supra is applicable to the facts of this case on hand with regard 
to maintainability of the Industrial Dispute as per new circular dated 08.04.205. The Scheme introduced 
by the Respondent Bank dated 6.06.2006 relates to payment of ex-gratia lump sum amount in lieu of 
compassionate appointment. The scheme introduced by the Respondent Bank on 08.04.20I5 came into 
force w.e.f. 08.05.20I4. The cases that occurred on or after 05.08.20I4 will only be covered under the 
scheme. While the death of the deceased employee of the Respondent Bank in the present case on hand 
was happened on 30.0.204 and cases prior to 05.08.20l4 i.e, 4.2.2005 to 04.08.20l4 will be dealt 
with as per circular dated 6.06.2006. 


9. As per claim statement, the deceased employee of the Respondent Bank died on 30.0.20]4. 
Therefore, provisions of circular dated 08.04.20I5 will be applicable and as per that circular, dependent 
of bank employee, those who are, described above in para no. 3 of this Award and as per the list of 
dependent Mother of deceased bank employee is not a legal heir. 


20. The question arises that whether this circular is based on principles of natural justice. Any person 
of general prudence may answer it in negative because, Mother of any person is very nearer legal heir in 
comparison of any other person in the absence of spouse, son and daughter. Admittedly, deceased 
employee was unmarried. So, there was no occasion for spouse or children. In the absence of spouse and 
children, the Mother of deceased employee is the very next or nearer legal heir. The Mother who reached 
her old age and needs maximum financial assistance to meet out the old age expenses for her livelihood 
in comparison of unmarried brother or sister. It is also worth to mention that the Mother is class I legal 
heir under the Personal Succession Law. To exclude the Mother to get benefit of welfare scheme cannot 
be said as reasonable classification which is being driven to destitution. This classification i.e, to exclude 
Mother from the list of legal heir of deceased bank employee seems to be arbitrary and has no nexus 
with the object of the scheme. Therefore, this circular is discriminatory with regard to exclusion of Mother 
without rational basis. Therefore, in view of the above, the Mother of deceased employee Mrs. N.Baby 
Saroja, (mother of late N.Bama) is entitled to get the amount of ex-gratia under the scheme framed by the 


Respondent Bank.

2l. This Tribunal is conscience enough to understand that it does not have power to struck down the 
policy of the Respondent Bank. But, this Tribunal is empowered not to enforce any contrary conditions 
imposed by the employer while deciding the industrial dispute which comes in the nature of unfair labour 
practice. Therefore, this Tribunal is inclined to pass an Award in favour of the Petitioner and hold that she 


is entitled to get ex-gratia from the Respondent/Management. 
AWARD 


The Industrial Dispute raised by the Petitioner is allowed. The Respondent/Management is directed to pay 
ex-gratia amount to the Petitioner within a period of two months after the publication of Award along 


with interest @ 6% per annum and cost of Rs.20,000/-. without any interest. Ordered accordingly. 
The reference is answered accordingly.

l]. The first point that arises for determination is whether this Industrial Dispute is maintainable 


under the provisions of the 2A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947 ? 
Section 2A describes the following conditions:- 


a) An employer discharges / dismisses / retrenches or otherwise terminates the service of any 


individual workman; 


b) Any dispute or difference between the workman and his employer connected with or arising out of 


such discharge, dismissal, retrenchment or termination shall be deemed to be an industrial dispute. 


2. The Petitioner in his claim statement stated that he worked continuously from May, 2007 to January, 
204 and he provided year-wise break up of working days at page No.| of the paper book. The statement 
given by the Petitioner gets rectification from paper no.2. Paper no.2 is a copy of letter written by 
complainant to the competent authority, Bank of Baroda that he has worked from 0.05.2007 till 
8.03.2008 and number of days was 063. 


3. This letter was written on 8.03.2008. The Respondent also admitted that Petitioner submitted an 
application for absorption under the Scheme. Thus, this fact is established that Petitioner worked for more 
than 240 days and denied the work to the workman, after working more than 240 days, which comes 


under the category of retrenchment / removal from service. Therefore, this ID is maintainable. 


4. The second point that arises for determination is whether the Petitioner is entitled for absorption as 


per the scheme of settlement arrived at between the employees union and the Respondent/Management? 


5. The Respondent in its reply describes the terms of settlement that casual / temporary peons / 


sweepers who had worked for more than 90 days from ..982 to 3.2.989 and who are still working 


7742 THE GAZETTE OF INDIA : AUGUST ।, 2026 / SHRAVAN 0, 948 [PART II—SEC. 3(ii)] 


will be absorbed at the first phase. Certainly, the Petitioner does not eligible for absorption at the stage of 
I“ phase. 


6. The workman who have worked for more than 240 days consecutively for a calendar of 2 months 
between 0.0.2009 to 29.02.996 who are still working will be absorbed in phase 2. 


The Petitioner certainly does not fall under this category also. 


7. The persons who have worked for 240 days or more in consecutive 2 months between 0.03.996 
and 28.07.2007 who are still working will be absorbed in phase III. 


8. The Petitioner as per claim statement stated that he joined the service of Respondent Bank on 
0.05.2007 and as per the Scheme, persons who have worked for more than 240 days or more between 
0.03.996 and 28.07.2007 will be absorbed. The Petitioner has only worked for 88 days. Therefore, under 
the scheme, he is not entitled for absorption as per the settlement arrived at between the employees union 


and the Respondent/Management. 


9. The third point that arises for determination is whether the Petitioner was removed from service 


in violation of the provisions of section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947? 


20. It is observed while deciding issue No.| itself that the Petitioner had worked for more than 240 
days. By an oath, the Petitioner submitted that he was removed by oral direction. The 
Respondent/Management in its reply also admitted that Petitioner was denied the wok along with other 


employees. 


2. Section 257 of the Industrial Disputes Act, [947 describe the conditions precedent to retrenchment 
of workman, who has completed continuous service of 240 days ina calendar year, then one month 
notice must be given to the workman indicating reasons for retrenchment or must have provided one 
month wages in lieu of notice period plus retrenchment compensation equivalent to 5 days average pay 
for every completed years of service or part thereof in excess of six months. These conditions are 
mandatory as per provisions of section 25F of the Act and non-compliance makes the retrenchment 
invalid. Therefore, removal of the Petitioner from service was in violation of the provisions of section 
25F of the Act. 


22. To what relief the workman is entitled? 


23. This fact is admitted by the Petitioner himself that he has started a small business in the name of 
Hareesh Broilers and Evening tiffin stall at Coimbatore. In such situation, there is no need to pass an order 
of reinstatement into service and it will fulfill the requirement of law, if the Petitioner is awarded 


compensation amount payable u/s.25F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 947. 
AWARD 
The Industrial Dispute raised by the Petitioner is allowed as per the following conditions: - 


(i) The Respondent Bank is directed to pay the Petitioner one moth salary along with interest 
payable at 6%per annum payable from the date of removal from service till the date of 


actual payment;

l]. The learned counsel appearing on behalf of the Petitioner stated that the Petitioner is not willing to

validity of enquiry proceedings and its report. 


2. Now, I proceed to decide quantum of punishment as to whether it is grossly disproportionate 


and shocking to the conscience of this Tribunal or not? 
3. The following facts has been admitted by the Petitioner in its claim petition:- 


(i) On 26.0.20I3 (Saturday), the Petitioner had handed over the cash box to the Cash 
Officer confirming cash balance of Rs.99,979/-; 


Gi) On 28.0.20l3 (Monday), when the Circle Auditor commenced his audit at the

branch and as per his statement, he experienced chest pain and went to hospital for 


treatment. He has mentioned this fact as under:- 


“On 26.0.20l3(Monday) the petitioner came to branch and started working. While so, 


he had severe chest pain. Therefore, after informing the Branch Manager and after

permission he went to hospital. The Doctor after examination informed the petitioner 


that he had mild heart attack and advised to take bed rest.” 


4. At the time of argument, I suggest the learned counsel appearing on behalf of the petitioner to 
submit the prescription provided by the Doctor to the Petitioner on 26.0.203, for which she agreed to 
submit the same. But, later on, she failed to submit the prescription slip and specifically mentioned that 
the Petitioner does not possess such prescription slip. The Petitioner in his claim petition supported by his 
affidavit raised a defense of his absence on 28.0.203, while the Circle Auditor commenced his audit in 
the bank and this defense is totally false. Had the Petitioner been a patient of mild heart attack, the Doctor 
would have admitted him in the hospital and would have provided him a prescription for medicine/test for 
treatment of mild heart attack. This defense was raised by the Petitioner himself during the course of 
arguments and his advocate assured this Tribunal that Petitioner will submit the prescription and another 
document with reference to the treatment of mild heart attack. But, later on she denied to have possession 


of such prescription and the course of treatment in the hospital. 


5. With reference to charge No.2, though the Petitioner stated in the claim petition that owing to 
health reasons / hospitalization, the Petitioner obtained leave on two spells i.e., from 30.09.20l3 to 
2.0.20I3 and 28.0.20I3 to 3.0.20I3, the Petitioner has failed to prove the same with any 
documentary evidence i.e., medical certificate / prescription /fitness certificate before the Respondent 
bank. Though he submitted several documents which are marked Ex.W] to Ex.W9, none of these 
documents support the claim of leave on medical grounds sanctioned by the competent authority, as 
claimed by the Petitioner. Therefore, the Petitioner remained unauthorized absent from duty for 26 days 
without any authority on two spells cited above and thus, he failed to explain the charge no.2 levelled 


against the Petitioner with regard to his unauthorised absence too. 


6. As I have already stated in the initial part of this Award that the Petitioner chose not to press 
validity of domestic enquiry. Thus it may be stated that domestic enquiry conducted by the Respondent 


Bank was fair and proper and charges were proved. 


7. As per Ex.M2, the Circle Auditor after auditing the cash chest intimated that there was shortage 
of Rs.45,90/-. This fact is established that the petitioner has initially run away from the bank to avoid 
any confrontation with the Circle Audit team. He falsely stated that he had chest pain and went to the 
Doctor for treatment. It is nothing but a cooked up story with an object to gain sympathy of the bank 


authorities. 


8. As per Ex.M7 (at page 33 of the paper book) “in the branch circle audit started at 9.30 am on

During that cash box of the Petitioner was opened in the presence of bank officials and the Petitioner,

Rs.45,90/- in the cash box of the Petitioner. The Petitioner was not attending the call over his mobile.” 


9. This report clearly suggests that the petitioner was not ina position to face the circle audit team 


with reference to cash verification and shortage of cash. 


20. As per Ex.M8 (page 34 of the paper book) also suggests that there was cash shortage of 


Rs.45,90/- and the cash inventory sheet was signed by the branch officials / Manager and the witnesses.
